short_explanation: Air India was nationalised in 1953, the Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India in 1955, the first elected communist government came to power in Kerala in 1957, and Goa was liberated in December 1961. So the order is 3-2-1-4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Puts Goa (1961) first, though it is the latest of the four events.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Puts Goa (1961) first and places Air India (1953) last, reversing the true order.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Places the Kerala government (1957) before the SBI renaming (1955).

common_traps: Remembering the EMS Namboodiripad ministry as the 'first' event because it is the most famous; the Air India and SBI changes came earlier in the 1950s.

topic_name: Right to life and personal liberty
short_explanation: In the Puttaswamy judgment (2017) a nine-judge bench held that privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and of the freedoms guaranteed throughout Part III.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Article 14 is equality before law; the 42nd Amendment added words like 'socialist' and 'secular', not privacy.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and Directive Principles are not enforceable rights.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Article 24 bars child labour in hazardous work; the 44th Amendment is not the source of privacy.

common_traps: Linking privacy to the 44th Amendment because it strengthened Article 21 during emergencies; the right itself flows from Article 21 as read by the Court.

short_explanation: Barley, finger millet (ragi), groundnut and sesamum are among the crops for which the CCEA announces MSP. Areca nut, coffee and turmeric are plantation or spice crops with no MSP. So 2, 4, 5 and 6 only.
explanation_text: MSP is announced on the recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices for 22 mandated crops: 14 kharif crops (including ragi, groundnut and sesamum), 6 rabi crops (including barley) and 2 commercial crops (jute and copra), plus a Fair and Remunerative Price for sugarcane. Plantation crops such as coffee and areca nut and spices such as turmeric are outside this list.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes areca nut, coffee and turmeric, which have no MSP, and omits ragi, groundnut and sesamum.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes areca nut and coffee, which have no MSP, and omits barley.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes areca nut, coffee and turmeric, which have no MSP.

common_traps: Assuming every commercially important crop has an MSP; coffee, areca nut and turmeric do not.

short_explanation: Pakhui (also called Pakke) Wildlife Sanctuary, now Pakke Tiger Reserve, lies in the East Kameng district of Arunachal Pradesh, bordering Nameri in Assam.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Manipur's well-known protected area is Keibul Lamjao, not Pakhui.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Meghalaya's sanctuaries include Nongkhyllem and Balpakram, not Pakhui.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Nagaland's protected areas include Intanki and Fakim, not Pakhui.

common_traps: Confusing Pakhui with the Assam side of the same forest block (Nameri), which lies across the state border.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the PSLV mainly puts remote-sensing satellites into polar sun-synchronous orbit, while the GSLV is built for heavier communication satellites. Statement 2 is incorrect: appearing fixed in the sky describes geostationary satellites, which the GSLV places, not PSLV payloads. Statement 3 is incorrect: GSLV Mk III has three stages (two solid strap-ons, a liquid core stage and a cryogenic upper stage). So 1 only.
explanation_text: GSLV Mk III (now LVM3) uses two S200 solid strap-on boosters, the L110 liquid core stage and the C25 cryogenic upper stage. It is therefore a three-stage vehicle, and no stage runs on a solid motor above the strap-ons.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect, and it omits statement 1, which is correct.

common_traps: Treating the four-stage PSLV layout (solid, liquid, solid, liquid) as if it described the GSLV Mk III.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: government capital infusion into public sector banks rose and fell from year to year over the decade rather than increasing steadily. Statement 2 is correct: the five associate banks of SBI, along with Bharatiya Mahila Bank, were merged into SBI on 1 April 2017. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; the infusion was uneven, not steady.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is correct.

common_traps: The word 'steadily' makes statement 1 false even though the total amount infused over the decade was large.
key_note: The stem is garbled (stray numerals '2. 2. 2.' split statement 1 in two). Read as the two statements the options refer to: 1 on capital infusion, 2 on the merger of associate banks with SBI.

short_explanation: Hulled cereal grains (unbranded), birds' eggs in shell whether fresh, preserved or cooked, and printed newspapers (even with advertising material) are all on the GST nil-rate list. Processed and canned fish is taxed. So 1, 2 and 4 only.
explanation_text: The exemption for fish covers fresh or chilled fish. Once fish is processed and put into cans or other packaged forms, it attracts GST. Eggs remain exempt as long as they are in shell, including when cooked.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits cooked eggs and newspapers, which are also exempt.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes canned fish, which is taxable, and omits hulled cereal grains and newspapers.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes canned fish, which is taxable.

common_traps: Assuming that 'cooked' takes eggs out of the exemption; the entry covers eggs in shell whether fresh, preserved or cooked.
Assuming advertising content makes newspapers taxable; printed newspapers are exempt regardless.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Section 2(b) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 defines 'critical wildlife habitat'. Statement 2 is correct: the Baigas of Madhya Pradesh were the first community to receive habitat rights, in 2015-16. Statement 3 is incorrect: habitat rights are recognised through the gram sabha and district-level committee process under the FRA, which the Ministry of Tribal Affairs administers, not by MoEFCC. So 1 and 2 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming that because forests are involved, the Environment Ministry decides forest-dweller rights; the FRA's nodal ministry is Tribal Affairs and the process starts at the gram sabha.

short_explanation: All four carry plant pathogens: birds move seeds, spores and insects; dust and wind carry fungal spores and bacteria over long distances; and rain splashes pathogens from leaf to leaf and plant to plant. So 1, 2, 3 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits dust and wind, which also spread spores.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits birds and dust, which also carry pathogens.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits rain, whose splash is a major route for bacterial and fungal diseases.

common_traps: Thinking only living carriers (birds, insects) count as vectors; non-living agents like wind and rain splash spread disease too.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: NPOP is run by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not the Ministry of Rural Development. Statement 2 is correct: APEDA acts as the Secretariat for NPOP. Statement 3 is correct: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Linking organic farming to Rural Development or Agriculture; NPOP began as an export-certification programme, which is why it sits with Commerce and APEDA.

topic_name: Types of bills and the legislative process
short_explanation: Article 110 lists appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India as a Money Bill matter, not appropriation out of the Contingency Fund. So statement c is the one that is not correct.
explanation_text: Article 110(1) covers: taxes; government borrowing and guarantees; custody of the Consolidated Fund and the Contingency Fund, and payments into or withdrawals from them; appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund; declaring expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund; and receipts into, custody and audit of the Consolidated Fund or public account. Withdrawals from the Contingency Fund are made by the President as advances and later regularised by Parliament through a normal appropriation from the Consolidated Fund.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: a bill dealing only with imposing, abolishing, remitting, altering or regulating a tax is a Money Bill under Article 110(1)(a).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund is a Money Bill matter under Article 110(1)(c).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: regulating government borrowing or guarantees is a Money Bill matter under Article 110(1)(b).

common_traps: Custody of the Contingency Fund is a Money Bill item, but appropriation out of it is not; the question turns on that one word.

topic_name: The President and the Union Executive
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: an MLA's vote value is the state's population divided by its number of MLAs, then by 1000, so it differs from state to state. Statement 2 is incorrect: every elected MP, Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha, has the same vote value, found by dividing the total value of all MLAs' votes by the number of elected MPs. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; MPs of both Houses have equal vote value.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is correct.

common_traps: Assuming the directly elected Lok Sabha carries more weight; Article 55 gives all elected MPs one common vote value.

short_explanation: India's Additional Protocol with the IAEA, in force since 2014, gives the Agency wider information and access rights over the civilian nuclear facilities India has placed under safeguards. Military facilities stay outside it.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: India's separation plan keeps military installations outside IAEA inspection; the protocol does not change that.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Access to NSG supply came from the 2008 NSG waiver, not from ratifying the protocol.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: NSG membership needs consensus of the members; India is still not a member.

common_traps: Mixing up the 2008 NSG waiver, which allowed nuclear trade, with NSG membership, which India has not obtained.

short_explanation: ASEAN has free trade agreements with China, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand. From the list, Australia, China, India and Japan qualify; Canada and the USA had no FTA with ASEAN. So 1, 3, 4 and 5.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Canada, which had no FTA with ASEAN, and omits China.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes the USA, which has no FTA with ASEAN, and omits Australia.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Canada and the USA and omits Australia and Japan.

common_traps: Assuming the USA, ASEAN's large trade partner, has an FTA with it; it has only dialogue-partner status.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: GACSA was launched at the UN Climate Summit in New York in September 2014, not at Paris in 2015. Statement 2 is correct: it is a voluntary alliance and membership creates no binding obligations. Statement 3 is incorrect: India was not a driving force in its creation. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, both incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, both incorrect.

common_traps: Tying every climate initiative to the 2015 Paris conference; GACSA predates it by a year.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is not an aim: Digital India does not aim to build home-grown internet firms on China's model. Statement 2 is not an aim: data-localisation rules for multinationals were not part of the plan. Statement 3 is an aim: rural broadband connectivity and public Wi-Fi are core to its digital-infrastructure pillar. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which are not aims, and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is not an aim.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which are not aims.

common_traps: Reading later debates on data localisation back into the 2015 Digital India programme.

topic_name: World political geography and regions in news
short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Aleppo is in Syria. Pair 2 is incorrect: Kirkuk is in Iraq, not Yemen. Pair 3 is incorrect: Mosul is in Iraq, not Palestine. Pair 4 is correct: Mazar-i-Sharif is in Afghanistan. So 1 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2; Kirkuk is in Iraq.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pairs 2 and 3, both wrong (both towns are in Iraq), and omits pair 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3 (Mosul is in Iraq) and omits pair 1.

common_traps: Kirkuk and Mosul are both northern Iraqi cities; matching them to other conflict zones in the news is the trap.
key_note: The stem is garbled: the column header 'Towns sometimes mentioned in news – Country' is numbered 1, which shifts every pair down by one. The options follow the original numbering: 1 Aleppo, 2 Kirkuk, 3 Mosul, 4 Mazar-i-Sharif. This explanation uses that numbering.

topic_name: Constitutional reforms and Government of India Acts
short_explanation: The Government of India Act, 1935 split powers into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent lists and vested residuary powers in the Governor-General, who could assign a residuary subject to the federal or a provincial legislature by public notification.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Federal Legislature got only what the Governor-General assigned to it; the power itself lay with him.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Provincial Legislatures had only the Provincial List and could get residuary subjects only if the Governor-General chose.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Provincial Governors had no role in allotting residuary powers.

common_traps: Carrying over the Indian Constitution's rule (residuary powers with Parliament, Article 248) into the 1935 Act.

topic_name: Presiding officers, privileges and office of profit
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: under Article 179 the Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Assembly. Statement 2 is incorrect: on dissolution the Speaker stays in office until just before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; the Speaker does not vacate on dissolution.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is correct.

common_traps: The word 'immediately' is what makes statement 2 wrong; the proviso to Article 179 keeps the Speaker in office until the new House first meets.
key_note: The two statements are unnumbered in the stem; they are read in order as 1 and 2.

short_explanation: Liberty in the political sense exists only within a framework of law: laws restrain others from interfering with each person's freedom. Without law, the strong would dominate the weak and no one would be secure, so there would be no liberty.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Treats law and liberty as opposites; good laws protect liberty rather than reduce it.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Speaks about who makes laws (democracy), not about the basic link between law and liberty.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: May be true in practice, but it is a remark about stability of law, not the core relationship.

common_traps: Picking the libertarian reading (more laws, less liberty); the question asks for the most appropriate relationship, which is that law is a condition of liberty.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Article 361(2) bars criminal proceedings of any kind against a Governor in any court during the term of office. Statement 2 is correct: Article 158(4) says the Governor's emoluments and allowances shall not be diminished during the term. So both 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct (Article 158(4)).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is also correct (Article 361(2)).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

common_traps: Thinking immunity covers only official acts; for criminal proceedings Article 361(2) gives complete protection during the term.

short_explanation: Bani Thani, painted by Nihal Chand in the mid-18th century at the court of Raja Sawant Singh, is the best-known work of the Kishangarh school of Rajasthani painting, famous for its elongated eyes and sharp profile.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Bundi painting is known for lush landscapes and hunting scenes, not for Bani Thani.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Jaipur is a separate Rajasthani school; Bani Thani was made at Kishangarh.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Kangra is a Pahari school of the hills, not Rajasthani.

common_traps: Assuming a famous Rajasthani painting must belong to the larger Jaipur school.

short_explanation: THAAD is a United States missile-defence system, built by Lockheed Martin, that intercepts short and medium range ballistic missiles in their final phase. It was in the news when deployed in South Korea in 2017.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Israel's systems are Iron Dome and Arrow; THAAD is American.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: India's programme is the Ballistic Missile Defence programme with Prithvi and Advanced Air Defence interceptors.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: THAAD was deployed in South Korea by the US; it is not a Japan-South Korea project.

common_traps: Its deployment in South Korea leads some to think it is a Korean or joint Asian system.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: most of Tyagaraja's kritis praise Lord Rama, not Krishna. Statement 2 is correct: he created several new ragas. Statement 3 is incorrect: Annamacharya lived in the 15th century and Tyagaraja in the 18th-19th century. Statement 4 is correct: Annamacharya's kirtanas praise Lord Venkateswara of Tirumala. So 2 and 4 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Both composers wrote Telugu devotional songs, so they are often assumed to be contemporaries; Annamacharya died in 1503 and Tyagaraja was born in 1767.

short_explanation: Limitation of powers (1), equality before law (2) and protection of liberty and civil rights (4) are core features of the rule of law. 'People's responsibility to the Government' (3) is not; the rule of law makes the government answerable to law, not the people answerable to the government. So 1, 2 and 4 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3, which is not a feature, and omits items 2 and 4.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits limitation of powers (item 1), a core feature.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3, which is not a feature.

common_traps: Item 3 reverses the direction of accountability, which is easy to miss on a quick read.

short_explanation: All three contributed. The Charter Act of 1813 set aside one lakh rupees a year for education. The General Committee of Public Instruction of 1823 was set up to oversee that spending. The Orientalist-Anglicist controversy within that committee was settled in favour of English by Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's resolution of 1835. So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy, whose resolution in 1835 actually introduced English education.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits the Charter Act of 1813 and the controversy.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits the General Committee of Public Instruction, the body within which the controversy was fought.

common_traps: Treating the 1813 Act as purely Orientalist; it began state funding of education, which led to the later choice of English.

topic_name: Lakes, waterfalls and inland water bodies
short_explanation: Kodaikanal Lake is man-made: it was created in 1863 by damming a stream, under the Madurai collector Sir Vere Henry Levinge. The others are natural lakes.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Kolleru is a natural freshwater lake between the Krishna and Godavari deltas.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Nainital is a natural lake of tectonic origin in the Kumaon hills.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Renuka is a natural lake in Sirmaur district.

common_traps: Assuming hill-station lakes are all natural; Kodaikanal's star-shaped lake was built.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, not the Ministry of Labour and Employment. Statement 2 is correct: its training includes soft skills, entrepreneurship, and financial and digital literacy. Statement 3 is correct: it aligns the skills of the unregulated workforce with the National Skills Qualification Framework, including through Recognition of Prior Learning. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assigning a jobs-related scheme to the Labour Ministry; skilling moved to its own ministry in 2014.

topic_name: Early nationalism and the moderate phase
short_explanation: In 1920 the All India Home Rule League, founded by Annie Besant in 1916, renamed itself Swarajya Sabha and chose Gandhi as its president; it then merged into the Congress-led non-cooperation effort.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The Hindu Mahasabha kept its name; it was not renamed Swarajya Sabha.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The South Indian Liberal Federation became the Justice Party, not Swarajya Sabha.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Servants of India Society, founded by Gokhale in 1905, kept its name.

common_traps: Confusing Swarajya Sabha (1920) with the Swaraj Party formed by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru in 1923.
tag_note: Topic should be Home Rule Movement and the start of the Gandhian phase. The Home Rule League (1916) and its 1920 renaming fall after the moderate phase.

short_explanation: Dinabandhu Mitra's Neel Darpan, on the indigo planters' cruelty, was written in 1858-59 and published in 1860. Satyendranath Tagore cleared the ICS in 1863, Arya Samaj was founded in 1875 and Anandmath was written in 1882, so Neel Darpan is the earliest.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Dayanand founded Arya Samaj in 1875, later than Neel Darpan.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Anandmath appeared in 1882, the latest of the four.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Satyendranath Tagore passed the ICS in 1863 and joined in 1864, after Neel Darpan.

common_traps: Treating Satyendranath Tagore's success as the earliest because 'first Indian' sounds early; it came a few years after Neel Darpan.

short_explanation: Item 1 is not a consequence: removing sand lets sea water push further up the river mouth, so salinity tends to rise, not fall. Item 2 is a consequence: loss of the sand filter and exposure of the aquifer allow pollutants to reach groundwater. Item 3 is a consequence: the riverbed deepens and the sand that stores water is removed, so the water table drops. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Item 1 is not a consequence, and it omits items 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 1, which is not a consequence, and omits item 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 1, which is not a consequence.

key_note: The stem reads 'heavy and mining'; it is taken as 'heavy sand mining' of riverbeds.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: organic matter acts like a sponge and increases soil's water-holding capacity. Statement 2 is incorrect: soil is a key sulphur reservoir, where microbes convert organic sulphur into plant-usable sulphate. Statement 3 is correct: poorly drained irrigation raises the water table and leaves salts behind on evaporation, salinising the land. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, both incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 1 uses 'drastically reduces', the opposite of the real effect; read the direction of the claim carefully.

short_explanation: PAGE was launched in 2013 in response to the call in 'The Future We Want', the outcome document of the UN Conference on Sustainable Development (Rio+20) held in Rio de Janeiro in 2012, to support countries moving to green economies.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The 2002 Johannesburg summit predates the green-economy agenda that produced PAGE.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: PAGE existed before the 2015 Paris climate conference.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The 2016 World Sustainable Development Summit in New Delhi is a TERI forum; PAGE predates it.

common_traps: 'Green economy' was the headline theme of Rio+20; linking it to the better-known Paris 2015 meeting is the common slip.

topic_name: States of matter and material properties
short_explanation: 3D printing (additive manufacturing) is used in all five: printed chocolate and sugar confectionery, bionic ears built from cells and electronics, car prototypes and parts, custom implants for reconstructive surgery, and the making of electronic and data-processing hardware. So 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits bionic ears and data-processing hardware, which are also applications.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits confectionery and reconstructive surgery, which are also applications.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits bionic ears, the automotive industry and data-processing hardware.

common_traps: Assuming 3D printing is only for engineering parts; food and medicine are among its fastest-growing uses.
key_note: Item 5 (data processing technologies) is loosely worded; it is read as 3D printing of electronic and computing hardware, which supports the key.
tag_note: Topic should be Emerging technologies (3D printing / additive manufacturing). The question tests applications of a technology, not states of matter.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only confirmed active volcano. Statement 2 is incorrect: it lies about 138 km north-east of Port Blair, far north of Great Nicobar. Statement 3 is incorrect: after 1991 it erupted again in 1994-95, 2005 and in later years, including 2017. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect, and it omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: 1991 was the first eruption in about two centuries, not the last one.

short_explanation: Prosopis juliflora, brought to India as a fuel and hedge plant, is an aggressive invasive shrub: it forms dense thickets, draws down groundwater and suppresses native grasses and trees, reducing local biodiversity.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: It is not known for cosmetic use; its fame is as an invader.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: It is not a pesticide source; it is in the news for its ecological damage.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: reef-building corals need warm, clear, shallow tropical water. Statement 2 is correct: Indonesia, Australia and the Philippines together hold well over a third of the world's reef area. Statement 3 is correct: coral reefs host 32 of the 34 animal phyla, far more than tropical rainforests. So 1, 2 and 3.
explanation_text: Rainforests are richer in species, especially insects, but reefs are richer in animal phyla, the broad body-plan groups. Statement 3 speaks of phyla, which is why it is correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statements 1 and 2, which are also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

common_traps: Confusing species richness, where rainforests lead, with phylum diversity, where reefs lead.

short_explanation: Momentum for Change is a UNFCCC secretariat initiative that showcases climate action; its 'Climate Neutral Now' strand, launched in 2015, encourages individuals and organisations to measure, reduce and offset their emissions.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The IPCC assesses climate science; it does not run action campaigns.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: UNEP is a separate UN programme; this initiative belongs to the UNFCCC secretariat.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The WMO deals with weather and climate data, not emission-neutrality campaigns.

common_traps: UNEP and UNFCCC are both UN climate bodies; this initiative is run by the convention's secretariat.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is incorrect: the Sanskrit College at Benaras was founded in 1791 by Jonathan Duncan, not William Jones. Pair 2 is correct: Warren Hastings founded the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781. Pair 3 is incorrect: Fort William College (1800) was founded by Lord Richard Wellesley, not his brother Arthur Wellesley. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 1; the Benaras college was founded by Jonathan Duncan.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pairs 1 and 3, both wrong, and omits pair 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Pair 3 names Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, not the Governor-General Richard Wellesley.

common_traps: Pair 3 has the right surname but the wrong person: Arthur Wellesley was a soldier, while Richard Wellesley was Governor-General.

topic_name: World political geography and regions in news
short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Catalonia is in Spain. Pair 2 is incorrect: Crimea belongs to Ukraine (annexed by Russia in 2014), not Hungary. Pair 3 is correct: Mindanao is in the Philippines. Pair 4 is incorrect: Oromia is a region of Ethiopia, not Nigeria. So 1 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2; Crimea is not in Hungary.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 4 (Oromia is in Ethiopia) and omits pair 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pairs 2 and 4, both wrong.

common_traps: Oromia sounds West African, but it is Ethiopia's largest region.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the IRNSS (NavIC) constellation has three satellites in geostationary orbit and four in inclined geosynchronous orbit. Statement 2 is incorrect: it covers India and about 1,500 km beyond its borders, not 5,500 sq km. Statement 3 is incorrect: IRNSS is a regional system with no plan for full global coverage by 2019. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: Statement 2 swaps a distance (1,500 km) for an area in square kilometres, and inflates the number.

short_explanation: Item 1 is a prediction: gravity bends light, confirmed during the 1919 solar eclipse. Item 2 follows from the theory: its equations describe a universe that expands, as Friedmann and Lemaitre showed and Hubble observed. Item 3 is a prediction: mass curves space-time, and that curvature is gravity. So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 3, which is the central idea of the theory.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 1 and 2, which also follow from the theory.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 2; an expanding universe is a solution of the theory's equations.

common_traps: Excluding expansion because Einstein initially resisted it; the theory's equations still predict it.
key_note: Einstein himself first added a cosmological constant to keep the universe static; expansion is a consequence of his equations rather than something he championed. Accepted as the prediction UPSC intends.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the bacterial genes in GM mustard (barnase and barstar from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, plus bar) give male sterility, fertility restoration and herbicide tolerance, not pest resistance. Statement 2 is correct: the barnase-barstar system lets breeders cross-pollinate and produce hybrids. Statement 3 is incorrect: DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University's Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, both incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, both incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming all GM crops carry Bt pest-resistance genes like Bt cotton; GM mustard's genes serve hybrid seed production.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is incorrect: Belle II is a particle-physics experiment at Japan's KEK collider, not an artificial intelligence project. Pair 2 is correct: blockchain technology underlies digital currencies. Pair 3 is incorrect: CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool, not particle physics. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 1; Belle II is particle physics.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3; CRISPR-Cas9 is gene editing.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pairs 1 and 3, both wrong.

common_traps: The contexts of pairs 1 and 3 are swapped with each other; both are real science terms, just matched to the wrong field.
key_note: The stem is garbled: the column header 'Terms sometimes seen in news – Context/Topic' is numbered 1, shifting each pair down by one. The options follow the original numbering: 1 Belle II, 2 Blockchain, 3 CRISPR-Cas9. This explanation uses that numbering.

short_explanation: Carbon fertilisation is the boost in photosynthesis and plant growth when atmospheric carbon dioxide rises, since CO2 is a raw material for photosynthesis.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Describes global warming, the greenhouse effect of CO2.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Describes ocean acidification.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Describes climate adaptation, not a CO2 growth effect.

short_explanation: Everyday devices (alarm, geyser, mirror, fridge, lights, car) sensing data and talking to each other over the internet to act on their own is exactly the Internet of Things.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol routes traffic between networks on the internet backbone; it is not about smart devices.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Internet Protocol is the basic addressing rule for all internet traffic, not the idea of connected household things.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A VPN is a secure tunnel over a public network, not device automation.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: India had almost no silicon wafer manufacturing and relied on imports, mostly from China. Statement 2 is incorrect: solar tariffs are discovered through competitive bidding and adopted by the electricity regulators (CERC and state commissions); SECI only runs auctions and buys power. So neither 1 nor 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; India is not a major wafer maker.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; SECI does not set tariffs.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: SECI conducts many solar auctions, so it is easy to think it fixes the tariff; tariff-setting and adoption are regulatory functions.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Statement 2 is a fine point: SECI's auctions discover tariffs, but the power to determine or adopt them lies with the regulatory commissions, which is the reading the key rests on.

short_explanation: In the mid-18th century the Company's main exports from Bengal were cotton textiles, raw and woven silk, saltpetre (for gunpowder) and, increasingly, opium.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Raw cotton and oilseeds became big exports only in the 19th century.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Salt, zinc and lead were not export staples from Bengal; sugar was minor.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The Company brought silver into Bengal to pay for goods; tea came from China, not Bengal.

common_traps: Listing gold and silver as exports; in this period bullion flowed into India to pay for its goods.

short_explanation: Champaran (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, taken up for indigo cultivators forced into the tinkathia system; it brought peasant grievances into the national movement.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The movement was local to Bihar; all-India participation of students and women came with Non-Cooperation.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It was a movement of indigo peasants, not specifically Dalit or tribal communities.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: It won concessions on the tinkathia system; it did not cause a sharp fall in cash-crop cultivation.

short_explanation: Hind Mazdoor Sabha was founded in 1948 by socialists who left the Congress-led INTUC, including Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam, G.G. Mehta, Basawon Singh and R.S. Ruikar.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: These were Kerala communist leaders linked to AITUC, not HMS.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya was a Jana Sangh leader and M.N. Roy a radical humanist; neither founded HMS.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: These were a Travancore dewan, a Congress leader and a social reformer, not trade union founders.

short_explanation: Sthanakvasi is a Svetambara Jain sect that rejects idol worship and prays in plain halls (sthanaks) instead of temples.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Buddhist schools are Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana; Sthanakvasi is not Buddhist.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Vaishnava sects include Vallabha and Gaudiya; Sthanakvasi is not among them.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Shaiva sects include Lingayat and Pashupata; Sthanakvasi is not Shaiva.

common_traps: Confusing Sthanakvasi with Svetambara Terapanthi; both are non-idolatrous Jain sub-sects.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Buland Darwaza and the Fatehpur Sikri buildings are built of red sandstone; white marble appears only as inlay and trim (the white marble tomb of Salim Chishti is a separate building). Statement 2 is incorrect: the Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza were built of brick with lime plaster, not red sandstone and marble. So neither 1 nor 2.
explanation_text: Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri is the classic red sandstone city. Asaf-ud-Daula's Lucknow monuments of the 1780s used lakhori bricks and lime stucco, partly because good stone was scarce in Awadh and partly because the work was a famine-relief project.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; red sandstone is the building material.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; the Lucknow buildings are brick and lime plaster.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

key_note: Accepted as defensible. Buland Darwaza does carry white marble inlay, so statement 1 could be read as partly true; the key reads it as naming the building material, which was red sandstone.

short_explanation: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a French jewel merchant who made six journeys to India in the 17th century, described the Golconda diamond mines such as Kollur in detail and bought famous stones, including the one later known as the Hope diamond.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Bernier was a physician who wrote on Mughal politics and land, not diamonds.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Thevenot described general travel in India, not the diamond mines in detail.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Carre wrote on travel and French company affairs, not diamond mining.

common_traps: Bernier is the best-known French traveller of the period, so candidates pick him by reflex.

short_explanation: Maitreya is the future Buddha in Buddhist tradition, the bodhisattva who now waits in Tushita heaven and will be born on earth to teach the dharma anew.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Avalokiteshvara is the bodhisattva of compassion, not the future Buddha.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Lokeshvara is another name for Avalokiteshvara.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Padmapani, the lotus-bearer, is also a form of Avalokiteshvara.

common_traps: Three of the options are names of the same bodhisattva, Avalokiteshvara.

topic_name: East India Company expansion and subsidiary alliance
short_explanation: Subsidiary Alliance aimed at British paramountcy, a large army paid for by Indian rulers, and keeping French and Napoleonic influence out. The subsidy or ceded land paid for the stationed troops; securing a fixed income for the Company was not its stated purpose.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: This is a core aim: the allied ruler paid for British troops stationed in his state.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: This is an aim: rulers had to expel Frenchmen and other Europeans, guarding against Napoleon.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: This is the central aim: rulers accepted British supremacy and a Resident at court.

common_traps: Seeing the subsidy payment as income; it was earmarked for maintaining the stationed force.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. The subsidy or ceded territory did bring the Company money, but it was tied to the upkeep of the troops (option a), not meant as a fixed revenue income, which is the reading the key takes.

topic_name: Money and banking: RBI and monetary policy
short_explanation: Legal tender is money that the law says a creditor must accept in settlement of a debt; in India, RBI notes and government coins are legal tender.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Court fees are paid in any accepted form; this is not what legal tender means.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Cheques and drafts are bank money that a creditor may refuse; they are not legal tender.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Legal tender includes paper notes, not only metallic coins.

common_traps: Treating cheques as legal tender; a creditor can refuse a cheque but not currency notes.

short_explanation: Nothing is truly free: the resources used to provide the good still have alternative uses. When the government gives it free, the cost is paid from taxes, so the opportunity cost shifts from the users to the taxpaying public.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Resources still have alternative uses, so the opportunity cost is not zero.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The cost is not ignored; it is borne by someone else.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The government has no money of its own; it spends taxpayers' money, so they bear the cost.

common_traps: Stopping at 'the government pays'; the government only passes the cost on to taxpayers.
tag_note: Topic should be Public finance and opportunity cost. The question tests who bears the cost of free public provision, not demand, supply or equilibrium.

short_explanation: Economic development means rising welfare for people, not just output. If poverty and unemployment grow while real GNP rises, the growth is not reaching people, so it does not mean higher development.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Sectoral balance between industry and agriculture is not the test of development.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Agriculture lagging industry is normal structural change, not a sign of no development.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A trade deficit does not by itself mean welfare is falling.

common_traps: Equating growth with development; development asks whether the gains reduce poverty and unemployment.

short_explanation: Item 1 is incorrect: accumulating more capital is physical capital formation, not human capital. Item 2 is correct: human capital formation means raising people's knowledge, skills and capacities. Item 3 is incorrect: tangible wealth is physical capital. Item 4 is correct: skills and knowledge are intangible wealth. So 2 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 1, which describes physical capital, and omits item 4.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 4, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 1 and 3, which describe physical capital.

common_traps: Human capital is wealth, but intangible wealth; 'tangible' refers to machines and buildings.
key_note: The stem is garbled: the lead sentence 'Human capital formation ... a process which enables' is numbered 1, shifting the four statements down by one. The options follow the original numbering: 1 accumulate more capital, 2 increasing knowledge and skills, 3 tangible wealth, 4 intangible wealth. This explanation uses that numbering.

short_explanation: The capital-output ratio is the capital needed to produce one extra unit of output. If it is high, capital is used inefficiently, so even a high savings rate adds little to output.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Weak administration can slow projects, but it is not the direct link between capital and output.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Illiteracy affects labour quality, not the capital-to-output relation the question is about.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Population density does not by itself decide how much output capital produces.

short_explanation: Measure 1 is correct: after the 1855-56 uprising the British carved out the Santhal Parganas as a separate district with its own administration. Measure 2 is correct: tenancy laws for the Santhal Parganas barred Santhals from transferring land to non-Santhals. So both 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits measure 2, which was also adopted.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits measure 1, the creation of the Santhal Parganas.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both measures were adopted.

key_note: The two measures are unnumbered in the stem; they are read in order as 1 and 2.

short_explanation: Under British rule in the 19th century, cash demands of land revenue and new export markets pushed farmers to grow cash crops such as indigo, cotton, jute and opium for sale; this is the commercialisation of agriculture.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Indian handicraft exports fell sharply as British machine goods flooded the market.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Indian-owned factories grew only slowly, from the late 19th century onwards.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Urban population actually stagnated or fell as old craft towns declined.

common_traps: Assuming colonial rule urbanised India; it caused de-industrialisation and a shift back to agriculture.

short_explanation: Under Article 356(1)(b), when President's Rule is imposed the President may declare that the powers of the State Legislature shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.
explanation_text: Article 356 lets the President assume the executive functions of the State and transfer the State Legislature's powers to Parliament. Article 357 then allows Parliament to confer law-making power on the President, or on an authority he names. The Assembly may be dissolved or kept in suspended animation; after S. R. Bommai (1994) dissolution should normally wait until Parliament has approved the proclamation.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Assembly is not automatically dissolved; it may be kept in suspended animation, and dissolution is a separate decision.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Article 19 is suspended only under a national emergency on grounds of war or external aggression (Article 358), not under Article 356.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The President can make laws for the State only if Parliament delegates that power under Article 357; it does not flow directly from the proclamation, so option b is the accurate description.

common_traps: Assuming President's Rule automatically dissolves the Assembly.
Mixing up Article 356 with Article 358, which suspends Article 19 during an external emergency.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Another reading set aside: option d is conditionally true because Parliament may delegate law-making for the State to the President under Article 357, but that is a delegated power, whereas option b is the direct effect of the proclamation.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Puthukkuli shawls are the embroidered shawls of the Toda community of the Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu. Pair 2 is incorrect: Sujni embroidery belongs to Bihar (Muzaffarpur), not Maharashtra. Pair 3 is incorrect: Uppada Jamdani saris are woven at Uppada in Andhra Pradesh, not Karnataka. So only 1.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2; Sujni is from Bihar.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Pair 3 is wrong; Uppada is in Andhra Pradesh.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both pairs 2 and 3 are wrong.

common_traps: Jamdani is linked in memory with Bengal and Dhaka, so candidates guess a coastal state other than Andhra Pradesh for the Uppada variety.

short_explanation: GPS gives both location and a very precise time signal. Mobile networks use it for location services and to synchronise base stations, banks use GPS time to timestamp and synchronise transactions, and power grids use it to synchronise and control the grid. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits banking and grid control, which also rely on GPS timing.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits mobile phone operations, the most familiar GPS use.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits banking operations, which use GPS time stamps to synchronise transactions.

common_traps: Thinking of GPS only as a map and location tool and missing its role as a precise clock for networks.
key_note: The stem is truncated after item 3 ('Controlling'); the original item reads 'Controlling the power grids'. The answer does not change.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the RBI manages and services State Government securities (State Development Loans) as well as Government of India securities. Statement 2 is correct: Treasury bills are issued only by the Government of India; States do not issue them. Statement 3 is correct: Treasury bills are zero-coupon instruments issued at a discount and redeemed at par. So 2 and 3.
explanation_text: The RBI is the debt manager for the Centre by law (RBI Act) and for the States by agreement, so it handles auctions and repayment for both. Treasury bills are short-term (91, 182 and 364 days) Central borrowings; State Governments meet short-term gaps through Ways and Means Advances from the RBI instead.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming the RBI handles only Central debt because States are separate borrowers.
key_note: The stem reads 'but any State Government Securities'; the intended wording is 'but not any', which is how statement 1 is judged here.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the geomagnetic field has reversed many times, on average every few hundred thousand years. Statement 2 is incorrect: the early atmosphere had almost no free oxygen and was rich in carbon dioxide, water vapour and nitrogen. Statement 3 is correct: photosynthesising life added oxygen and drew down carbon dioxide, transforming the atmosphere. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which reverses the early atmosphere.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 2 sounds precise because of the figure 54%, but it inverts the real picture: little oxygen, much carbon dioxide.
key_note: Reversals are irregular (the last was about 780,000 years ago), but 'every few hundred thousand years' is the usual average and statement 1 is accepted as correct.

short_explanation: WannaCry and Petya (with its variant NotPetya) were ransomware attacks that spread worldwide in 2017, and EternalBlue was the leaked Windows file-sharing exploit that let them spread from computer to computer. All three are names from cyber-attacks.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not exoplanet names; these are malware and exploit names.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Ransomware demanded Bitcoin payments, but the terms name the attacks, not cryptocurrencies.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Not satellite names.

common_traps: Because the ransom was paid in Bitcoin, some link the names to cryptocurrency.

short_explanation: Conservation Agriculture rests on three principles: minimum soil disturbance (item 2), permanent soil cover such as crop residues (item 4) and crop diversification through rotations and sequencing (item 5). Avoiding plantation crops (item 3) is not a principle, and every option except c includes item 3. So 2, 4 and 5.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3 and omits minimum tillage and crop rotation.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3, avoiding plantation crops, which is not a Conservation Agriculture principle.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3 and omits soil cover with crop residues.

common_traps: Reading 'conservation' as avoiding commercial or plantation crops; the concept is about how the soil is managed, not which crop is grown.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Item 1 (avoiding monoculture) overlaps with crop diversification, but the official framing lists rotation (item 5) as the principle, and no option pairs item 1 with 2, 4 and 5 without also including item 3.

short_explanation: The 'sixth extinction' refers to the present, human-driven wave of species loss caused by over-exploitation of resources, habitat loss and fragmentation, pollution and climate change. Five earlier mass extinctions occurred in the geological past.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Monoculture farming is only one small contributor, not what the term refers to.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The meteorite impact 65 million years ago caused the fifth extinction; the sixth is not about a future impact.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: GM crops and food biodiversity are a narrow concern, not the meaning of the term.

common_traps: Linking 'extinction' with the dinosaur-ending asteroid and so picking option b.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Capital Adequacy Ratio is the capital a bank must hold, measured against its risk-weighted assets, to absorb losses when borrowers default. Statement 2 is incorrect: the minimum CAR is set by the regulator, the RBI, following Basel norms, not by each bank. So 1 only.
explanation_text: Under the RBI's Basel III rules Indian banks must maintain a total CAR of 9% plus a capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, which is stricter than the Basel minimum of 8%. A bank may hold more than the minimum, but it cannot set a lower requirement for itself.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; the RBI prescribes CAR.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: A bank may choose to hold more capital, which tempts candidates to say CAR is decided by each bank; the required minimum is regulatory.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: open APIs mean any device or application can be integrated with Aadhaar authentication through published interfaces. Statement 2 is correct: the authentication API supports biometric checks, including iris scans, online. So both 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; iris-based online authentication is supported.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; open APIs let devices integrate with the platform.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

common_traps: The word 'any' in statement 1 looks like an overstatement, but it is exactly what an open API offers: integration is not tied to a particular vendor's device.

short_explanation: Armed conflict drove Yemen's civil war and South Sudan's internal war into severe hunger around 2016-2017; the UN declared famine in parts of South Sudan in February 2017 and warned of famine in Yemen, with lakhs facing starvation.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not the conflict-driven famine cases in the news at the time.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Not the conflict-driven famine cases in the news at the time.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Venezuela faced an economic crisis and food shortages, not a war-driven famine, and Colombia did not.

common_traps: Venezuela's food shortages were in the news too, but they arose from economic collapse rather than war or ethnic conflict.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Dispatch (1854) introduced a system of grants-in-aid to private schools. Statement 2 is correct: it recommended universities on the London model, founded at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857. Statement 3 is incorrect: it wanted English for higher education but vernacular languages at the school level, not English at all levels. So 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3 and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Confusing Wood's Dispatch with Macaulay's Minute (1835), which pushed English-medium education.

short_explanation: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation examines whether the rule-making powers delegated to the executive by the Constitution or by Parliament are being exercised within their limits, and reports to the House.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Committee on Government Assurances tracks promises made by ministers on the floor of the House.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The Rules Committee deals with the House's own rules of procedure.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Business Advisory Committee allots time for the House's business.

common_traps: Picking the Rules Committee because the stem mentions rules; it handles the House's own procedural rules, not delegated legislation.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: under the RTE Act minimum teacher qualifications are laid down by an academic authority notified by the Centre, which is the National Council for Teacher Education, not a State council. Statement 2 is correct: a candidate must pass a Teacher Eligibility Test held under NCTE guidelines. Statement 3 is incorrect: most teacher education institutions are privately run, not directly under State Governments. So 2 only.
explanation_text: Section 23 of the RTE Act empowers an academic authority authorised by the Central Government to fix minimum qualifications, and the NCTE was so notified in 2010. The NCTE then made passing the TET an essential qualification. Teacher education in India expanded mostly through private, self-financing institutions, which account for over 90% of the sector.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; qualifications are set by the NCTE.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements 1 and 3 are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect; the sector is mostly private.

common_traps: Statement 3 reverses the real share: over 90% are private, not State-run.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Chapchar Kut is the spring festival of Mizoram. Pair 2 is correct: Khongjom Parba is a Manipuri ballad about the Battle of Khongjom (1891). Pair 3 is incorrect: Thang-Ta is the martial art of Manipur, not Sikkim. So 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pair 2, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Pair 3 is wrong; Thang-Ta belongs to Manipur.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3, which is wrong.

common_traps: Assigning Thang-Ta to another north-eastern state because it looks like a Himalayan term.
key_note: The stem has lost the pair numbers; the pairs are read as 1 Chapchar Kut, 2 Khongjom Parba (spelt 'Khongiom' in the stem), 3 Thang-Ta.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 consolidated food laws and replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, among others. Statement 2 is incorrect: FSSAI is a statutory body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare headed by its own Chairperson and run by a Chief Executive Officer, not by the Director General of Health Services. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; FSSAI is not under the DGHS.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: Since FSSAI sits under the Health Ministry, candidates assume the ministry's DGHS runs it.

short_explanation: The two-state solution is the proposal to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict by having an independent State of Palestine alongside Israel, broadly along pre-1967 lines.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not about China; 'One China' is the unrelated term used there.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Not about Iraq.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Not about Yemen, though Yemen was once two separate states.

common_traps: Recalling that Yemen was once North and South Yemen and picking option d.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Act covers priority households and Antyodaya households, up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population, not only BPL families. Statement 2 is correct: the eldest woman aged 18 or above is head of household for the ration card. Statement 3 is incorrect: pregnant women and lactating mothers get a free meal or take-home ration of 600 calories, not 1600, plus maternity benefit of at least ₹6,000. So 2 only.
explanation_text: Schedule II of the Act sets nutritional norms: 600 calories and 18-20 g protein a day for pregnant and lactating women through the anganwadi. Section 13 makes the eldest woman, not below 18 years, the head of household for issuing ration cards.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; eligibility is not limited to BPL families.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements 1 and 3 are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect; the norm is 600 calories.

common_traps: The 1600 figure in statement 3 is close enough to the real 600 to be mistaken on a quick read.

short_explanation: India enacted the GI Act, 1999 to meet its obligations under the WTO's TRIPS Agreement, which requires members to protect geographical indications.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The ILO deals with labour standards, not intellectual property.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The IMF deals with monetary cooperation and the balance of payments.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: UNCTAD is a UN forum on trade and development without binding IP obligations.

common_traps: Picking UNCTAD because it has 'trade' in its name; binding IP rules come from TRIPS under the WTO.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: since the MMDR Amendment Act, 2015, State Governments auction non-coal major mineral blocks. Statement 2 is incorrect: Andhra Pradesh (Ramagiri and Chigargunta belts) and Jharkhand (for example Parasi) have gold deposits. Statement 3 is correct: Rajasthan has iron ore mines, for instance in Jaipur and Jhunjhunu districts. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements 1 and 2 are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; States do auction non-coal mines.

common_traps: Assuming auctions are a Central function because coal blocks are auctioned by the Centre.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: BHIM, built on UPI, lets users send money to anyone with a UPI-enabled bank account. Statement 2 is incorrect: a chip-and-PIN debit card uses two factors (the card you have and the PIN you know), not four. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: Counting the chip, the magnetic strip, the card number and the PIN as separate factors; they collapse into possession and knowledge.

short_explanation: Delhi lies at about 77.2° E. Bengaluru is at about 77.6° E, closest of the four; Hyderabad is at about 78.5° E, Nagpur about 79.1° E and Pune about 73.9° E.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Hyderabad is about 78.5° E, farther east than Bengaluru.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Nagpur is about 79.1° E, nearly 2° east of Delhi.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Pune is about 73.9° E, well west of Delhi.

common_traps: Picking Nagpur because it is central and nearer to Delhi in distance; the question asks about longitude, not proximity.

topic_name: Social security, pensions and labour welfare
short_explanation: ILO Convention 138 fixes the minimum age for admission to employment and Convention 182 targets the worst forms of child labour; India ratified both in 2017. They are core conventions on child labour.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The ILO has no convention with these numbers on farm adaptation to climate change.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Food prices are not an ILO subject; that is the FAO's field.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Gender parity at work is covered by Conventions 100 and 111.

common_traps: Confusing these with Conventions 100 and 111, the other pair of core conventions, which deal with equal pay and discrimination.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha was the Communist Party of India; the Swatantra Party was founded only in 1959. Statement 2 is correct: a Leader of the Opposition was first recognised in 1969 (Ram Subhag Singh). Statement 3 is incorrect: the convention requires one-tenth of the House's strength (55 members), not 75. So 2 only.
explanation_text: The one-tenth rule comes from a Speaker's direction and from the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977, which recognises the leader of the largest opposition party; in practice Speakers have required one-tenth of the House, the quorum, which is 55 in a House of 545.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements 1 and 3 are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; the threshold is 55, one-tenth of the House.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 3 uses a plausible but wrong number; the working threshold is 55, one-tenth of the House.

short_explanation: All three help desert plants cut water loss: hard, waxy leaves slow evaporation (item 1), tiny leaves reduce the surface that loses water (item 2), and thorns in place of leaves, as in cacti, almost eliminate it (item 3). So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits hard and waxy leaves, a common desert adaptation.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits waxy leaves and thorns.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits waxy leaves and tiny leaves.

short_explanation: The NSSO's 70th Round (2013) surveyed farm households. Statement 1 is correct: Rajasthan had the highest share of agricultural households among its rural households, about 78%. Statement 2 is incorrect: OBCs made up about 45% of agricultural households, not a little over 60%. Statement 3 is correct: in Kerala about 61% of agricultural households earned most of their income from non-farm sources. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2 and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming a high agricultural share in Punjab or Uttar Pradesh rather than Rajasthan.
tag_note: Topic should be Agriculture — farm households and rural income. The question tests findings of an agricultural household survey, not population or demography.

topic_name: Environment Protection Act and pollution control bodies
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: both are statutory; the NGT was set up under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 and the CPCB under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, not by executive order. Statement 2 is correct: the NGT gives speedy environmental justice and eases the load on higher courts, while the CPCB's mandate is to promote cleanliness of streams and wells and improve air quality. So 2 only.
explanation_text: The CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water Act and was later given functions under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. Its stated aims under these laws are to promote cleanliness of streams and wells and to improve the quality of air.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; the CPCB is statutory.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is correct.

common_traps: Assuming a regulator like the CPCB must be an executive creation because it sits under a ministry.

topic_name: Parts and Schedules of the Constitution
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Parliament can place a law in the Ninth Schedule, by a constitutional amendment under Article 31B. Statement 2 is incorrect: in I. R. Coelho (2007) the Supreme Court held that laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure. So 1 only.
explanation_text: The 24 April 1973 date is the day of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, which laid down the basic structure doctrine. Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after that date are protected from challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds only if they do not damage the basic structure.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: Statement 2 was true before 2007; the I. R. Coelho judgment ended total immunity.

short_explanation: The Merchant Discount Rate is the fee a merchant pays to its bank, shared with the card network and issuing bank, for accepting card payments from customers; it is usually a percentage of the transaction.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: MDR is a charge on the merchant, not an incentive to it.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: MDR is not a refund to cardholders; cashback is a different thing.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Government incentives for digital payments are separate from MDR, though the government has at times borne MDR on small payments.

common_traps: Assuming 'discount' means a benefit to the merchant; it is the amount deducted from what the merchant receives.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct as UPSC frames it: members trade among themselves in nuclear material and technology under NSG guidelines, which gives access to advanced nuclear technology. Statement 2 is incorrect: NSG membership does not automatically make a country a party to the NPT, which is a separate treaty. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is accepted as correct.

common_traps: Because NSG members are normally NPT parties, candidates think one membership brings the other; it works the other way, and each is joined separately.
key_note: Statement 1 is loosely worded ('latest and most efficient'), but it is accepted as the intended benefit of membership.
