short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the equalisation levy was introduced through Chapter VIII of the Finance Act, 2016 as a standalone levy, not as part of the Income Tax Act. Statement 2 is incorrect: because it is outside the Income Tax Act, it is not a tax covered by the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements, so non-residents cannot claim credit for it at home. So neither.
explanation_text: Keeping the levy outside the Income Tax Act was deliberate: DTAAs cover taxes on income, and a separate levy on gross payments for online advertising falls outside them. That is why foreign platforms cannot offset it against their home tax.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; the levy sits in the Finance Act, 2016.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; DTAAs do not cover the levy.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming any tax on non-residents is under the Income Tax Act and therefore creditable under a DTAA.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the FRBM Review Committee (N. K. Singh, 2017) recommended a general government debt of 60% of GDP by 2023, 40% for the Centre and 20% for the States. Statement 2 is incorrect: it reverses the figures; the Centre's domestic liabilities were about 49% of GDP and the States' about 21%. Statement 3 is correct: Article 293(3) requires a State to get the Centre's consent to borrow while any Central loan to it is outstanding. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2 and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which reverses the figures.

common_traps: Statement 2 swaps the Centre's and States' shares; spot it by remembering the Centre carries the larger debt.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: India imports roughly 60-70% of the edible oil it consumes, so imports have exceeded domestic production for years. Statement 2 is incorrect: edible oil imports attract customs duty, which the government raises or lowers to balance farmers' and consumers' interests. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; customs duty is levied.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: The words 'any' and 'all' in statement 2 make it absolute; duty rates change, but duty is not waived on all edible oils.

topic_name: Early nationalism and the moderate phase
short_explanation: Lala Lajpat Rai wrote biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Shri Krishna, lived in the United States from 1914 to 1920, where he founded the Indian Home Rule League of America, and was elected to the Central Legislative Assembly in 1926.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Aurobindo Ghosh studied in England and never lived in America or sat in the Central Assembly.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Bipin Chandra Pal wrote and lectured abroad but is not the author of these biographies.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Motilal Nehru was in the Central Assembly but did not write these biographies or live in America.

common_traps: Bipin Chandra Pal, as the third member of Lal-Bal-Pal, is a tempting guess.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act says the Aadhaar number is not proof of citizenship or domicile. Statement 2 is incorrect: UIDAI can omit or deactivate an Aadhaar number under Section 23(2)(g) of the Act and its regulations. So neither.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: Because Aadhaar is widely used as identity and address proof, candidates assume it proves citizenship too.
key_note: The stem reads 'citizenship of domicile'; the intended wording is 'citizenship or domicile'.

topic_name: Degradation of lakes and inland water bodies
short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: the Aral Sea shrank drastically after its feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, were diverted for irrigation. Item 2 is not: the Black Sea has not shrunk. Item 3 is not: Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake, faces pollution but has not dried up. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Neither the Black Sea nor Lake Baikal has shrunk.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The Black Sea has not shrunk.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Lake Baikal has not dried up.

common_traps: Confusing pollution threats to Lake Baikal or the Black Sea with shrinkage.

short_explanation: The Rule of Law Index is published by the World Justice Project, an independent organisation in Washington DC, which scores countries on factors such as constraints on government power, absence of corruption and fundamental rights.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Amnesty International publishes human rights reports, not this index.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states and publishes no rankings.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The UN human rights office does not publish this index.

common_traps: Assuming a rule-of-law ranking must come from a UN or judicial body.
key_note: Option d reads 'World Justice Report'; the publisher is the World Justice Project. The intended option is clear.

short_explanation: The National Payments Corporation of India runs the National Financial Switch, which links the ATMs of banks across India so that any card works at any bank's ATM.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Indian Banks' Association is an industry body, not a switching network.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: NSDL is a securities depository.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The RBI regulates payment systems but does not itself operate the ATM switch.

common_traps: Picking the RBI because it oversees payment systems; the operator of the switch is NPCI.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: fertilised agricultural soils emit nitrous oxide and nitric oxide through microbial action. Statement 2 is correct: cattle dung and urine release ammonia. Statement 3 is correct: poultry litter releases ammonia and other reactive nitrogen compounds. So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; cattle are a major ammonia source.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; farm soils emit nitrogen oxides.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statements 1 and 3, which are also correct.

key_note: The stem has lost its statement numbers; they are read in the order given.

topic_name: Lakes, waterfalls and inland water bodies
short_explanation: Aliyar (Tamil Nadu), Isapur (Maharashtra, on the Penganga) and Kangsabati (West Bengal) are all dams with reservoirs built for irrigation.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: None of these is a uranium find.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: None of these is a rain forest.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: None of these is a cave system.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: H-CNG reduces carbon monoxide emissions but does not eliminate them. Statement 2 is correct: it cuts carbon dioxide and hydrocarbon emissions. Statement 3 is correct: hydrogen of up to about 18-20% by volume can be blended with CNG. Statement 4 is incorrect: H-CNG costs more than CNG because hydrogen is costly to produce. So 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 overstates the benefit; CO is reduced, not eliminated.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 4 is incorrect; H-CNG is costlier.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 4, which are incorrect.

common_traps: 'Elimination' in statement 1 is the absolute word that makes a true idea (lower CO) false.
key_note: The trials cited an 18% hydrogen blend, which statement 3 rounds to one-fifth; it is accepted as correct.

short_explanation: Dew forms when the ground cools enough by losing heat at night for moisture to condense. On a cloudy night the clouds send the Earth's outgoing heat radiation back to the ground, so the surface stays too warm for dew to form.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Clouds do absorb outgoing radiation, but what stops dew is that the heat is returned to the ground; absorption alone is only half the process.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The opposite is true: cloudy nights are warmer at the surface.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Clouds do not push wind down to the ground.

common_traps: Choosing option c by thinking clouds make nights cooler, when they act like a blanket.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Physically clouds absorb and re-emit long-wave radiation, so option a is partly true, but option b states the effect that keeps the ground warm, and the key is the one accepted.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: it was the 39th Amendment (1975) that inserted Article 329A placing the Prime Minister's election beyond judicial review; the 44th Amendment (1978) repealed it. Statement 2 is correct: in 2015 the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment, which set up the National Judicial Appointments Commission, for violating judicial independence. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; that was the 39th Amendment.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is correct.

common_traps: Attaching the Emergency-era change to the 44th Amendment, which in fact undid many Emergency amendments.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: under Section 3 of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 the Speaker may admit or refuse to admit the motion. Statement 2 is incorrect: the Constitution does not define 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'. Statement 3 is correct: the procedure is laid down in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Statement 4 is correct: each House must pass the motion by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting. So 3 and 4.
explanation_text: Article 124(4) sets the special majority and Article 124(5) leaves the procedure to Parliament, which enacted the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. A motion needs 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members to give notice; if the Speaker or Chairman admits it, a three-member committee investigates before any vote.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 4, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; the Speaker can reject the motion.

common_traps: Assuming the Speaker must accept a validly signed motion; the Act gives the Speaker discretion to refuse it.
key_note: Statement 4 garbles the second limb ('two-thirds of total members of that House present and voting') and attributes the majority to 'the law' though it is in Article 124(4); its intended meaning is correct and it is judged correct.

topic_name: Parts and Schedules of the Constitution
short_explanation: The Ninth Schedule was added by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, together with Article 31B, to shield land reform laws from challenge; Jawaharlal Nehru was Prime Minister.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister only in 1964.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Indira Gandhi's governments added many laws to the Schedule but did not create it.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Morarji Desai's government (1977-79) came much later.

common_traps: Linking the Ninth Schedule with Indira Gandhi because many laws were placed in it during her tenure.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: coking coal (1971-72) and non-coking coal (1973) mines were nationalised under Indira Gandhi. Statement 2 is incorrect: since the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 blocks are allocated by auction or allotment to public entities, not by lottery. Statement 3 is incorrect: India still imports coal, especially coking coal. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 2 and 3 are both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect; India still imports coal.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, which are incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 3 mixes a true trend (rising domestic output) with a false claim of self-sufficiency.

topic_name: Presiding officers, privileges and office of profit
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 lists offices whose holders are not disqualified from being MPs. Statement 2 is correct as keyed: the Act has been amended several times, with UPSC taking the count as five. Statement 3 is incorrect: the Constitution does not define 'office of profit'; its meaning comes from court rulings. So 1 and 2.
explanation_text: Articles 102(1)(a) and 191(1)(a) disqualify a member who holds an office of profit under the government, except offices Parliament or the State legislature has declared exempt by law. Courts have built the tests: who appoints, who can remove, who pays, and whether the office carries real profit.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect; the term is not defined in the Constitution.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming a term used in the Constitution must be defined there.
key_note: The exact number of amendments to the 1959 Act is hard to corroborate; the key is accepted on UPSC's count of five.

topic_name: Special provisions for states and areas
short_explanation: In Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997), the Supreme Court read the Fifth Schedule, which protects Scheduled Areas and tribes, to hold that transfer of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private parties for mining is null and void.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Third Schedule contains forms of oaths.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The Ninth Schedule protects listed laws from Fundamental Rights challenges.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Twelfth Schedule lists municipal functions.

common_traps: Choosing the Ninth Schedule because it deals with land reform laws; protection of tribal land in Scheduled Areas comes from the Fifth Schedule.

short_explanation: The Himalayan nettle yields a strong natural fibre from its stem bark, used for yarn and fabric, and Uttarakhand has promoted it as a sustainable source of textile fibre.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: It is not a source of an anti-malarial drug.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It is not grown for biodiesel.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Its fibre is used for textiles, not as paper pulp.

key_note: Option b reads 'blodiesel', a misprint for 'biodiesel'.

short_explanation: All three can be estimated from satellite data: chlorophyll through vegetation indices from reflected light (item 1), greenhouse gas emissions from paddies by mapping flooded rice area and plugging it into emission models (item 2), and land surface temperature from thermal infrared bands (item 3). So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 1, the most common remote sensing use.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 1 and 2.

common_traps: Assuming gas emissions can only be measured on the ground; satellites estimate them indirectly.

short_explanation: In the India State of Forest Report 2017, forest cover as a share of area was about 16.5% for Maharashtra, 25.1% for Madhya Pradesh, 33.0% for Odisha and 41.1% for Chhattisgarh. So the ascending order is Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh: 3-2-4-1.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Puts Madhya Pradesh first, but Maharashtra has the lower share.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Puts Madhya Pradesh first; Maharashtra's share is lowest.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Places Chhattisgarh below Odisha; Chhattisgarh has the highest share.

common_traps: Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area in absolute terms, which tempts candidates to rank it high; the question asks for percentage of area.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: warming seas and thawing permafrost can destabilise hydrates and release methane. Statement 2 is correct: large deposits lie in Arctic permafrost and under the seafloor on continental margins. Statement 3 is correct: methane lasts about a decade in the air before it oxidises to carbon dioxide and water. So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

short_explanation: Burning crop residue directly releases carbon monoxide (item 1), methane (item 2) and sulphur dioxide (item 4), and its nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons form ozone (item 3) in the smoke plume. So 1, 2, 3 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits ozone and sulphur dioxide.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits carbon monoxide, a major product of incomplete burning.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits methane and ozone.

common_traps: Ozone is a secondary pollutant, not emitted directly, so candidates drop it; UPSC counts it among the pollutants released by residue burning.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Ozone forms from the smoke's nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons rather than being emitted directly; on a strict reading only carbon monoxide, methane and sulphur dioxide are emitted directly, but no option lists those three alone, and the key is the one accepted.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Albania borders the Adriatic. Pair 2 is incorrect: Croatia lies on the Adriatic, not the Black Sea. Pair 3 is correct: Kazakhstan borders the Caspian. Pair 4 is correct: Morocco has a Mediterranean coast. Pair 5 is incorrect: Syria is on the Mediterranean, not the Red Sea. So 1, 3 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2; Croatia is on the Adriatic.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both pairs 2 and 5 are wrong.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Pairs 2 and 5 are wrong.

common_traps: Morocco is often thought of as only an Atlantic country, but its northern coast lies on the Mediterranean.

short_explanation: India has been the world's largest rice exporter since 2011-12, shipping more than Thailand and Vietnam, thanks to large surpluses of both basmati and non-basmati rice.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: China is the largest producer and consumer, but not a major exporter.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Myanmar exports much less than India.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Vietnam is a leading exporter but ranks behind India.

common_traps: Confusing the largest producer (China) with the largest exporter (India).

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: the Yamuna rises from the Yamunotri glacier on the Bandarpunch massif. Pair 2 is correct: Bara Shigri feeds the Chandra, a headstream of the Chenab. Pair 3 is incorrect: the Milam glacier feeds the Goriganga, not the Mandakini. Pair 4 is correct: Siachen feeds the Nubra. Pair 5 is incorrect: the Zemu glacier feeds the Teesta, not the Manas. So 1, 2 and 4.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3; Milam feeds the Goriganga.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 5, which is wrong, and omits pairs 1 and 4.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Pairs 3 and 5 are both wrong.

common_traps: Pair 2 looks wrong because Bara Shigri drains into the Chandra, but the Chandra is a headstream of the Chenab.

short_explanation: Carbofuran, methyl parathion, phorate and triazophos are highly toxic insecticides used in agriculture; their residues and poisoning cases have led to restrictions and bans in India.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: They are not food preservatives.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Calcium carbide and ethylene are ripening agents, not these chemicals.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: They are not used in cosmetics.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Ramsar Convention asks parties to conserve listed Ramsar sites and make wise use of wetlands; it does not oblige India to protect all its wetlands. Statement 2 is incorrect: the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010 were framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, not on Ramsar's recommendations. Statement 3 is correct: the Rules covered the drainage or catchment area of wetlands as determined by the authority. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements 1 and 2 are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which are incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 1 turns on 'all': Ramsar obligations attach to designated sites and wise use, not every wetland.

short_explanation: Kalyana mandapas, ornate pillared halls for the ritual marriage of the deity, are a hallmark of Vijayanagara temple architecture, as at the Vitthala temple in Hampi.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Chalukya temples do not feature kalyana mandapas.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Chandela temples at Khajuraho follow the northern Nagara style without kalyana mandapas.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Rashtrakuta temples such as Ellora's Kailasa do not feature kalyana mandapas.

common_traps: Confusing kalyana mandapas with the ordinary mandapa found in most Hindu temples.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Amil was the revenue collection officer in the Sultanate's administration. Statement 2 is incorrect: the Iqta system was a West Asian institution brought in by the Turkish rulers, not an ancient Indian one. Statement 3 is incorrect: Mir Bakshi was a Mughal office, created under Akbar, not by the Khaljis. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; the Iqta was imported, not indigenous.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect; Mir Bakshi is Mughal.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, which are incorrect.

common_traps: Mixing up Sultanate and Mughal offices; the Sultanate had the Ariz-i-Mumalik for the army, the Mughals the Mir Bakshi.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Nimbarka lived around the 12th-13th century, centuries before Akbar. Statement 2 is incorrect: Kabir (15th century) died before Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (1564-1624) was born, so could not have been influenced by him. So neither.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; Nimbarka predates Akbar.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; Sirhindi came after Kabir.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: Sirhindi was a contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir; linking him with the Bhakti saints of that era is chronologically wrong for Kabir.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Gandhi campaigned against indentured labour in South Africa and India, and the system was ended in 1917. Statement 2 is incorrect: at Lord Chelmsford's War Conference in Delhi (April 1918) Gandhi supported the resolution on recruiting Indians for the war. Statement 3 is correct: after the Salt Satyagraha the Congress was declared illegal in 1930. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; Gandhi supported the recruitment resolution.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2 and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming Gandhi, as an apostle of non-violence, opposed war recruitment; in 1918 he actively supported it.

topic_name: Early nationalism and the moderate phase
short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Tej Bahadur Sapru led the All India Liberal Federation, the Moderates' party, and served as its President. Pair 2 is correct: K. C. Neogy was elected to the Constituent Assembly from West Bengal. Pair 3 is correct: P. C. Joshi was the first General Secretary of the Communist Party of India (1935-47). So all three pairs match.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pairs 2 and 3, which are also correctly matched.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pair 3; P. C. Joshi was indeed the CPI's General Secretary.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pairs 1 and 2, which are also correctly matched.

common_traps: K. C. Neogy is best remembered as Chairman of the First Finance Commission, which makes candidates doubt his Constituent Assembly membership; he held both roles.

short_explanation: The title 'Tansen' is traditionally said to have been conferred by Raja Vikramajit of Gwalior; Akbar honoured him with the title 'Mian'. So statement a is the one that is not correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: Tansen's dhrupads include many compositions on Hindu deities such as Ganesha and Shiva.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: he composed songs in praise of his patrons, including Akbar.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: ragas such as Miyan ki Todi, Miyan ki Malhar and Darbari Kanada are credited to him.

common_traps: Mixing up the two titles: 'Mian' (from Akbar) and 'Tansen' (from the Gwalior court).

short_explanation: Under Jahangir the Mughal atelier moved away from large illustrated manuscripts towards albums (muraqqa) of single paintings, portraits and nature studies by painters such as Abul Hasan and Mansur.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Humayun brought Persian masters (Mir Sayyid Ali, Abd al-Samad) and laid the foundation; he did not make this shift.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Akbar's workshop concentrated on illustrated manuscripts such as the Hamzanama and Akbarnama.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Shah Jahan continued the album tradition he inherited; the shift in emphasis came under Jahangir.

common_traps: Picking Akbar because his atelier was the largest; the question asks who changed the emphasis, which was Jahangir.

short_explanation: The Valley of Flowers National Park in Uttarakhand lies at roughly 3,200 to 6,700 metres, entirely within the temperate and alpine zone of the Western Himalaya.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Manas lies in the Himalayan foothills of Assam, with tropical and subtropical forests and grasslands.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Namdapha spans from about 200 m to over 4,500 m, so it runs from tropical rainforest to alpine, not completely alpine.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Neora Valley in Darjeeling ranges from subtropical to temperate forest; it is not wholly alpine.

common_traps: Choosing Namdapha because it reaches alpine heights; the word 'completely' rules it out.

short_explanation: The Atal Innovation Mission, announced in 2016 to promote innovation and entrepreneurship (Atal Tinkering Labs, Atal Incubation Centres), is set up under NITI Aayog.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Department of Science and Technology runs its own innovation schemes, but AIM is not under it.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: There is no link between AIM and the employment ministry.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The skill ministry handles skilling and entrepreneurship training, not AIM.

common_traps: Assuming an innovation programme must sit under the Department of Science and Technology or the skill ministry.

short_explanation: On 21 June the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so all places on and north of the Arctic Circle get 24 hours of daylight and the Sun does not set there.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: On 21 June the Antarctic Circle has 24 hours of darkness; the Sun does not rise there.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The Sun is overhead at noon on the Equator around the equinoxes (21 March and 23 September).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer on 21 June; it is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn around 22 December.

common_traps: Swapping the two circles or the two tropics; on 21 June everything favours the Northern Hemisphere.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: a jagir was a revenue assignment given in lieu of salary for state service, chiefly maintaining troops under the mansab system, not for judicial and police duties, and zamindars did have other duties such as keeping order and supplying men. Statement 2 is incorrect: it reverses the facts, since jagirs were transferable and not hereditary while zamindari rights were hereditary. So neither.
explanation_text: Under the mansabdari system a mansabdar was paid either in cash or through a jagir, the right to collect revenue from a territory equal to his salary. Jagirs were deliberately transferred every few years so that no noble could build a local base, which is why they were not hereditary. Zamindars were local holders of hereditary rights over land revenue; besides collecting revenue they kept local order and often maintained armed retainers.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which misstates what jagirs were given for.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which reverses the hereditary position of jagirs and zamindari rights.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 2 sounds right because both words suggest landed power; the trap is the reversal: zamindari was hereditary, the jagir was transferable.

short_explanation: The central aim of land reforms after independence was redistributive: to abolish intermediaries and give surplus land to the tillers and the landless. The other options misdescribe the ceiling laws or their outcome.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Early ceiling laws applied to individual landholders; only after the 1972 national guidelines did most States make the family the unit, so 'not individual holdings' is not true as a general statement.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Land reforms did not make cash crops the predominant form of cultivation; food crops remained dominant.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Ceiling laws had many exemptions, such as plantations, orchards, religious and charitable trusts and efficiently run farms.

common_traps: Treating option a as correct because the family became the unit after 1972; the statement's 'not individual holdings' ignores the earlier laws.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. The word 'all' in option b overstates what land reforms could deliver; the key reads it as the stated redistributive aim. Another reading set aside: option a, because ceiling laws covered individual holdings until the 1972 guidelines made the family the unit.

short_explanation: The Global Competitiveness Report, which ranks economies on the factors that drive productivity, is published by the World Economic Forum, based in Geneva.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The IMF publishes the World Economic Outlook and Global Financial Stability Report, not this report.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The World Bank published the Doing Business report, a different ranking.

common_traps: Confusing the WEF's competitiveness ranking with the World Bank's Doing Business ranking.

topic_name: Constitutional reforms and Government of India Acts
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly in India but kept its monopoly on tea and trade with China. Statement 2 is correct: the Act asserted the Crown's 'undoubted sovereignty' over the Company's Indian territories. Statement 3 is incorrect: the Company kept control of Indian revenues, subject to rules laid down by the Act. So 1 and 2 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; the Act did not hand Indian revenues to Parliament's control.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3 and omits statement 2, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: The 1813 Act ended the India monopoly but not the tea and China monopoly, which went only in 1833; candidates mix up the two Acts.

topic_name: Early nationalism and the moderate phase
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: boycott of foreign goods revived indigenous crafts, handloom and swadeshi enterprises such as textile mills, soap and match factories. Statement 2 is correct: the National Council of Education was set up in 1906 as part of the movement's programme of national education. So both.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the National Council of Education grew directly out of the movement.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; reviving indigenous industry was a core aim of swadeshi.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League in 1932, later renamed the Harijan Sevak Sangh. Pair 2 is correct: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was the first President of the All India Kisan Sabha (1936). Pair 3 is correct: E. V. Ramaswami Naicker (Periyar) led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pairs 2 and 3, which are also correctly matched.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pair 3; Periyar led the Self-Respect Movement.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pair 1; Gandhi founded the Anti-Untouchability League.

common_traps: Assuming the Anti-Untouchability League was Ambedkar's organisation; Ambedkar founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, while the League was Gandhi's.

short_explanation: Sohgaura, in Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh, is known for a Mauryan-era copper plate inscription, not for Harappan remains. The other three are Harappan sites.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Chanhudaro in Sindh is a Harappan bead-making centre.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Kot Diji in Sindh has pre-Harappan and Harappan levels.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Desalpur in Kutch, Gujarat, is a fortified Harappan settlement.

short_explanation: At Kanganahalli, near Sannati in Karnataka, a stupa relief shows a king with his queens, labelled 'Raya Asoko' (King Ashoka), the only known portrait of Ashoka identified by an inscription.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Sanchi reliefs show scenes connected with Ashoka but carry no such labelled portrait.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Shahbazgarhi has a rock edict of Ashoka, not a portrait relief.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Sohgaura has a copper plate inscription, not a relief sculpture of Ashoka.

common_traps: Picking a site famous for Ashokan edicts; the question asks for a labelled portrait relief, which is Kanganahalli.

short_explanation: Item 1 is a feature: Mahayana treats the Buddha as a divine saviour. Item 2 is a feature: its ideal is the Bodhisattva who delays nirvana to help others. Item 3 is a feature: Mahayana brought in image worship and devotional rituals. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 2 and 3, which are also Mahayana features.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 3; image worship is characteristic of Mahayana.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 1; the deification of the Buddha is central to Mahayana.

short_explanation: Gupta-period inscriptions list vishti (forced, unpaid labour) among the dues the State could claim from villagers, so it functioned as a kind of tax paid in labour.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Inscriptions mention vishti across the empire, including western regions such as Kathiawar and central India.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Vishti was unpaid labour; there was no weekly wage.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No rule sent the eldest son; the obligation fell on villagers generally.

short_explanation: Tobacco, cocoa and rubber (Hevea) were all domesticated in the Americas and taken to the Old World after 1492.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Cotton was domesticated independently in both worlds, including in the Indus region, so it is not a New World introduction.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Coffee (Ethiopia) and sugarcane (New Guinea and South Asia) are Old World crops.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Coffee and wheat (Fertile Crescent) are Old World crops.

common_traps: Rubber is now grown mostly in Southeast Asia, but it came from Brazil.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: wild Asiatic lions survive only in and around Gir in Gujarat. Statement 2 is incorrect: the double-humped Bactrian camel is native to Central Asia (Mongolia, China); India's Nubra valley has only a small population. Statement 3 is incorrect: the one-horned rhinoceros is also found in Nepal. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; Bactrian camels are mainly found in Central Asia.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; Nepal's Chitwan also has one-horned rhinos.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, which are incorrect.

common_traps: The word 'only' is the test: rhinos and Bactrian camels occur in India but not only in India.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: Pandharpur stands on the Chandrabhaga, as the Bhima is called there. Pair 2 is correct: Tiruchirappalli lies on the Cauvery. Pair 3 is incorrect: Hampi lies on the Tungabhadra; the Malaprabha flows past Aihole, Pattadakal and Badami. So 1 and 2 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3; Hampi is on the Tungabhadra.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3 and omits pair 2, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 3, which is incorrect.

common_traps: The Malaprabha is linked to Chalukyan temple sites, not Hampi; both are in north Karnataka.

short_explanation: A poverty line is the money needed to buy a fixed basket of consumption, so States with higher prices get higher poverty lines; the Tendulkar and Rangarajan methods both adjust State lines for price differences.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Poverty rates are the result of applying the line, not the reason the line differs.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Gross State Product does not enter the calculation of the poverty line.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: PDS quality affects living standards but is not how official lines are set.

common_traps: Confusing cause and effect: the poverty rate is computed from the line, it does not set it.

short_explanation: Thinning cirrus clouds (so more heat escapes to space) and injecting sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere (to reflect sunlight) are geoengineering ideas proposed to counter global warming.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Artificial rain uses cloud seeding with silver iodide or salt, not these techniques.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: These methods aim at cooling the whole planet, not specifically at tropical cyclones.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Solar wind is handled by Earth's magnetic field; these techniques have nothing to do with it.

short_explanation: Pyrolysis (heating waste without oxygen) and plasma gasification (breaking waste down with a plasma torch into syngas) are technologies for converting waste into energy.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Rare earths are extracted by mining and chemical separation, not these processes.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Natural gas extraction uses drilling and fracking, not pyrolysis.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Hydrogen vehicles use fuel cells; these terms relate to treating waste.

short_explanation: The Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve on the Kerala-Tamil Nadu border includes the Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney Wildlife Sanctuaries and the Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: These areas belong to the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: These are Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu areas outside Agasthyamala; Mukurthi lies in the Nilgiris.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: These are in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, far from Agasthyamala.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the green turtle is mainly a herbivore that feeds on seagrass and algae. Statement 2 is correct: parrotfish and surgeonfish graze on algae. Statement 3 is correct: dugongs and manatees are herbivorous marine mammals. Statement 4 is correct: many snakes, such as sea snakes and several vipers, give birth to live young. So all four.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statements 2 and 4, which are also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; the green turtle is herbivorous.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statements 1 and 3, which are also correct.

common_traps: Assuming all snakes lay eggs; many species are viviparous.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is correct: the blue-finned mahseer is found in the Cauvery. Pair 2 is incorrect: the Irrawaddy dolphin lives in Chilika Lake and coastal waters; the Chambal has the Ganges river dolphin. Pair 3 is correct: the rusty-spotted cat occurs in the Eastern Ghats. So 1 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2 and omits pair 3, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2 and omits pair 1, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 2; the Chambal dolphin is the Ganges river dolphin.

common_traps: Mixing up India's two dolphins: the Ganges river dolphin (Ganga, Chambal, Brahmaputra) and the Irrawaddy dolphin (Chilika, Sundarbans coast).

short_explanation: Microbeads are tiny plastic particles from cosmetics and cleansers that pass through sewage treatment into rivers and seas, where they persist, absorb toxins and are eaten by marine organisms.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: There is no established link between microbeads and skin cancer in children.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The main concern is aquatic, not uptake by crops in irrigated fields.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Microbeads are not known as food adulterants.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: shutting out the physical world is virtual reality, not augmented reality. Statement 2 is incorrect: overlaying computer images on real surroundings is augmented reality, not virtual reality. Statement 3 is correct: AR keeps the user in the real world and adds to it through a phone or PC camera. Statement 4 is correct: VR closes off the real world for full immersion. So 3 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which swap the definitions of AR and VR.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which are incorrect, and omits statement 4.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which correctly describes AR.

common_traps: Statements 1 and 2 are accurate descriptions with the labels swapped.

short_explanation: Denisovans are an extinct archaic human group known from fossils in Denisova Cave in Siberia; their DNA survives in some present-day Asian and Oceanian populations.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Denisovans are hominins, not dinosaurs.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Denisova Cave is in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, not North-East India.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: It is not the name of a geological period.

short_explanation: Making synthetic DNA, copying DNA outside a cell by PCR, and growing plant and animal cells in culture are all routine laboratory work. The key treats option a, building a functional chromosome by joining DNA segments from different species, as the claim that is not correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: artificial DNA is synthesised in labs routinely.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: the polymerase chain reaction copies DNA in a test tube.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: plant and animal cells divide in tissue culture in petri dishes.

key_note: Accepted as UPSC's key. Option a is contestable, since artificial chromosomes (for example yeast artificial chromosomes carrying foreign DNA) are made in labs; the key treats a functional chromosome assembled from different species' DNA as not established.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: an electronic record identifying the issuing certifying authority is a digital certificate. Statement 2 is incorrect: serving as proof of identity to access information or a server is also the role of a digital certificate. Statement 3 is correct: a digital signature is an electronic way of signing a document that also shows the content has not been changed. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which describes a digital certificate.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which describes a digital certificate.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which describe a digital certificate, not a signature.

common_traps: Treating 'digital signature' and 'digital certificate' as the same; the certificate proves identity, the signature signs and protects integrity.

short_explanation: Item 1 is done: GPS-enabled wearables identify location. Item 2 is done: fitness bands and smartwatches monitor sleep. Item 3 is done: hearing aids and smart hearing devices assist the hearing impaired. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 2 and 3, which wearables also do.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 1; wearables with GPS identify location.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 1 and 2, which wearables also do.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: RNAi silences specific genes and underpins gene-silencing therapies. Item 2 is correct: it is being used to develop cancer therapies by silencing cancer-related genes. Item 3 is incorrect: hormone replacement means supplying a hormone, which RNAi does not do. Item 4 is correct: RNAi is used to make crops resistant to viruses. So 1, 2 and 4.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3 and omits items 1 and 4, which are correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3, which RNAi does not do.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 2; RNAi is used in cancer therapy research.

common_traps: RNAi switches genes off; it cannot add a missing hormone, so hormone replacement does not fit.

short_explanation: The LIGO detectors recorded ripples in spacetime from merging black holes, the first direct detection of gravitational waves predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Higgs boson was found at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, not from black hole mergers.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The observation said nothing about wormholes or intergalactic travel.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The signal came from outside the black holes and did not reveal the singularity.

short_explanation: Item 1 is incorrect: resistance develops in the microbes, not from people's genes. Item 2 is correct: wrong doses and incomplete courses let resistant strains survive. Item 3 is correct: antibiotic use in livestock spreads resistance. Item 4 is incorrect: having chronic diseases does not itself create drug-resistant microbes. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 1; human genetic predisposition does not cause microbial drug resistance.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 1 and 4 and omits item 2, the misuse of antibiotics.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 4; chronic illness is not a cause of resistance.

common_traps: Confusing a patient's vulnerability to infection with the cause of drug resistance, which is antibiotic overuse and misuse.

short_explanation: Cas9 is the enzyme in the CRISPR-Cas9 system that cuts DNA at a site chosen by a guide RNA, which is why it is called molecular scissors for gene editing.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Cas9 is not a biosensor, although other CRISPR enzymes have been adapted for diagnostics.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Cas9 is a bacterial protein, not a plant pest-resistance gene such as Bt.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Cas9 is not a herbicide.

short_explanation: Hepatitis B has a safe vaccine that is part of India's immunisation programme; it is Hepatitis C that has no vaccine. So statement b reverses the facts and is the one not correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: Hepatitis B spreads through blood, sexual contact and mother to child, as HIV does.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: many more people live with Hepatitis B and C than with HIV.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Correct statement: both infections can stay silent for years before liver damage shows.

common_traps: Remembering that one of B and C lacks a vaccine but mixing up which one.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: High Courts can strike down central laws under Article 226, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court. Statement 2 is incorrect: since Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court can strike down an amendment that violates the basic structure. So neither.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; High Courts do exercise judicial review over central laws.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; amendments can be tested against the basic structure.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: Article 368(4), which barred review of amendments, was itself struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: PPP rates compare what the same basket of goods and services costs in different countries. Statement 2 is incorrect: in PPP terms India is the third largest economy, after China and the United States. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; India ranks third in PPP terms, not sixth.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which correctly defines PPP.

common_traps: Mixing up India's rank at market exchange rates (then sixth or fifth) with its rank by PPP (third).

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: rice has by far the largest kharif area. Statement 2 is incorrect: kharif oilseeds (soybean, groundnut) cover far more area than jowar. Statement 3 is correct: cotton covers roughly twice the area of sugarcane. Statement 4 is incorrect: sugarcane area has moved up and down with prices and rainfall, not fallen steadily. So 1 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 4 and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 4, which are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 4, which are incorrect.

common_traps: 'Steadily decreased' in statement 4: sugarcane area fluctuates year to year; it has not declined steadily.

short_explanation: India imports a large share of its edible oil, mainly palm oil from Indonesia and Malaysia and soybean and sunflower oil, making vegetable oils its largest agricultural import by value.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: India is a net exporter of spices.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Fresh fruit imports are much smaller in value.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Pulses are a large import but have been well below vegetable oils in value.

common_traps: Pulses imports get much attention, but edible oil imports are larger in value.

short_explanation: In political theory liberty is best understood positively, as the conditions and opportunity for a person to develop fully, not merely freedom from restraint.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Protection against tyranny is one part of liberty, not a full definition.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Absence of restraint is the narrow negative view; some restraints are needed for liberty to exist for all.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Doing whatever one likes is licence, which would destroy others' liberty.

common_traps: Picking 'absence of restraint' because it sounds like the textbook definition; the question asks for the most appropriate one.

short_explanation: An expansionary monetary policy cuts interest rates and adds liquidity, which pushes capital out and weakens the rupee further; to defend the rupee the RBI tightens instead.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Curbing imports and promoting exports reduce demand for dollars, which supports the rupee.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Masala bonds bring in foreign money while leaving the currency risk with investors, supporting the rupee.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Easier external commercial borrowing brings in dollars, which supports the rupee.

short_explanation: The RBI's April 2018 directive on storage of payment system data requires payment system operators to keep all such data only in India. Statement 1 is correct: this is the core requirement. Statement 2 is incorrect: there is no requirement for public sector ownership. Statement 3 is incorrect: the system audit report goes to the RBI, not the CAG. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; private operators may run payment systems.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3 and omits statement 1, the actual requirement.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, which are incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming an audit report must go to the CAG; the CAG audits government accounts, while the RBI regulates payment systems.

short_explanation: The General Data Protection Regulation is the European Union's data protection law, adopted in April 2016 and enforced from 25 May 2018.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Australia's privacy law is the Privacy Act 1988.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Canada's law is PIPEDA, not the GDPR.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The United States has no single federal law of this kind.

short_explanation: India and Russia have long cooperated on nuclear power, notably at Kudankulam. The Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field was signed during President Putin's visit to India in October 2018.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not the partner in this agreement; India and Japan signed a civil nuclear agreement in 2016.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Not the partner named in the agreement.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Not the partner in this agreement; the India-US civil nuclear deal dates from 2008.

short_explanation: The money multiplier grows when people keep less cash and more bank deposits, because deposits can be lent on again; a stronger banking habit therefore raises it.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A higher cash reserve ratio leaves banks less to lend, so the multiplier falls.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A higher statutory liquidity ratio also reduces lendable funds, lowering the multiplier.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Population size by itself does not change the multiplier.

common_traps: Thinking a higher reserve ratio raises the multiplier; reserve ratios and the multiplier move in opposite directions.

short_explanation: The Service Area Approach (1989) gave each rural and semi-urban bank branch a set of villages to plan credit for, and it was implemented under the Lead Bank Scheme.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Integrated Rural Development Programme was a poverty scheme, not a framework for bank planning.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: MGNREGS is a wage employment scheme from 2005.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The National Skill Development Mission deals with skilling.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: ordinary sand used for building is a minor mineral under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. Statement 2 is incorrect: States both grant leases and make the rules for minor minerals. Statement 3 is correct: States can make rules to prevent illegal mining. So 1 and 3 only.
explanation_text: Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act lists ordinary sand among minor minerals. Section 15 gives State Governments the power to make rules for granting quarry leases and mining leases for minor minerals, and Section 23C lets States frame rules to prevent illegal mining, transport and storage of minerals.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; rule-making for minor minerals lies with the States.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; sand is a minor mineral under the Act.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 2 splits leasing and rule-making between the States and the Centre; for minor minerals both lie with the States.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: most of India's external debt is owed by non-government borrowers, through commercial borrowings, NRI deposits and trade credit; the government's share is about a fifth. Statement 2 is incorrect: a large part is in US dollars, but part is in rupees, yen, SDR and euro. So neither.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; non-government debt dominates.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; the debt is in several currencies, including rupees.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: The word 'all' in statement 2 is the giveaway; rupee-denominated debt such as masala bonds exists.

short_explanation: Deposits are money a bank owes its customers, so they are a liability. Advances, investments and money at call and short notice are assets.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Advances (loans) are a bank's main earning asset.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Investments in government and other securities are assets.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Money lent at call and short notice is a short-term asset.

short_explanation: Item 1 reduces the risk: IT export earnings bring in foreign currency. Item 2 does not: higher government spending can widen deficits and imports, adding to pressure on the rupee. Item 3 reduces the risk: remittances are a large, steady source of foreign exchange. So 1 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 3; remittances are a major foreign exchange inflow.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits items 1 and 3 and picks item 2, which does not reduce currency risk.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 2; more government spending does not reduce currency risk.

short_explanation: The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State relations (set up in 1983) recommended that a Governor be an eminent person from outside the State, detached and without recent active politics.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The First ARC dealt with administrative reform; this Governor criterion is associated with Sarkaria.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The Rajamannar Committee was set up by Tamil Nadu on State autonomy and did not frame this criterion.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The NCRWC (2000) reviewed the Constitution broadly; this formulation is Sarkaria's.

common_traps: The Punchhi Commission and the NCRWC later echoed Sarkaria, but the recommendation originates with Sarkaria.

short_explanation: Participatory Notes are offshore derivative instruments issued by registered foreign portfolio investors to overseas investors who want exposure to Indian shares without registering with SEBI.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A certificate of deposit is a money market instrument issued by banks.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Commercial paper is short-term unsecured debt issued by companies.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A promissory note is a written promise to pay, not a route to Indian equities.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 creates a National Authority and State Authorities (CAMPA). Statement 2 is incorrect: the Act does not make people's participation mandatory in compensatory afforestation, which was a criticism of it. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; the Act has no mandatory people's participation clause.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; CAMPA exists at both levels.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: Parliament can set up ad hoc committees to review a regulator. Item 2 is correct: departmentally related standing committees examine the regulators of their ministries. Item 3 is incorrect: the Finance Commission recommends tax-sharing between Centre and States. Item 4 is incorrect: the FSLRC drafted financial law reforms, it does not review regulators. Item 5 is incorrect: NITI Aayog is a policy think tank. So 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 3 and 4 and omits item 2.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 3, 4 and 5, none of which reviews regulators.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 5 and omits item 1.

common_traps: The FSLRC wrote about regulators and proposed a new framework, but writing a report is not the same as reviewing them.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Second Plan (Mahalanobis model) pushed heavy, basic and capital goods industries to substitute imports. Statement 2 is correct: the Fourth Plan aimed at 'growth with stability' and at correcting the concentration of wealth and economic power. Statement 3 is incorrect: the financial sector was not made an integral part of the Plan for the first time in the Fifth Plan. So 1 and 2 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; the Second Plan's heavy-industry push is its defining feature.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: PVTGs live in 18 States and one Union Territory (Andaman and Nicobar Islands). Statement 2 is correct: a stagnant or declining population is one criterion, along with pre-agricultural technology, low literacy and a subsistence economy. Statement 3 is incorrect: 75 PVTGs are notified, not 95. Statement 4 is correct: the Irular (Tamil Nadu) and Konda Reddi (Andhra Pradesh) are PVTGs. So 1, 2 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3 and omits statement 4.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3 and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; the number notified is 75.

common_traps: The count is the trap: 75 PVTGs, not 95.

short_explanation: The sentence says ordinary laws cannot limit the Supreme Court's power under Article 142 to do complete justice. Option b restates exactly that.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The sentence is about Article 142, the Supreme Court's power; Election Commission decisions can be challenged in court.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Article 360 emergencies need the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers; this has nothing to do with Article 142.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: This describes limits on State legislation, not the Supreme Court's powers.

common_traps: In practice the Court has said Article 142 cannot be used to override express statutory provisions (Supreme Court Bar Association, 1998); the question asks only what the sentence could mean.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: under Article 176 the Governor addresses the Assembly at the start of the first session each year. Statement 2 is correct per UPSC's key: where a State Legislature has no rule on a matter, it follows the Lok Sabha's rule and practice. So both.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which UPSC's key treats as correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; the Governor's annual address is required by Article 176.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are treated as correct.

common_traps: The Governor's address is at the first session of each year, and also after each general election.
key_note: Accepted as UPSC's key. Statement 2 reflects parliamentary practice followed by State legislatures rather than an express constitutional provision, so it is harder to corroborate.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the protocol on smuggling of migrants is attached to UNTOC, not UNCAC. Statement 2 is correct: UNCAC (2003) is the first legally binding global anti-corruption instrument. Statement 3 is incorrect: the asset-recovery chapter is in UNCAC (Chapter V), not UNTOC. Statement 4 is correct: UNODC supports implementation of both conventions. So 2 and 4 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, which swap features of UNCAC and UNTOC.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; asset recovery is a UNCAC chapter.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 3, which are incorrect.

common_traps: Statements 1 and 3 give real features of the two conventions but attach them to the wrong one.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the 2017 amendment to the Indian Forest Act removed bamboo grown outside forest areas from the definition of 'tree'; it gave no right to fell bamboo in forest areas. Statement 2 is correct: the Forest Rights Act, 2006 lists bamboo as minor forest produce. Statement 3 is correct: the Act recognises the right to ownership of minor forest produce. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; the amendment concerned bamboo grown on non-forest land.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the Act lists bamboo as minor forest produce.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

common_traps: The 2017 amendment applies to bamboo outside forests, not in forest areas.

topic_name: Right to life and personal liberty
short_explanation: The Supreme Court, notably in Shafin Jahan (2018), held that the right to marry a person of one's choice is part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Article 19 guarantees freedoms such as speech and movement, not choice of spouse.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Article 25 protects freedom of religion.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Article 29 protects the culture of minorities.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes plants, seeds and essentially biological processes for producing plants from patentability. Statement 2 is incorrect: when the question was set (2019) the Intellectual Property Appellate Board existed, having been set up in 2003. Statement 3 is correct: plant varieties cannot be patented and are protected instead under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001. So only 3.
explanation_text: Section 3(j) lists what is not an invention: plants and animals in whole or in part (other than micro-organisms), including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for their production or propagation. India chose a separate, sui generis law for plant varieties, the PPV&FR Act, 2001, as permitted under Article 27(3)(b) of the TRIPS Agreement. Micro-organisms and non-biological (microbiological) processes remain patentable.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect: biological processes for producing seeds are excluded under Section 3(j).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which was incorrect in 2019: the Intellectual Property Appellate Board was then functioning.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, both incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 2 has since changed: the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 abolished the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and moved its work to the High Courts. The question must be read as of 2019.
Micro-organisms can be patented; candidates sometimes extend the Section 3(j) exclusion to them.
key_note: Statement 2 is judged as of 2019, when the Intellectual Property Appellate Board existed; it was abolished in 2021, which would make statement 2 true today.

topic_name: Environment Protection Act and pollution control bodies
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 does not itself lay down any requirement or procedure for public participation; public hearings come later, through notifications such as the EIA Notification. Statement 2 is correct: Section 3(2) empowers the Centre to lay down standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources. So only 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect: the Act has no provision on public participation.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is correct: setting emission and discharge standards is a core power under Section 3.

common_traps: Public hearings under the EIA Notification are issued under powers of the Environment (Protection) Act, so candidates credit the Act itself with a public-participation requirement.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. A broader reading of statement 1 (public hearing under the EIA Notification, which is issued under the Act) is set aside because the Act itself contains no such provision.

short_explanation: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 set out detailed criteria for choosing sites for landfills and waste-processing facilities (distance from habitation, water bodies, airports, flood plains and so on), so option c is correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Generators must segregate waste into three streams (biodegradable, non-biodegradable and domestic hazardous), not five.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The Rules go well beyond these bodies: they cover urban agglomerations, census towns, notified areas, railways, airports, ports, special economic zones, defence establishments, places of pilgrimage and more.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Rules contain no ban on moving waste from one district to another.

common_traps: The 2016 Rules widened coverage beyond municipal areas; the word 'only' in option b is the trap.

topic_name: Social security, pensions and labour welfare
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the 2018 amendment extended fixed-term employment to all sectors, and a fixed-term contract simply ends on its date without retrenchment procedure, which makes it easier for firms to shed workers. Statement 2 is correct: the amended rules state that no notice of termination is necessary in the case of a temporary workman. So both.
explanation_text: Fixed-term employment was first allowed in apparel manufacturing (2016) and extended to all sectors by the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018. A fixed-term worker gets the same hours, wages and benefits as a permanent worker, pro rata, but the contract ends on expiry, so no retrenchment compensation or notice is needed. The same idea was later carried into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct: the rules dispense with termination notice for temporary workmen.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is also correct: a fixed-term contract ends on its own term without retrenchment formalities.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

key_note: Statement 1 is an evaluative claim rather than a verbatim rule; accepted as the intended reading.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: AIIB had well over 80 approved members by 2019 and has more than 100 today. Statement 2 is incorrect: China is the largest shareholder; India is the second largest. Statement 3 is incorrect: AIIB has many non-regional members, such as the United Kingdom, Germany and France. So only 1.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect: China, not India, is the largest shareholder, and members come from outside Asia too.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect: several European, African and Latin American countries are members.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect.

common_traps: India is the second-largest shareholder and also the largest borrower; candidates mistake this for 'largest shareholder'.

short_explanation: The Inter-Creditor Agreement of July 2019, drawn up under Project Sashakt, binds lenders in a consortium to a lead lender's resolution plan so that stressed accounts of Rs 50 crore or more are resolved faster; it was a bad-loan resolution tool, so option d is correct.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The agreement is among lenders over stressed loans; it has nothing to do with the fiscal or current account deficit.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It does not finance infrastructure projects; it deals with resolving loans that have already turned stressed.
