option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3 (it is not legally binding) and statement 5 (India was not a signatory at inception).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 2, which are correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 5, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 4.

common_traps: Assuming a declaration launched at a UN summit must be legally binding; it is a voluntary pledge.
Assuming India, a large forest nation, signed at launch; it did not.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: friction in vehicle brakes sheds iron-rich particles, including magnetite. Item 2 is correct: fuel combustion in engines produces magnetite nanoparticles. Item 3 is incorrect: microwave stoves do not burn fuel or grind metal, so they are not a recognised source. Item 4 is correct: high-temperature combustion in power plants emits them. Item 5 is incorrect: telephone lines generate no such particles. So 1, 2 and 4.
explanation_text: Magnetite is an iron oxide. Tiny rounded magnetite particles form mainly in high-temperature combustion and from friction of iron parts, which is why they are found near busy roads. Studies that found such particles in human brain tissue matched them to traffic and combustion sources, raising concern about links with neurodegenerative disease.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes microwave stoves and telephone lines (items 3 and 5), which are not sources, and omits power plants.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 3 and 5, which are not sources, and omits brakes and engines.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes microwave stoves and telephone lines, which do not generate magnetite.

common_traps: Linking 'magnetic' particles to electromagnetic devices such as microwaves or telephone lines; the source is combustion and friction, not electromagnetic fields.

short_explanation: An oyster draws water over its gills and strains out plankton and fine organic particles, which is filter feeding.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Catfish are bottom-feeding fish that scavenge or hunt; they do not strain food out of water.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: An octopus is an active predator that catches crabs and fish with its arms.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A pelican scoops fish into its throat pouch; it catches prey rather than filtering fine particles.

common_traps: Reading the pelican's pouch-scooping as filter feeding; it drains water to swallow whole fish, not to sieve plankton.

short_explanation: Phosphorus has no significant gaseous phase, so its main reservoir is rock; weathering of phosphate rocks releases it into soil and water, from where plants take it up.
explanation_text: Biogeochemical cycles are either gaseous (the main reservoir is the atmosphere, as in the carbon and nitrogen cycles) or sedimentary (the main reservoir is the Earth's crust). Phosphorus is the classic sedimentary cycle. Sulphur is partly sedimentary too, but it also moves through the air as sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide, so weathering is not its single main entry point.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The carbon cycle's main reservoir is atmospheric carbon dioxide, entering living things through photosynthesis.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Nitrogen enters the living world mainly from the atmosphere through nitrogen fixation, not rock weathering.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Sulphur has a large atmospheric component (volcanic and industrial gases), so rock weathering is not its main source.

common_traps: Choosing sulphur because it is also partly sedimentary; phosphorus is the cycle with no meaningful gaseous stage.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: earthworms eat decaying leaves and organic matter in soil. Item 2 is incorrect: jellyfish are predators that sting plankton and small fish. Item 3 is correct: millipedes feed on dead leaves and rotting wood. Item 4 is incorrect: seahorses are predators of tiny crustaceans. Item 5 is correct: woodlice feed on decaying plant matter. So 1, 3 and 5.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes jellyfish and seahorses (items 2 and 4), which are predators, and omits millipedes and woodlice.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes jellyfish and seahorses, which are predators, and omits earthworms.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes jellyfish and seahorses, which are not detritivores.

short_explanation: The Common Carbon Metric, developed under UNEP's Sustainable Buildings and Climate Initiative, is a standard way to measure energy use and greenhouse gas emissions from the operation of existing buildings, so that building performance can be compared across countries.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It is not a carbon-trading tool for farms; it measures the operational footprint of buildings.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: National footprints are reported through UNFCCC inventories, not this building-level metric.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: It does not estimate the world's total fossil-fuel emissions over time; its scope is building operations.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: corals, which are cnidarians, host photosynthetic algae called zooxanthellae in their tissues. Item 2 is correct: fungi form lichens with algae and mycorrhizae with plant roots. Item 3 is correct: flagellate protozoa in a termite's gut digest the wood it eats. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits protozoa (item 3), which include the termite-gut symbionts.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits cnidarians (item 1), which include reef-building corals with algal partners.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits fungi (item 2), which form lichens and mycorrhizae.

common_traps: Thinking of protozoa only as parasites that cause disease; many live in mutually beneficial partnerships.

short_explanation: When more people keep money in banks instead of as cash, more of each rupee returns to banks as deposits and can be lent again, so the money multiplier rises.
explanation_text: The money multiplier is broad money divided by reserve money. It falls when banks must hold more reserves and when the public holds more cash relative to deposits. A stronger banking habit lowers the cash that leaks out of the banking system in each round of lending, so each rupee of reserve money supports more deposits.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: A higher Cash Reserve Ratio forces banks to keep more with the RBI, which lowers the multiplier.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: A higher Statutory Liquidity Ratio locks more deposits into liquid assets, reducing lending and the multiplier.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Population size by itself does not change the ratio of cash to deposits or the reserve ratios that set the multiplier.

common_traps: Confusing an increase in reserve requirements with an increase in money creation; higher CRR or SLR shrinks the multiplier.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: expansionary monetary or fiscal policy raises aggregate demand. Item 2 is correct: a fiscal stimulus adds government spending or tax relief, pushing demand up. Item 3 is incorrect: indexing wages to inflation raises costs, which is cost-push inflation (the wage-price spiral). Item 4 is correct: higher purchasing power lets people buy more. Item 5 is incorrect: rising interest rates curb borrowing and spending, reducing demand. So 1, 2 and 4.
explanation_text: Demand-pull inflation happens when total demand grows faster than the economy's ability to supply goods. Cost-push inflation happens when production costs such as wages or raw materials rise. Inflation-indexed wages belong to the second type, because they raise firms' costs every time prices rise.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes wage indexation (cost-push) and rising interest rates (which reduce demand), and omits items 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 3 and 5, which do not cause demand-pull inflation, and omits higher purchasing power.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes wage indexation and rising interest rates, which do not add to demand-pull inflation.

common_traps: Treating every cause of inflation as demand-pull; wage indexation raises costs, so it is cost-push.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: retail investors can buy Treasury Bills and government dated bonds in the primary market through non-competitive bidding, including through stock exchange platforms linked to demat accounts. Statement 2 is correct: NDS-OM is the RBI's electronic, anonymous order-matching platform for trading government securities. Statement 3 is incorrect: CDSL was promoted by the Bombay Stock Exchange together with banks, not by the RBI. So 1 and 2.
explanation_text: The RBI regulates the government securities market and runs its trading platform, but it does not promote depositories. India's two depositories are NSDL (promoted by NSE with IDBI and UTI) and CDSL (promoted by BSE with leading banks), both regulated by SEBI.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; NDS-OM is indeed the RBI's government securities trading platform.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only statement 3, which is incorrect because the RBI did not promote CDSL.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

common_traps: Assuming the RBI promoted a depository because it manages government securities; depositories are promoted by stock exchanges and banks and regulated by SEBI.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: WaterCredit gives small loans so poor households can pay for water connections and toilets. Statement 2 is incorrect: it is an initiative of the non-profit Water.org, not the WHO and the World Bank. Statement 3 is correct: it aims to meet water and sanitation needs through affordable finance rather than subsidies or charity. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect because WaterCredit comes from Water.org, and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Assuming any global water or health initiative must be run by the WHO or the World Bank.

topic_name: Money and banking: RBI and monetary policy
short_explanation: Item 1 is incorrect: lending to trade and industry is ordinary commercial banking, not a central bank's last-resort role. Item 2 is correct: as lender of last resort, the RBI provides emergency liquidity to banks facing a temporary crisis so that a solvent bank does not fail for want of cash. Item 3 is incorrect: lending to governments is the RBI's role as banker to the government. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 1; lending to trade and industry is not the lender-of-last-resort function.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 3; financing government deficits falls under the banker-to-government role.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only item 3 and omits item 2, which is the actual lender-of-last-resort role.

common_traps: Mixing up the RBI's separate roles: lender of last resort to banks versus banker to the government.

short_explanation: R2, or Responsible Recycling, is a standard for electronics recyclers that sets practices for safe handling of electronic waste, data security and environmental and worker protection.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Ramsar sites are managed under the Ramsar Convention's own wise-use guidelines, not the R2 standard.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: R2 has nothing to do with farming on degraded land; it covers electronics recycling.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Environmental Impact Assessment is a separate appraisal process for projects, not the R2 recycling standard.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: smelting is not known for releasing lethal quantities of carbon monoxide. Statement 2 is correct: copper slag can leach heavy metals such as lead, arsenic and cadmium into soil and water. Statement 3 is correct: copper ores are sulphides, so smelting releases sulphur dioxide. So 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits sulphur dioxide (statement 3).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits slag leaching (statement 2).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; carbon monoxide in lethal quantities is not the concern with copper smelters.

common_traps: The word 'lethal' in statement 1: some carbon monoxide may form in any furnace, but lethal releases are not the recognised concern.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: furnace oil is a heavy residual fraction left after crude oil distillation in refineries. Statement 2 is correct: industries burn it in boilers and captive power units. Statement 3 is correct: it has a high sulphur content, so burning it releases sulphur dioxide. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3; furnace oil is a high-sulphur fuel.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; furnace oil is a refinery product.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; industries do use it to generate power.

short_explanation: Blue carbon is the carbon stored by oceans and coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows, much of it locked in their waterlogged soils.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Carbon held in forests and farm soils is called green carbon.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Carbon in petroleum and natural gas is fossil carbon, sometimes called brown or black carbon in this context.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Atmospheric carbon is not a stored carbon pool; blue carbon is carbon removed from the air and held by marine ecosystems.

common_traps: Confusing blue carbon with black carbon, which is soot from incomplete combustion.

short_explanation: Item 1 is incorrect: ferns have true roots and need soil or at least accumulated humus. Item 2 is correct: lichens grow on bare rock and help break it down. Item 3 is correct: mosses have no true roots and can cling to rock surfaces. Item 4 is incorrect: mushrooms are fungi that need decaying organic matter to feed on. So 2 and 3.
explanation_text: Lichens and mosses are pioneer species of primary succession on bare rock. Lichens release acids that weather the rock, and dead lichen and moss add organic matter, slowly building the first thin soil in which ferns and other plants can later grow.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes ferns and mushrooms, which need soil or organic matter, and omits lichens and mosses.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits moss (item 3), which also grows on bare surfaces.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes ferns and mushrooms and omits lichens, the classic survivors on bare rock.

common_traps: Picking mushrooms because they grow on logs; they still feed on decaying organic matter.

topic_name: Money and banking: RBI and monetary policy
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: under Section 8 of the RBI Act, 1934, the Central Government appoints the Governor. Statement 2 is incorrect: the power to issue directions to the RBI in public interest comes from Section 7 of the RBI Act, not the Constitution. Statement 3 is correct: the Governor's powers come from the RBI Act. So 1 and 3.
explanation_text: The RBI is a statutory body, not a constitutional one. Section 7 of the RBI Act lets the Central Government, after consulting the Governor, give the RBI directions it considers necessary in the public interest.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; the power of direction is statutory (Section 7 of the RBI Act), not constitutional.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect because the Constitution has no such provision.

common_traps: Treating the RBI as a constitutional body; it was created by the RBI Act, 1934, and all its governing powers come from that Act.

topic_name: Social security, pensions and labour welfare
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: EPF coverage depends on the establishment (mandatory only where 20 or more persons are employed) and a wage ceiling, so not all casual workers are covered. Statement 2 is correct: labour law caps normal working hours and requires overtime pay for any worker, casual or regular. Statement 3 is correct: the 2017 amendment to Section 6 of the Payment of Wages Act lets the government, by notification, require an establishment or industry to pay wages only by cheque or bank transfer. So 2 and 3.
explanation_text: The word 'All' in statement 1 is what fails it. The Employees' Provident Funds Act applies to notified establishments employing 20 or more persons, so a casual worker in a small shop or farm falls outside it. Hours of work and overtime, by contrast, attach to the worker under wage and factory laws whatever the nature of the job.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which fails because EPF covers only establishments above the size threshold, and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; not all casual workers are entitled to EPF coverage.

common_traps: 'All casual workers' in statement 1: EPF is tied to establishment size, so the universal claim is false.
key_note: UPSC's key treats statement 2 as correct on the basis that working-hour limits and overtime apply to every worker; in practice enforcement for informal casual work is weak, but the legal entitlement is what the statement tests.

short_explanation: In a recession private demand collapses, so the government raises spending on public projects to create jobs and income, which revives demand through the multiplier.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The tax cut helps, but raising interest rates at the same time chokes borrowing and investment, the opposite of what a recession needs.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Raising taxes takes income away from households and firms and deepens the slump, even if interest rates are cut.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Cutting public spending further reduces demand and worsens a recession.

common_traps: Picking a mixed option because it contains one correct measure; both halves must point towards expansion.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: if a substitute gets dearer, buyers switch to this good. Statement 2 is incorrect: if a complement gets dearer, buyers use less of the pair, so demand falls. Statement 3 is incorrect: for an inferior good, higher income makes people buy less of it. Statement 4 is correct in the loose sense UPSC uses: a fall in its own price raises the quantity bought in the market. So 1 and 4.
explanation_text: Strictly, a change in a good's own price moves buyers along the demand curve (a change in quantity demanded), while changes in the prices of related goods or in income shift the whole curve (a change in demand). Statement 4 counts as correct only if 'demand' is read loosely as the quantity demanded.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3; a dearer complement and higher income for an inferior good both reduce demand.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; for an inferior good demand falls as income rises.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, which reduce demand, and omits statement 4.

common_traps: Forgetting that an inferior good behaves opposite to a normal good when income rises.
Mixing up substitutes and complements: a dearer substitute helps this good, a dearer complement hurts it.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. A strict reading would say a fall in own price changes quantity demanded, not demand, which would leave only statement 1 (not an option); the key reads statement 4 loosely.

topic_name: Cooperative banks and regional rural banks
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: urban cooperative banks are regulated by the RBI for banking matters and by the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies (or the Central Registrar for multi-state banks) for management, not by local boards. Statement 2 is correct: since the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020, they can issue equity, preference and special shares, subject to RBI rules. Statement 3 is correct: they were brought under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 with effect from 1966. So 2 and 3.
explanation_text: Urban cooperative banks long faced dual control: the RBI supervised banking functions while state registrars controlled registration, management and audit. The 2020 amendment strengthened RBI oversight and opened new routes to raise capital, including share issues to members and others.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only statement 1, which is incorrect because there are no state 'local boards' regulating these banks.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; supervision lies with the RBI and the Registrar of Cooperative Societies, not local boards.

common_traps: Confusing the state Registrar of Cooperative Societies with an invented 'local board'.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: changes in US Federal Reserve rates shift global capital flows and so affect demand for Indian bonds. Item 2 is correct: the RBI's policy rate, liquidity operations and bond purchases or sales directly move yields. Item 3 is correct: higher inflation and short-term rates push investors to demand higher yields. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 3; inflation and short-term rates are basic drivers of bond yields.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only the RBI; global and inflation factors also move Indian yields.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only inflation and short-term rates, omitting the Fed and the RBI.

common_traps: Assuming a domestic bond market is untouched by foreign central banks; foreign investors move money when US rates change.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: foreign currency convertible bonds, once converted into equity under FDI rules, count towards foreign direct investment. Item 2 is correct: portfolio investment that crosses the 10 percent stake threshold is reclassified as FDI, which is the 'certain conditions' in the item. Item 3 is correct: global depository receipts represent underlying Indian shares and are counted within FDI under the depository receipt scheme. Item 4 is incorrect: non-resident external deposits are bank deposits, not investment in a company's equity. So 1, 2 and 3.
explanation_text: FDI means a lasting stake and some control in an enterprise, usually equity. Instruments that end up as shares of an Indian company, such as convertible bonds and depository receipts, are recorded within the FDI framework. NRE deposits are counted in the banking capital account of the balance of payments.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only GDRs and omits FCCBs and qualifying foreign institutional investment.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes NRE deposits (item 4), which are bank deposits, and omits items 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes NRE deposits, which are not FDI, and omits items 2 and 3.

common_traps: Treating NRE deposits as investment because they come from abroad; they are deposits, not equity stakes.
key_note: Classification of FCCBs and GDRs depends on their conversion into equity under FDI rules; the key's reading is accepted.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: after devaluation each unit of foreign currency buys more domestic goods, so exports become cheaper abroad and more competitive. Statement 2 is incorrect: devaluation lowers, not raises, the foreign value of the domestic currency. Statement 3 is incorrect: the trade balance improves only if export and import demand respond enough, and it often worsens at first. So 1 only.
explanation_text: Whether devaluation improves the trade balance depends on the price elasticities of exports and imports (the Marshall-Lerner condition). In the short run the import bill can rise before volumes adjust, so the balance first worsens and then improves, a pattern called the J-curve. That is why 'necessarily' makes statement 3 false.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; devaluation reduces the foreign value of the currency.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 3, which fails because the trade balance does not necessarily improve.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect, and omits statement 1.

common_traps: The word 'necessarily' before the list: price competitiveness always improves, but the trade balance need not.

short_explanation: Black money is income hidden from the tax authorities, so its most direct and serious cost to the government is lost tax revenue, which weakens the exchequer and forces higher burdens on honest taxpayers.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Real estate diversion is a common use of black money, but it is a symptom rather than the government's main worry.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Buying gold and jewellery is another use of black money, not the chief concern of the exchequer.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Political funding is a concern, but 'growth of regionalism' is not an effect of black money, and revenue loss is the main worry.

short_explanation: Printing new money (monetisation) to pay for a deficit adds fresh purchasing power to the economy without withdrawing any, so it is the most inflationary way to finance a deficit.
explanation_text: Borrowing from the public only moves existing money from savers to the government, so total money supply barely changes. Borrowing from banks can add to credit, but banks lend from existing deposits and reserves. Creating new money expands reserve money directly and, through the money multiplier, broad money too.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Repaying public debt returns money already in the system and is not especially inflationary.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Borrowing from the public only transfers existing money to the government, so it adds little to money supply.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Borrowing from banks can add some credit, but less than printing fresh money.

short_explanation: The Rapid Financing Instrument and the Rapid Credit Facility are IMF lending windows that give quick, low-conditionality emergency finance to member countries facing urgent balance-of-payments needs; the credit facility is concessional and meant for low-income countries.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Asian Development Bank lends for regional development projects and has no windows by these names.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The UNEP Finance Initiative is a partnership with private financial institutions on sustainability, not a lender.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The World Bank finances development projects; these rapid balance-of-payments facilities belong to the IMF.

common_traps: Confusing the World Bank with the IMF: the IMF handles balance-of-payments support, the World Bank project and development finance.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the RBI's NEER index is expressed so that a rise means the rupee has appreciated against a basket of currencies. Statement 2 is incorrect: a rise in REER means the rupee has appreciated in real terms, which makes exports costlier and hurts trade competitiveness. Statement 3 is correct: REER adjusts NEER for relative inflation, so higher domestic inflation than abroad pushes REER up faster than NEER and widens the gap. So 1 and 3.
explanation_text: NEER is a weighted average of the rupee's exchange rates against trading partners' currencies. REER is NEER adjusted for price differences between India and those partners. When Indian prices rise faster than partners' prices, REER rises even if NEER stays flat.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; a rising REER signals a loss, not a gain, in trade competitiveness.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; a real appreciation makes exports less competitive.

common_traps: Reading a rise in REER as a 'stronger' and therefore better position; for exporters a real appreciation is a loss of competitiveness.

topic_name: Liquidity instruments and open market operations
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: to fight high inflation the RBI sells government securities to absorb money, not buys them. Statement 2 is correct: selling dollars from reserves raises the supply of dollars and supports a falling rupee. Statement 3 is correct: lower US or EU interest rates draw capital into India, pushing the rupee up, so the RBI buys dollars to curb appreciation and build reserves. So 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; buying securities injects money and would worsen inflation.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; the RBI sells securities, not buys them, to fight inflation.

common_traps: Mixing up the direction of open market operations: buying securities injects liquidity, selling withdraws it.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the DSSI was agreed by the G20 in November 2020 and endorsed by the Paris Club creditors. Statement 2 is correct: it lets low-income countries with unsustainable debt seek coordinated, case-by-case debt restructuring from official creditors. So both.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the framework exists to help low-income countries with unsustainable debt.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; the Paris Club did endorse the framework alongside the G20.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: because the principal is protected against inflation, investors accept a lower coupon, which cuts the government's borrowing cost. Statement 2 is correct: indexing the principal to inflation protects investors from uncertainty about future prices. Statement 3 is incorrect: interest and capital gains on these bonds are taxable under normal income-tax rules. So 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; income from inflation-indexed bonds is not tax-free.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; there is no tax exemption on these bonds.

common_traps: Assuming government savings instruments are tax-free by default; these bonds carry no tax exemption.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: India permits foreign direct investment only in the marketplace model of e-commerce, and a foreign-owned platform may not hold and sell its own inventory. Statement 2 is incorrect as worded: since 2018 the rules bar a platform from letting any seller in which it or its group holds equity sell on its platform, so this is a prohibition, not a limit on how far it may own big sellers. So neither.
explanation_text: Press Note 2 of 2018 tightened the FDI policy for e-commerce. A foreign-invested marketplace cannot own the inventory sold on it, cannot control a seller's inventory, and cannot allow entities with its own or its group's equity participation to sell on its platform.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 1, but foreign-owned firms cannot sell their own goods through an inventory model.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 2, but the rules bar such ownership-linked sellers outright rather than limiting the degree of ownership.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect under India's FDI policy for e-commerce.

common_traps: Reading statement 2 as 'some restriction exists, so it is true'; the rule is an outright bar, which is why UPSC treats 'limited' as incorrect.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. A looser reading of statement 2 (any restriction counts as a limit) would favour option b; the key treats the 2018 rule as an outright bar on platform-linked sellers.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: harvesting crops produces goods, so it is real-sector activity. Item 2 is correct: turning cotton into fabric is manufacturing, also real sector. Item 3 is incorrect: a bank lending money is a financial transaction. Item 4 is incorrect: issuing rupee-denominated bonds abroad is raising finance, a financial-sector activity. So 1 and 2.
explanation_text: The real sector covers the production and sale of goods and services, such as farming, manufacturing and trade in goods. The financial sector covers the flow of money and financial claims: lending, borrowing, and issuing shares or bonds.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 3 and 4, which are financial activities, and omits farming.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 3 and 4, which are financial activities, and omits manufacturing.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes bank lending and bond issuance, which belong to the financial sector.

short_explanation: An indirect transfer is a sale of shares of a foreign company whose value comes substantially from assets in India; India taxes the gain on the ground that the underlying value lies in India.
explanation_text: Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, added retrospectively in 2012 after the Supreme Court's Vodafone ruling, deemed such gains to accrue in India. The retrospective part of this rule was withdrawn by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, which is why the term was often in the news.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: This is ordinary taxation of an Indian firm's foreign profits, not an indirect transfer of Indian assets.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: This is a foreign company paying tax at home on Indian profits; no transfer of shares holding Indian value is involved.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: This is a direct sale of foreign tangible assets by an Indian company, not an offshore share transfer deriving value from India.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: acquiring new technology creates a lasting asset for the company, so it is capital expenditure. Statement 2 is incorrect: debt and equity are ways of raising money, not kinds of expenditure, so neither is capital or revenue expenditure. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 2, which confuses sources of finance with categories of spending.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; buying new technology is capital expenditure.

common_traps: Confusing capital receipts or financing with capital expenditure; borrowing or issuing shares brings money in, it is not spending.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: banks, insurers and provident funds invest household savings in government securities, so a share of household financial savings finances government borrowing. Statement 2 is correct: dated securities sold at market-related rates through RBI auctions form the largest part of the Centre's internal debt. So both.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; dated securities are the biggest component of internal debt.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; household savings reach government borrowing through banks and funds.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

topic_name: Contempt of court and judicial accountability
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961) reviewed the law of contempt, and its report led to the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Statement 2 is correct: Articles 129 and 215 make the Supreme Court and High Courts courts of record with power to punish contempt of themselves. Statement 3 is incorrect: civil and criminal contempt are defined in the 1971 Act, not the Constitution. Statement 4 is correct: Parliament can legislate on contempt under Entry 77 of the Union List and Entry 14 of the Concurrent List. So 1, 2 and 4.
explanation_text: The Constitution creates the power to punish contempt but leaves the definitions to statute. Section 2 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil contempt (wilful disobedience of a court order or breach of an undertaking) and criminal contempt (acts that scandalise or lower the authority of a court, prejudice proceedings, or obstruct justice).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 4; Parliament does have power to make laws on contempt of court.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only statement 3, which is incorrect because the definitions are in the 1971 Act.

common_traps: Assuming that because the Constitution gives the power to punish contempt, it must also define the types of contempt.

topic_name: Legal profession and access to justice
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: under the Advocates Act, 1961, an advocate is an individual enrolled on a State Bar Council roll, so a legal firm is not recognised as an advocate, and the statement's neat split between included and excluded groups is wrong. Statement 2 is correct: under Section 7 of the Act, the Bar Council of India lays down standards of legal education and recognises universities and law colleges whose degrees qualify for enrolment. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 1, which is incorrect because firms are not recognised as advocates.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the Bar Council of India does regulate legal education and recognise law colleges.

common_traps: Assuming the UGC alone regulates law colleges; the Bar Council of India recognises them for the purpose of enrolment as advocates.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: a Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced in either House without the President's prior recommendation. Statement 2 is correct: since the 24th Amendment (1971), Article 368 obliges the President to give assent. Statement 3 is correct: each House must pass it by a special majority, and there is no joint sitting to resolve a deadlock. So 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; no prior presidential recommendation is needed.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Carrying over the Money Bill rule of prior recommendation to amendment bills.

topic_name: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Constitution does not rank ministers; the three-tier system of Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers comes from convention and practice. Statement 2 is correct: Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, 2003, caps the total number of ministers including the Prime Minister at 15 percent of the Lok Sabha's total strength. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 1; ministerial ranks are not classified in the Constitution.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the 15 percent cap is in Article 75(1A).

common_traps: Assuming a familiar practice must have a constitutional basis; ministerial ranks are conventional.

short_explanation: Item 1 is incorrect: a proclamation of emergency must be approved by both Houses of Parliament. Item 2 is correct: only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion, because the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to it under Article 75(3). Item 3 is incorrect: the President is impeached by both Houses under Article 61. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 1; emergency approval needs both Houses.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 1 and 3, both of which involve both Houses.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only impeachment, which is shared by both Houses.

common_traps: Treating the Lok Sabha's special role in approving revocation of an emergency as an exclusive power to ratify it.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: under the Tenth Schedule a nominated member may join a political party within six months of taking the seat; only joining after six months attracts disqualification. Statement 2 is correct: the law sets no time limit for the presiding officer to decide a defection petition. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 1, which reverses the rule: nominated members may join a party within six months.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the Tenth Schedule indeed has no deadline for deciding cases.

common_traps: Reversing the six-month rule for nominated members; the window is for joining, not a ban on joining.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Constitution gives the Attorney General (Article 88) and ministers the right to speak in Parliament, but the Solicitor General has no such right, so they are not 'the only officers' allowed. Statement 2 is incorrect: the Constitution says nothing about the Attorney General resigning with the government; that is only a convention. So neither.
explanation_text: Article 88 lets every minister and the Attorney General speak and take part in the proceedings of either House and its committees, without a right to vote. Article 76 says the Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and sets no fixed term.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 1, but the Solicitor General has no constitutional right to take part in Parliament.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Marks statement 2, but resignation with the government is a convention, not a constitutional rule.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: The words 'According to the Constitution' in statement 2: the practice exists but is conventional, not written.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: mandamus lies against a private body only when it performs a public duty. Statement 2 is accepted as correct: courts have held that mandamus does not lie against a company, even a government company, merely to enforce ordinary contractual or company obligations, since such a company is not a statutory authority with a public duty. Statement 3 is correct: quo warranto can be sought by any member of the public, not only an aggrieved person. So all three.
explanation_text: Mandamus commands a public authority to perform a public duty. In Praga Tools Corporation v. C.A. Imanual (1969) the Supreme Court held that mandamus would not issue against a government-owned company registered under the Companies Act to enforce a private dispute, because it was not a statutory body discharging a public duty. Quo warranto tests a person's right to hold a public office, and because public interest is at stake the petitioner need not be personally aggrieved.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3; any public-minded person can seek quo warranto.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; mandamus against a private body needs a public duty.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which the key treats as correct on the settled Praga Tools line.

common_traps: Assuming that because a government company is 'State' under Article 12 for fundamental rights, mandamus always lies against it.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Later case law allows writs against government companies performing public functions, which would make statement 2 doubtful and favour option c; the key follows the older rule that mandamus does not lie against a company as such.

topic_name: Health system and public health programmes
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: joining the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is voluntary for hospitals and other providers. Statement 2 is incorrect: citizens choose whether to create a health ID (ABHA), so no one is required to be part of it. Statement 3 is correct: a digital health record linked to the ABHA number can be accessed anywhere in the country. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2; participation is voluntary for both hospitals and citizens.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1; hospitals are not required to adopt the mission.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, both of which wrongly make participation compulsory.

common_traps: The words 'must' and 'every citizen should': the mission is voluntary by design, partly because of privacy concerns.

topic_name: Presiding officers, privileges and office of profit
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: under Rule 8 of the Lok Sabha Rules, the Deputy Speaker's election is held on a date fixed by the Speaker. Statement 2 is incorrect: there is no rule that the Deputy Speaker must come from the ruling or main opposition party; by convention the post has often gone to the opposition. Statement 3 is correct: when presiding, the Deputy Speaker has the Speaker's powers and no appeal lies against the rulings. Statement 4 is incorrect: the motion to elect the Deputy Speaker is moved by a member and seconded by another member; there is no practice of the Speaker moving it with the Prime Minister seconding. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; there is no mandatory party rule for the Deputy Speaker.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 4, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 4, both incorrect.

common_traps: Turning the convention of giving the post to the opposition into a 'mandatory provision'.

short_explanation: Flooded paddy fields create oxygen-poor soil where microbes release methane, and heavy nitrogen fertiliser use on rice releases nitrous oxide, making rice the leading crop source of both gases.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Cotton adds nitrous oxide through fertiliser but is grown in unflooded fields, so it produces little methane.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Sugarcane is not flooded like paddy, so its methane emissions are minor.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Wheat is a dryland crop; its main farm emission is nitrous oxide from fertiliser, not methane.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: SRI transplants single young seedlings at wide spacing, so it needs far less seed. Item 2 is correct: alternate wetting and drying keeps the soil aerated part of the time, cutting the methane made by microbes in flooded fields. Item 3 is correct: using less irrigation water means less pumping, so less electricity is used. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 3; less irrigation means less power for pumps.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 1; SRI uses far less seed because of single, widely spaced seedlings.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 2; intermittent drying cuts methane from paddy.

topic_name: Degradation of lakes and inland water bodies
short_explanation: Lake Faguibine in northern Mali, once one of West Africa's largest lakes, dried up after the droughts of the 1970s and reduced flooding from the Niger, and its bed is now largely desert.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Lake Victoria is in East Africa and still holds water; it is Africa's largest lake.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Lake Oguta is in south-eastern Nigeria and has not dried up.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Lake Volta in Ghana is a large man-made reservoir behind the Akosombo Dam, not a dried lake.

short_explanation: The Gandikota canyon in the Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh was carved by the Pennar (Penna) river cutting through the Erramala hills.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The Cauvery flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; it does not pass Gandikota.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The Manjira is a tributary of the Godavari in Telangana and Maharashtra, far from Gandikota.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Tungabhadra flows through Karnataka to join the Krishna; it does not form this canyon.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is incorrect: Namcha Barwa is at the eastern end of the Himalaya, near the Brahmaputra's great bend, not in the Garhwal Himalaya. Pair 2 is correct: Nanda Devi lies in the Kumaon Himalaya of Uttarakhand. Pair 3 is incorrect: Nokrek is the highest peak of the Garo Hills in Meghalaya, not part of the Sikkim Himalaya. So 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 1; Namcha Barwa is in the eastern Himalaya, not Garhwal.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pairs 1 and 3, both incorrect, and omits pair 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Marks only pair 3; Nokrek is in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya.

common_traps: Placing Nokrek in the Himalaya because it is in the north-east; it is in the Meghalaya plateau.

topic_name: World political geography and regions in news
short_explanation: The Levant is the region along the eastern shore of the Mediterranean, roughly covering Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan and nearby areas.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The North African coast from Egypt to Morocco is usually called the Maghreb and North Africa, not the Levant.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The Persian Gulf and Horn of Africa lie far to the south and east of the Levant.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The Levant is only the eastern part of the Mediterranean coast, not the whole of it.

short_explanation: Item 1 is incorrect: Azerbaijan lies west of the Caspian Sea and does not touch Afghanistan. Item 2 is incorrect: Kyrgyzstan is separated from Afghanistan by Tajikistan. Item 3 is correct: Tajikistan borders northern Afghanistan. Item 4 is correct: Uzbekistan has a short border along the Amu Darya. Item 5 is correct: Turkmenistan borders north-western Afghanistan. So 3, 4 and 5.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan, neither of which borders Afghanistan.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan and omits Turkmenistan.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan, which do not border Afghanistan.

common_traps: Assuming Kyrgyzstan borders Afghanistan because it is close; the narrow Wakhan corridor touches Tajikistan and China, not Kyrgyzstan.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: monazite is a phosphate mineral rich in rare earth elements. Statement 2 is correct: it contains thorium, which makes it an atomic mineral. Statement 3 is incorrect: it occurs in beach sands of certain coastal stretches (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh), not along the entire coast. Statement 4 is correct: because of its thorium, only government bodies such as Indian Rare Earths Limited may process or export it. So 1, 2 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; monazite is found only in some coastal sands, not all of them.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which fails because of the word 'entire'.

common_traps: The word 'entire' in statement 3: monazite is found in selected coastal placer deposits, not the whole coastline.

short_explanation: In the northern hemisphere the longest day falls at the summer solstice, usually on 21 June and sometimes on the 20th or 22nd, which is in the second half of June.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The solstice falls around 21 June, after the first half of the month.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: By early July the Sun has already moved south of its solstice position and days are shortening.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Late July days are clearly shorter than at the solstice.

short_explanation: Pair 1 is incorrect: Hokera (Hokersar) wetland is near Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir, not Punjab. Pair 2 is correct: Renuka wetland is in Sirmaur district of Himachal Pradesh. Pair 3 is correct: Rudrasagar lake is in Tripura. Pair 4 is incorrect: Sasthamkotta lake is in Kollam district of Kerala, not Tamil Nadu. So two pairs.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Two pairs, Renuka and Rudrasagar, are correctly matched, not one.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Only two pairs are correct; Hokera and Sasthamkotta are misplaced.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Hokera is in Jammu and Kashmir and Sasthamkotta in Kerala, so not all four are correct.

common_traps: Assuming a southern lake is in Tamil Nadu; Sasthamkotta, Kerala's largest freshwater lake, is in Kollam.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: the Aarogya Setu app's source code was released as open source. Item 2 is correct: CoWIN uses open-source building blocks, including the DIVOC platform for digital vaccine certificates. Item 3 is correct: DigiLocker is part of India's open, API-based digital public infrastructure. Item 4 is correct: DIKSHA is built on the open-source Sunbird platform. So all four.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits DigiLocker and DIKSHA; DIKSHA in particular runs on the open-source Sunbird platform.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits Aarogya Setu, whose source code was made open source.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits CoWIN, which also uses open-source components such as DIVOC.

key_note: How each platform uses open-source components is drawn from government announcements; the key's reading that all four qualify is accepted.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Web 3.0 aims to let users own and control their data instead of leaving it with platforms. Statement 2 is correct: social networks can be built on blockchains, with posts and identities held on decentralised ledgers. Statement 3 is correct: Web 3.0 is designed to be run collectively by users and node operators rather than by one corporation. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3; decentralised, user-run operation is central to Web 3.0.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; user control of data is the core idea of Web 3.0.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; blockchain-based social networks are possible in Web 3.0.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: SaaS customers can usually configure the interface, such as layout and branding, and add or change data fields within the vendor's settings. Statement 2 is correct: SaaS apps run in the cloud, so users can reach their data from mobile devices. Statement 3 is correct: web email services such as Outlook, Hotmail and Yahoo! Mail are everyday examples of SaaS. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3; web mail services are classic SaaS.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; SaaS buyers can configure the interface and data fields.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; cloud delivery lets SaaS data be reached from mobile devices.

common_traps: Assuming SaaS cannot be customised at all because the software is shared; configuration within the vendor's settings is standard.

short_explanation: A Fractional Orbital Bombardment System puts a warhead into a low orbit around the Earth and then brings it down on a target before a full orbit is complete, which lets it approach from unexpected directions and evade early-warning radars.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: FOBS is a weapons delivery system, not a planetary defence against asteroids.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Landing a spacecraft on another planet after several orbits describes a planetary mission, not a weapon system.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Matching a comet's speed to place a probe describes a mission like Rosetta, not FOBS.

common_traps: Reading 'fractional' as meaning the warhead never reaches orbit; it does enter orbit but is brought down before completing a full circuit.

short_explanation: A qubit (quantum bit) is the basic unit of information in quantum computing; unlike a classical bit that is either 0 or 1, it can exist in a superposition of both states.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Cloud services run on classical bits; qubits belong to quantum machines, even if some are offered over the cloud.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Visible light communication (Li-Fi) sends data by modulating light; it uses classical bits, not qubits.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Wireless communication encodes classical bits on radio waves; the term qubit does not arise there.

common_traps: Quantum computers are now offered as cloud services, which tempts some to pick option a; the term itself belongs to quantum computing.

short_explanation: Item 1 is correct: wireless CCTV cameras transmit over a short distance to a nearby receiver and are listed among short-range devices. Item 2 is correct: RFID tags are read within centimetres to a few metres. Item 3 is correct: a wireless LAN covers a building or campus. So all three.
explanation_text: Short-range devices are low-power radio transmitters meant to work over a few metres to a few hundred metres, such as RFID readers, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth equipment, remote controls and wireless alarm and CCTV links. In India several such bands are de-licensed for them by the Department of Telecommunications.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 3, which is also a short-range technology.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 1, which is also a short-range technology.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 2, which is also a short-range technology.

common_traps: CCTV is often thought of as a wired closed circuit and dropped from the list; wireless CCTV links are treated as short-range devices.
key_note: Accepted as the official key. CCTV counts as a short-range device in its wireless form; a wired CCTV system is not a radio device at all, so a strict reading could drop item 1.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: biofilms form on catheters, artificial joints and other implants and cause persistent infections. Statement 2 is correct: they form on food and on processing equipment such as pipes and steel surfaces. Statement 3 is correct: the slimy matrix shields the microbes, so a biofilm can survive antibiotic doses many times higher than free cells. So all three.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: probiotics include bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium and yeasts such as Saccharomyces boulardii. Statement 2 is incorrect: many probiotic organisms are normal residents of the human gut. Statement 3 is correct: lactic acid bacteria help break down lactose, the milk sugar. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 3, which are also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1, which is also correct.

common_traps: Statement 2 sounds plausible because probiotics are sold as supplements, but the same organisms live naturally in the gut.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Covishield uses a viral vector (a weakened chimpanzee adenovirus), not mRNA. Statement 2 is correct: Sputnik V uses two human adenovirus vectors. Statement 3 is correct: Covaxin uses whole inactivated coronavirus. So 2 and 3 only.
explanation_text: Vaccine platforms: mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna) deliver genetic instructions in a lipid coat; viral-vector vaccines (Covishield, Sputnik V) carry the spike gene in a harmless adenovirus; inactivated vaccines (Covaxin) use killed whole virus; protein-subunit vaccines (Corbevax) use a purified piece of the spike protein.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Covishield and Pfizer are both 'new-technology' vaccines, so candidates often assume both are mRNA; Covishield is a viral-vector vaccine.

short_explanation: Effect 1 is possible: storms disturb the ionosphere and degrade GPS signals. Effect 2 is not: tsunamis come from undersea earthquakes and landslides, not solar activity. Effect 3 is possible: induced currents can damage transformers and power grids. Effect 4 is possible: strong storms push auroras to unusually low latitudes. Effect 5 is not: solar storms do not ignite forests. Effect 6 is possible: a heated upper atmosphere increases drag on satellites and changes their orbits. Effect 7 is possible: shortwave radio blackouts are common on polar flight routes. So 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes effects 2 and 5, which are not possible effects, and omits effects 3, 6 and 7, which are also possible effects.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes effects 2 and 5, which are not possible effects, and omits effects 1 and 4, which are also possible effects.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes effects 2 and 5, which are not possible effects.

common_traps: Tsunamis and forest fires sound like large 'natural disaster' effects, but a solar storm acts through the magnetic field and upper atmosphere, not the ground or oceans.

short_explanation: The Climate Action Tracker is an independent scientific analysis produced by research organisations (Climate Analytics and the NewClimate Institute) that rates countries' climate targets and policies against the Paris Agreement goals.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It is not part of the IPCC (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change), which assesses science but does not rate national pledges.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: It is not a UNFCCC body; the UNFCCC runs its own transparency and review process.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: It is not an agency of UNEP or the World Bank; UNEP publishes a separate Emissions Gap Report.

common_traps: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report also compares pledges with goals, so candidates confuse the two; the tracker is a non-governmental research product.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the Climate Group is an international non-profit that builds and runs networks of businesses and governments. Statement 2 is incorrect: EP100 was launched by the Climate Group with the Alliance to Save Energy, not the International Energy Agency. Statement 3 is correct: EP100 brings together leading companies committed to energy productivity. Statement 4 is correct: several Indian companies are EP100 members. Statement 5 is incorrect: the Climate Group, not the IEA, is the secretariat of the Under2 Coalition. So 1, 3 and 4.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 5, which are incorrect, and omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 5, which are incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 4, which are also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 5, which are incorrect.

common_traps: The IEA appears twice to lend authority; in both statements the partner or secretariat role actually belongs to other bodies.
key_note: Statement 3 in the input reads 'lending companies committee'; this is read as 'leading companies committed', which is the evident intent.

short_explanation: Kidneys filter waste from the blood; wetlands do the same for water, as aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients and so purify it.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Describes the water cycle in wetlands, not their filtering role.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Describes wetlands as a food base, a productivity function rather than a cleansing one.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Sediment and soil stabilisation is a real function, but it does not match the filtering image of a kidney.

common_traps: Option c sounds close because wetlands trap sediment, but the kidney analogy is about removing pollutants from water.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the 2021 WHO guidelines set PM2.5 at 15 µg/m³ for the 24-hour mean and 5 µg/m³ for the annual mean. Statement 2 is incorrect: ozone peaks in sunny, hot, still weather, since it forms from sunlight acting on precursor gases. Statement 3 is incorrect: it is the finer PM2.5 that can cross the lung barrier into the blood; PM10 lodges in the airways and lungs. Statement 4 is correct: high ozone irritates airways and can trigger asthma. So 1 and 4 only.
explanation_text: The 2021 WHO Air Quality Guidelines tightened the earlier 2005 values: annual PM2.5 from 10 to 5 µg/m³ and 24-hour PM2.5 from 25 to 15 µg/m³. Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant made when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight, which is why it peaks on bright summer afternoons.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, which are incorrect, and omits statement 1, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 4, which is also correct.

common_traps: Swapping PM10 and PM2.5: only the fine fraction reaches the bloodstream.
Assuming pollution peaks in bad weather; ozone needs sunlight to form.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Gucchi is the morel mushroom, a fungus. Statement 2 is correct: it grows wild in Himalayan forests of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Statement 3 is incorrect: it is collected from the wild, not commercially cultivated, and is not associated with the north-eastern foothills. So 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 2, which are also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1, which is also correct.

common_traps: Its high price suggests a farmed product, but Gucchi is foraged from the wild, which is why it is so costly.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: polyester (PET) fibres are routinely blended with cotton and wool. Statement 2 is incorrect: PET is not suitable for storing every alcoholic beverage; it lets in oxygen and can interact with some spirits and wines over time, so 'any' makes it false. Statement 3 is correct: PET bottles are widely recycled into fibre, sheet and new bottles. Statement 4 is incorrect: burning PET releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. So 1 and 3.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 4, which are incorrect, and omits statements 1 and 3, which are also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 4, which is incorrect, and omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1, which is also correct.

common_traps: The word 'any' in statement 2 turns a partly true claim into a false one.

short_explanation: The Golden Mahseer is a large freshwater fish of Himalayan rivers, not a bird.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The Indian Nightjar is a nocturnal bird.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The spoonbill is a wading bird with a spoon-shaped bill.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The white ibis (black-headed ibis in India) is a wading bird.

common_traps: The word 'Golden' and an unfamiliar name can make it sound like a bird such as an oriole.

short_explanation: Alfalfa (item 1), chickpea (item 3) and clover (item 4) are legumes whose root nodules host Rhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen. Amaranth (item 2), purslane (item 5) and spinach (item 6) are not legumes and do not fix nitrogen. So 1, 3 and 4 only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 5 and 6, which are not nitrogen-fixing, and omits item 4, which is also nitrogen-fixing.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 2, 5 and 6, which are not nitrogen-fixing, and omits items 1 and 3, which are also nitrogen-fixing.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes items 2, 5 and 6, which are not nitrogen-fixing, and omits item 3, which is also nitrogen-fixing.

common_traps: Leafy greens such as spinach and amaranth are nutritious and nitrogen-rich, but they draw nitrogen from the soil rather than fix it.

short_explanation: Biorock technology passes a low-voltage current through a steel frame in seawater, which deposits limestone on it and gives coral fragments a base to grow on; it is used to restore damaged reefs, for example in the Gulf of Kutch.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Building materials from plant residues have nothing to do with the electrolytic mineral growth of biorock.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Shale gas exploration uses geological surveys, not biorock.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Salt licks are natural or placed mineral deposits for animals, not biorock structures.

short_explanation: The Miyawaki method, developed by the Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki, plants many native species densely in small plots so that they grow into a mini forest quickly; it is used for urban afforestation.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: It is a native-forest planting technique, not a method of commercial farming in dry areas.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: It uses native species, not genetically modified plants.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: It has nothing to do with harvesting wind energy.

tag_note: Topic should be Afforestation and urban forestry. The method creates dense native forests, not an agricultural practice.

topic_name: Constitutional reforms and Government of India Acts
short_explanation: Item 1, administration of justice, was reserved. Item 2, local self-government, was transferred to Indian ministers. Item 3, land revenue, was reserved. Item 4, police, was reserved. So 1, 3 and 4.
explanation_text: Under dyarchy in the Government of India Act 1919, reserved subjects stayed with the Governor and his executive council: law and order, police, justice, land revenue, irrigation and finance. Transferred subjects went to ministers responsible to the legislature: local self-government, education, public health, agriculture and similar 'nation-building' departments.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 2, which was a transferred subject, and omits item 4, which was also reserved.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 2, which was a transferred subject, and omits item 1, which was also reserved.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 2, which was a transferred subject, and omits item 3, which was also reserved.

common_traps: Local self-government sounds like an administrative subject, but it was the showpiece transferred subject.

short_explanation: The fanam was a small gold or silver coin used widely in South India, including the Vijayanagara empire, where it was a fraction of the gold pagoda (varaha).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Not a term for clothing; the fanam was a unit of money.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Not an ornament, though made of precious metal; it was a coin.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Not a weapon; it was a coin.

short_explanation: Name 1, Barindra Kumar Ghosh, led the Anushilan-Jugantar group in Bengal and was tried in the Alipore bomb case, not a Ghadar leader. Name 2, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee, belonged to the Anushilan Samiti and later the Hindustan Republican Association. Name 3, Rash Behari Bose, was actively involved in the Ghadar plan for an armed uprising in February 1915. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes names 1 and 2, who were not Ghadar figures, and omits name 3, who was the Ghadar associate.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes name 2, who was not a Ghadar figure, and omits name 3, who was the Ghadar associate.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes name 1, who was not a Ghadar figure.

common_traps: All three were Bengal revolutionaries, so candidates add Ghosh or Chatterjee; only Rash Behari Bose worked directly with the Ghadarites.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: under the Cripps proposals the provincial members of the Constituent Assembly were to be elected by the provincial assemblies by proportional representation; only the princely states' members were to be nominated. Statement 2 is correct: any province unwilling to accept the new constitution could stay out and make a separate agreement with Britain. So 2 only.
explanation_text: The Cripps Mission (March 1942) offered dominion status after the war, a constitution-making body elected by provincial assemblies with nominees of the princes, and a right for any province to stay out. The Congress rejected it partly because this opt-out opened a door to partition.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2, which is also correct.

common_traps: The word 'nominated' in statement 1 is the catch: provincial members were elected, princely states' members were nominated.
