common_traps: Picking the climate-change option because the passage opens with it; the opening is context, and the argument is about genetic uniformity.

short_explanation: Assumption I is valid: the passage warns that climate change may 'make some plant infections more common in all climatic zones', so diseases can appear where they were not common before. Assumption II is valid: the passage says selective breeding has bred out 'genetic variations that are not immediately useful', which is 'bad for coping with changes', so it rests on the value of the genetic diversity kept in wild relatives. So both.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits assumption II, which is also valid.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Omits assumption I, which is also valid.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Assumption I is valid, so 'neither' is wrong.

common_traps: Rejecting II because the passage never says 'wild relatives'; the loss of bred-out genetic variation is exactly what wild relatives preserve.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. The passage does not mention wild relatives by name; assumption II is read as the remedy implied by its point that genetic variation 'has been bred out' of high-value crops.

short_explanation: The International North-South Transport Corridor is a ship, rail and road route of about 7,200 km linking Mumbai to Iran's ports, then overland through Iran and the Caspian region to Russia, Central Asia and on to Europe. So it connects India to Central Asia and Europe via Iran.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The corridor runs through Iran, not China; India is not part of China-led overland routes.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: That describes eastern links such as the Kaladan project or the India-Myanmar-Thailand highway.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Azerbaijan lies on one branch of the route, but the core transit country is Iran.

common_traps: Picking Azerbaijan because it lies on the western branch; the corridor's defining transit country is Iran.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: the United States is the world's largest ethanol producer, well ahead of Brazil. Statement II is correct: US ethanol is made mainly from corn (maize), while Brazil's is made mainly from sugarcane. So I is not correct but II is.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect; the United States produces more ethanol than Brazil.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, the reverse of this option.

common_traps: Brazil's fame for sugarcane ethanol and flex-fuel cars makes candidates assume it is the bigger producer.

short_explanation: The author says the statesman must 'pray never to be left without opponents; for they keep him on the path of reason and good sense', and that national unity depends on 'a sufficiently even balance of political power'. So the opposition is indispensable for balance of power and good governance, as option D says.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Contradicts the passage: without opponents the statesman's supporters 'will push him to disaster'.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Contradicts the passage, which wants the balance of power to make it impracticable for opposition 'to be revolutionary and irreconcilable'.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The opposition's role is to show the rulers 'where the dangers are', not to provide support for their survival.

common_traps: Reading 'learns more from his opponents' as meaning rulers depend on the opposition's support (option C); the passage is about checks, not support.

short_explanation: Assumption I is not valid: the passage says a statesman should 'pray never to be left without opponents; for they keep him on the path of reason', so opposition is always needed, not only when the leader is indifferent. Assumption II is not valid: the passage wants an 'even balance of political power' so that opposition is not 'revolutionary and irreconcilable', which rules out 'the more aggressive the better'. So neither.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption I, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption II, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption I, which is not valid.

common_traps: Missing the restrictive 'only if' in assumption I.
Reading praise for opponents as praise for aggressive opposition; the passage asks for balance.

short_explanation: Statement I is accepted: the same warming that pushes wet-bulb readings past 35 °C also intensifies floods, cyclones and droughts, to which peninsular India is exposed. Statement II is correct: at a wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C sweat can no longer evaporate to cool the body, so humans and animals cannot shed heat and survival is threatened. So both.
explanation_text: Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity: it is the lowest temperature to which air can be cooled by evaporating water into it. Around 35 °C it matches skin temperature, so perspiration stops cooling the body, and even a healthy person resting in shade faces fatal heat stress within hours. The World Bank's 2022 report on India's cooling sector warned that India could be among the first places to cross this threshold routinely.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement II, which states the direct physiological meaning of a 35 °C wet-bulb temperature.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The key treats the wider climate risks in statement I as part of the implication as well.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is plainly correct.

common_traps: Reading wet-bulb temperature as ordinary air temperature; it is the humidity-adjusted measure that decides whether sweating can cool the body.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Statement II is the direct implication of a 35 °C wet-bulb temperature; Statement I is a broader climate-risk claim that the report does not tie to wet-bulb heat, and a strict reading would give option b. The key treats both as implications of the warming the report describes.

short_explanation: P, Q and R are siblings, S is their mother and T their father. Definitely true: I (S and T are a couple), III (T is Q's father), IV (S is P's mother) and VI (P, a brother, is S's son); II and V fail because Q's and R's genders are not given. So only four.
explanation_text: P is the brother of Q and R, so the three are siblings and P is male. S is R's mother, so S is mother of all three; T is P's father, so T is father of all three. That makes S and T a couple (I true), T the father of Q (III true), S the mother of P (IV true) and P the son of S (VI true). Statement II calls Q a son and statement V calls R a daughter, but the question never gives Q's or R's gender, so neither is definite.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Four statements are definitely true, not two.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Four statements are definitely true: I, III, IV and VI.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Only four; II and V depend on Q's and R's genders, which are not given.

solution_steps: P is the brother of Q and R, so the three are siblings and P is male.
S is the mother and T the father of all three siblings.
True for certain: I, III, IV, VI.
Not certain: II (Q's gender unknown) and V (R's gender unknown). So four.
common_traps: Assuming Q is male and R female from the names; neither gender is stated.
key_note: Accepted on the usual reading that P, Q and R are full siblings sharing both parents.

short_explanation: Gross primary deficit is the gross fiscal deficit minus interest payments: 50,000 − 1,500 = ₹48,500 crores. Non-debt capital receipts are already counted inside the fiscal deficit, so they are not used again.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: ₹51,500 crores comes from adding the interest to the fiscal deficit instead of subtracting it.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: ₹58,500 crores comes from adding the ₹10,000 crores of non-debt capital receipts back and then subtracting interest.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

solution_steps: Gross fiscal deficit is given as ₹50,000 crores; non-debt capital receipts have already been netted off in arriving at it.
Gross primary deficit = gross fiscal deficit − interest payments.
formula_used: Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit − Interest payments
common_traps: Using the ₹10,000 crores of non-debt capital receipts a second time; it is a distractor figure.

short_explanation: Each code is the product of the letters' alphabet positions: N = 14, O = 15, T = 20, E = 5, S = 19. NOTES = 21000 × 19 = 399000.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 420000 multiplies by 20 (the value of T) instead of 19 for S.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 440000; the working gives 21000 × 19 = 399000.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 630000; the working gives 21000 × 19 = 399000.

solution_steps: S is the 19th letter, so NOTES = 21000 × 19 = 399000.
formula_used: Code = product of alphabet positions
common_traps: Miscounting S as the 20th letter.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: the Commission recommended ₹4,800 crore from 2022–23 to 2025–26 as incentive grants for improving educational outcomes. Statement II is incorrect: the vertical share of States is 41% of the divisible pool, not 45%. Statement III is correct: it proposed ₹45,000 crore as performance incentives for States carrying out agricultural reforms. Statement IV is correct: it reintroduced tax effort (2.5% weight) in the devolution formula. So I, III and IV.
explanation_text: The Fourteenth Finance Commission had set the States' share at 42%. The Fifteenth cut it to 41% for 2021–26, the one point reflecting the reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir into Union Territories. Its horizontal formula gave weight to income distance, population (2011), area, forest and ecology, demographic performance and tax effort.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II; the share is 41%, not 45%.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II (the share is 41%) and omits statement III, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II and omits statement I, which is correct.

common_traps: Confusing 41% (Fifteenth) with 42% (Fourteenth); 45% belongs to neither.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: the IBRD lends to and guarantees for middle-income and creditworthy lower-income countries. Statement II is incorrect: it works as one arm of the World Bank Group alongside IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID, and with other partners, not single-handedly. Statement III is correct: it was set up in 1944 at Bretton Woods, and its first loans went to rebuilding post-war Europe (France, 1947). So I and III.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II; the IBRD works within the World Bank Group, not alone.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II and omits statement I, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Words like 'single-handedly' turn a broadly true mission statement into a false one.

short_explanation: From FRANCE = 654321, E = 1 and N = 3; from GERMANY = 9158437, M = 8 and Y = 7. So YEMEN = 7, 1, 8, 1, 3 = 71813.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 54321 is part of FRANCE's code, not YEMEN's.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 81913 codes Y as 8 and M as 9; Y is 7 and M is 8.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 71913 codes M as 9 (G's digit); M is 8.

solution_steps: GERMANY = 9158437: G 9, E 1, R 5, M 8, A 4, N 3, Y 7 (consistent with FRANCE).
YEMEN: Y 7, E 1, M 8, E 1, N 3, giving 71813.
common_traps: Reading off the digit of the neighbouring letter in GERMANY.

short_explanation: P = 3T with T not 0 gives T, P as 1, 3; 2, 6; or 3, 9. R, Q, S are R, R + 3, R + 7, so R is 0, 1 or 2. Keeping all digits different leaves 4 numbers: 35291, 63072, 64182, 94183.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Misses one; the four valid numbers are 35291, 63072, 64182 and 94183.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Overcounts; every other combination repeats a digit (for example T = 1, R = 0 makes P and Q both 3).

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Overcounts; only 4 of the 9 combinations of T and R keep all five digits different.

solution_steps: T is 1, 2 or 3, so P is 3, 6 or 9.
Q = R + 3 and S = Q + 4 = R + 7 ≤ 9, so R is 0, 1 or 2, with Q, S = 3, 7; 4, 8; 5, 9.
T = 1, P = 3: R = 2 gives 35291 (R = 0 and R = 1 repeat 3 or 1).
T = 2, P = 6: R = 0 gives 63072, R = 1 gives 64182 (R = 2 repeats 2).
T = 3, P = 9: R = 1 gives 94183 (R = 0 repeats 3, R = 2 repeats 9). Total 4.
common_traps: Forgetting to check that T and P do not repeat one of Q, R, S, which gives 9 instead of 4.
tag_note: Topic should be Digit puzzles and counting. The item counts numbers meeting digit conditions; no LCM, HCF or divisibility is involved.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: RTGS settles each transaction individually in real time, while NEFT settles in half-hourly batches. Statement II is incorrect: the RBI has made inward transactions free for customers in both RTGS and NEFT. Statement III is incorrect: both systems have run round the clock, all 365 days, since December 2020 for RTGS and December 2019 for NEFT. So I only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II; no charge is levied on inward RTGS or NEFT transactions.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement III; RTGS has operated 24x7 since December 2020.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is incorrect and statement I is correct.

common_traps: Remembering the old RTGS timings; both systems have been available 24x7 since 2019–2020.

short_explanation: UPI can be used for merchant payments abroad through NPCI International partnerships. The UAE accepts it, France accepts it (starting with the Eiffel Tower in 2024) and Singapore accepts it. Germany does not, and UPI merchant acceptance had not been launched in Bangladesh. So only three.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The UAE, France and Singapore all accept UPI merchant payments, so three.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Only three; Germany and Bangladesh are not among the accepting countries.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Germany and Bangladesh do not accept UPI merchant payments.

common_traps: Confusing cross-border UPI remittance links (such as with Singapore's PayNow) with merchant acceptance, or assuming Bangladesh is covered because Sri Lanka and Mauritius were launched in 2024.
key_note: Country coverage of UPI changes often; the key's count of three (UAE, France, Singapore) is accepted, with Bangladesh's status not independently verified.

short_explanation: X takes 18 days, Y 24 days and Z 16 days for the whole job. Taking the work as 144 units, their daily rates are 8, 6 and 9. Y's 8⅔ days do 52 units, so 23n = 92 and n = 4.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 3; the working gives 23n = 144 − 52 = 92, so n = 4.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 5; the working gives 23n = 92, so n = 4.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 6; the working gives 23n = 92, so n = 4.

solution_steps: X: one-third in 6 days, whole in 18. Y: whole in 24. Z: three-fourths in 12, whole in 16.
Work = LCM(18, 24, 16) = 144 units; rates 8, 6 and 9 a day; together 23.
Y alone for 26/3 days: 6 × 26/3 = 52 units.
formula_used: Rate = Work ÷ Time
common_traps: Reading 'three-fourth of the work in 12 days' as Z needing 9 days (12 × 3/4) instead of 16 days (12 × 4/3).

short_explanation: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, launched in February 2024 under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, subsidises rooftop solar with up to 300 units of free power a month. Statement I is correct: it targets one crore households. Statement II is correct: the Ministry runs training on installation, operation, maintenance and repair at grassroots level. Statement III is correct: its capacity-building component aims to create over three lakh skilled workers. So all three.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement III; the capacity-building target is over three lakh skilled workers.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement II; grassroots training is part of the scheme.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement I; the scheme targets one crore rooftop installations.

key_note: Statement I says 'panels' where the scheme's target is one crore households; read loosely, it is correct.

topic_name: Number series — arithmetic and difference patterns
short_explanation: The gaps are the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. So X = 18 + 11 = 29, and 29 + 13 = 42 confirms it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 26; 26 + 16 would be needed to reach 42.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 27 comes from reading the gaps as 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 (odd numbers); then 42 − 27 = 15 does not continue it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 30; the prime gap after 7 is 11, giving 29.

solution_steps: These are consecutive primes; the next are 11 and 13.
common_traps: Taking the gaps as odd numbers after 2 and adding 9, which fails the check against 42.

short_explanation: The passage says demand-side behaviour change can give at best half the cut, and 'even that would require companies and governments to provide more incentives to change' by making 'low-carbon options cheaper and more widely available'. So low-carbon behaviour must be brought about through incentives, as option B says.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Contradicts the passage: at best half the reduction can come from households, and the word 'only' is not supported.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Reverses the logic: the passage wants supply-side investment to make low-carbon options cheaper, not low-carbon technology to make all goods cheaper.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Too specific: the passage speaks of incentives from companies and governments in general, not subsidies for manufacturing industries.

common_traps: Option A borrows the passage's opening words about household emissions but adds 'only', which the passage denies.

short_explanation: Gandhi turned the colonial charge of sedition into a badge of honour. The key places his remark 'sedition has become my religion' at the launch of the Quit India Movement in 1942, when he called for open defiance and the slogan 'Do or Die'.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Champaran (1917) was a limited agitation against indigo planters, not a call to defy the state as such.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: At Dandi Gandhi broke the salt law; the key does not link this remark to the Salt March.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: At the Second Round Table Conference Gandhi was negotiating, not proclaiming sedition.

common_traps: Linking it to Gandhi's 1922 sedition trial, where he spoke of Section 124A as 'the prince among the political sections'.
key_note: Accepted on the official key. The quotation's exact occasion is not settled in standard texts; some sources connect similar remarks with the Salt Satyagraha of 1930 (option b), which is set aside in favour of the key.

short_explanation: The 'Dancing Girl' of Mohenjo-daro is a small bronze figurine, about 10.5 cm tall, cast by the lost-wax technique and showing a girl wearing many bangles on one arm.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Carnelian was used for Harappan beads, not this figurine.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Many Harappan figurines are terracotta, but the Dancing Girl is metal.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No such gold figure exists; the figure is bronze.

common_traps: Confusing it with the terracotta mother-goddess figurines or the steatite 'priest-king'.

short_explanation: Assumption I is valid: the passage says behaviour change would 'require companies and governments to provide more incentives to change through supply-side investments to make low-carbon options cheaper and more widely available'. Assumption II is not valid: the passage says that incentives are needed to reach the scale of cuts required, not that people are incapable of low-carbon behaviour on their own. So I only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption II, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption II, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Assumption I is valid, so 'neither' is wrong.

common_traps: Reading 'would require companies and governments' as 'people are not capable without them'; the passage is about the scale of the cuts, not about people's ability.
key_note: Assumption II sits close to the passage's 'even that would require companies and governments to provide more incentives'; the key rejects it because it turns a point about achieving the needed cuts into an absolute claim about people's capability.

short_explanation: After the Chauri Chaura violence of February 1922, many peasants were sentenced to death. Madan Mohan Malaviya argued their appeal in the Allahabad High Court, assisted by Krishna Kant Malaviya, and saved most of them from the gallows.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: C. R. Das was a leading lawyer, but he did not conduct the Chauri Chaura defence.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Kitchlew is linked with the Punjab agitation of 1919, not this trial.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Jinnah had no role in the Chauri Chaura defence.

short_explanation: The passage notes raw-material use has 'nearly quadrupled', less than 9% is reused, supply chains are risky, and concludes 'Reusing materials makes sense', with batteries sent back to factories for recovery. The balanced message is that a circular economy benefits sustainable growth, as option C says.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Overreaches with 'not possible without'; the passage says reuse 'makes sense', not that a green economy is impossible otherwise.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Overreaches with 'every sector' and 'immediately'; the passage speaks mainly of batteries and gives no timeline.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Overreaches with 'the only option' and 'survival'; the passage speaks of costs and risks, not the survival of industries.

common_traps: For 'most logical, rational and pragmatic' questions, extreme words such as 'only', 'every', 'immediately' and 'not possible' usually signal an overreach.

short_explanation: Assumption I is not valid: the passage says old batteries 'should go back to a factory where their ingredients can be recovered', a proposal, and does not describe automobile factories as already circular. Assumption II is valid: against consumption that 'has nearly quadrupled' with 'less than 9%' reused, the passage says 'reusing materials makes sense', so it rests on growth and circular use of minerals going together. So II only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption I, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes assumption I, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Assumption II is valid, so 'neither' is wrong.

common_traps: Taking the passage's 'should go back to a factory' as a description of what automobile factories already do.

short_explanation: After the Poona Pact of September 1932 settled the Depressed Classes' representation, Gandhi made removal of untouchability a central programme: he founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh and the weekly Harijan, and toured the country in 1933–34 for Harijan upliftment.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) dealt with civil disobedience and the Round Table Conference.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: By 1942 the Harijan programme was already a decade old.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The 1935 Act came after Gandhi's Harijan campaign had begun.

short_explanation: Papaya, pineapple and guava are all New World fruits that the Portuguese brought to India in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, alongside crops such as chilli, tobacco, maize and cashew. So all three.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: All three are American fruits brought by the Portuguese.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: All three, not two.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: All three reached India through the Portuguese.

common_traps: Assuming guava is native because it is now so common in India.

short_explanation: Per pipe, set X fills 0.25% a minute, set Y fills 0.625% and set Z empties 0.15625%. With 10 X pipes, 5 Y pipes and all 16 Z pipes the net fill is 2.5 + 3.125 − 2.5 = 3.125% a minute, so 50% takes 16 minutes.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 8 minutes comes from keeping all 10 pipes of set Y open: 2.5 + 6.25 − 2.5 = 6.25% a minute; only 5 of them are open.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 10; the working gives 50 ÷ 3.125 = 16 minutes.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 12; the working gives 50 ÷ 3.125 = 16 minutes.

solution_steps: Set X: 70% in 14 minutes = 5% a minute for 20 pipes, 0.25% per pipe.
Set Y: 37.5% in 6 minutes = 6.25% a minute for 10 pipes, 0.625% per pipe.
Set Z: 50% in 20 minutes = 2.5% a minute for 16 pipes (emptying).
Time for 50% = 50 ÷ 3.125 = 16 minutes.
formula_used: Net rate = filling rates − emptying rate
common_traps: Halving set Z as well; all 16 emptying pipes stay open.
tag_note: Topic should be Pipes and cisterns. The item is a filling-and-emptying rate problem, not a percentage change.

short_explanation: The United Kingdom has more than four time zones once its overseas territories are counted. Denmark has five, with Greenland and the Faroe Islands. New Zealand has five, with the Chatham Islands and its realm territories. Australia has more than four, including its external territories. Brazil has exactly four, which is not 'more than four'. So only four.
explanation_text: Countries with far-flung territories accumulate time zones. France leads the world, and the UK, the US and Russia follow. Brazil's four zones cover its mainland and Atlantic islands such as Fernando de Noronha, and it has no distant territories to add more.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Brazil has exactly four time zones, not more than four.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Four countries, not three; all but Brazil exceed four.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Only Brazil fails the test, so four qualify.

common_traps: Counting only the mainland zones: the UK, Denmark and New Zealand look like single-zone countries until overseas territories are included.
'More than four' excludes a country with exactly four.

short_explanation: For n = 1, 1 + 2 = 3 leaves remainder 3. For n of 2 or more, 2ⁿ is a multiple of 4, so 1 + 2ⁿ leaves remainder 1. Only two remainders occur: 3 and 1.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A remainder always exists; 3 and 1 both occur.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: n = 1 gives 3 while every larger n gives 1, so there are two remainders, not one.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No third remainder occurs; from n = 2 on the remainder is always 1.

solution_steps: n = 1: 1 + 2 = 3, remainder 3.
n ≥ 2: 2ⁿ = 4 × 2ⁿ⁻², so 1 + 2ⁿ leaves remainder 1.
Distinct remainders: 3 and 1, which is two.
common_traps: Forgetting the case n = 1, which gives the second remainder.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: Anadyr and Nome lie on either side of the International Date Line, so at breakfast time in each town the two are on different calendar days. Statement II is incorrect: Anadyr, west of the Date Line, is ahead, so when it is Monday in Anadyr it is Sunday in Nome.
explanation_text: Anadyr keeps UTC+12 and Nome UTC−9 (UTC−8 in summer), about 20 to 21 hours apart. Crossing the Date Line from Asia to America takes a traveller back one day. So the Siberian town is almost a full day ahead of its Alaskan neighbour.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II reverses the direction; Nome is behind, so it is Sunday there.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is correct.

common_traps: Thinking the eastern town is ahead, as it is for places not separated by the Date Line.
key_note: The two towns are several hundred kilometres apart rather than 'a few kilometers'; the loose distance does not affect the point of Statement I.

short_explanation: QQQ = Q × 111 = Q × 3 × 37, and 481 = 13 × 37. Q is a single digit, so it can never supply the 13; the HCF is always 37.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The factor 37 is always shared, so the HCF is never 1.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 13 divides 481 but not 111, and a single digit Q cannot be 13.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 481 would have to divide QQQ, which needs a factor 13 that QQQ never has.

solution_steps: Common factor: 37 (Q from 1 to 9 has no factor 13). HCF = 37.
formula_used: QQQ = 111 × Q
common_traps: Assuming a repeated-digit number shares nothing with 481 and choosing 1.

short_explanation: The Self-Respect Movement was founded by 'Periyar' E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker in 1925 in the Madras Presidency to fight caste hierarchy and Brahmin dominance and to promote rationalism.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha and founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, not this movement.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Bhaskarrao Jadhav was a leader of the non-Brahmin movement in Maharashtra.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Dinkarrao Javalkar was a non-Brahmin writer in Maharashtra.

short_explanation: Numbers 1 to 9 use 9 digits and 10 to 99 use 180, a total of 189. The remaining 300 digits cover exactly 100 three-digit numbers, 100 to 199, so the 489th digit is the last digit of 199, which is 9.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 0 is the 491st digit (the second digit of 200); the 489th is the last digit of 199.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 3; the working ends exactly on 199.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 6; the working ends exactly on 199.

solution_steps: Digits from 1 to 9: 9.
Digits from 10 to 99: 90 × 2 = 180. Running total 189.
Digits still needed: 489 − 189 = 300 = 100 three-digit numbers.
The 100th three-digit number is 199; its last digit, 9, is the 489th digit.
formula_used: Digits used = count of numbers × digits in each
common_traps: Taking the 100th three-digit number as 200 instead of 199.

short_explanation: Whichever of P, Q or R is the thief, some of the six statements turn out false, and the question never says who is truthful, so none of the three cases can be ruled out.
explanation_text: Test each suspect in turn. If P stole it, both of P's statements are false and all of Q's and R's are true. If Q stole it, P's statements are true, Q's 'I did not steal' is false and R's statement is true. If R stole it, R's 'I did not steal', P's 'Q stole it' and Q's 'R did not steal' are all false. Each case is possible because the question gives no rule about who tells the truth, so the thief cannot be identified.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: P fits only if we add an unstated rule that the thief lies and the innocent tell the truth; the question gives no such rule.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: If R stole it, three statements are false, but nothing given rules this case in or out.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: If Q stole it, Q's 'I did not steal' is false, but nothing given rules this case in or out.

solution_steps: Only one person is guilty, so test P, Q and R one at a time.
If P is guilty, P's two statements are false; if Q is guilty, Q's second statement is false; if R is guilty, one statement from each person is false.
Every case leaves some statement false, and the question does not say how many people are lying or who is truthful.
No case can be eliminated, so the thief cannot be concluded.
common_traps: Assuming the thief lies and the innocent tell the truth, a rule the question never states. Under that rule only P fits.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Another reading set aside: option A (P), which follows only if one assumes the guilty person lies throughout and the two innocent people tell the truth; the question states no truth-telling condition.
tag_note: Topic should be Truth-teller and liar logic puzzle. The item tests whether suspects' statements can be consistent, not matching categories to attributes.

short_explanation: Row I is correct: Botswana is among the world's largest diamond producers. Row II is correct: Chile holds one of the largest lithium reserves, in the Atacama salt flats. Row III is correct: Indonesia is the world's largest nickel producer. So all three.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: All three rows are correct.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: All three rows are correct, not two.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Each country is rich in the resource named.

topic_name: World political geography and regions in news
short_explanation: Row I is incorrect: Mallorca is a Spanish island in the Balearics. Row II is incorrect: Normandy is a region of France. Row III is incorrect: Sardinia is an Italian island. So none; the countries have been rotated.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: No row is correct; each region belongs to a different country from the one given.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: No row is correct.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: All three rows are wrong.

common_traps: Sardinia and Corsica sit side by side; Corsica is French, Sardinia Italian.

topic_name: Cost price, selling price and margin
short_explanation: Statement I is correct: the only results that fit are P drew 0–0 with Q, P beat R 1–0 and Q drew 1–1 with R. Statement II is correct: in that last match R scored 1 goal against Q. So both.
explanation_text: P has 3 points (a win and a draw), R has 1 (a draw and a loss), and each team scored exactly one goal. P's win must be 1–0, using P's only goal, so P's draw is 0–0. If P beat Q 1–0 and drew R 0–0, then R's loss is to Q, and R never scores, which breaks the rule that each team scored once. So P beat R 1–0 and drew Q 0–0. Q and R still need one goal each, so their match is a 1–1 draw. That gives P 3 points, Q 2 (two draws) and R 1, exactly as stated.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement II; R's one goal came in the 1–1 draw with Q.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement I; P and Q drew 0–0.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

solution_steps: Points: P has a win and a draw, R a draw and a loss.
P's win must be 1–0 because P scored only once, so P's draw is 0–0.
If P beat Q, then P drew R 0–0 and R lost to Q, so R never scores: impossible.
So P beat R 1–0 and drew Q 0–0, and Q and R drew 1–1.
R's one goal came against Q, and P–Q was 0–0: both statements hold.
common_traps: Assuming Q's 2 points come from a win and a loss; with each team scoring once, Q's 2 points are two draws.
tag_note: Topic should be Logical puzzles (tournament and points tables). The item has nothing to do with cost price or selling price.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: rare earth elements such as europium, terbium and yttrium go into the phosphors of flat-panel screens and monitors. Statement II is treated as not correct: the glow in screens comes from rare-earth-activated phosphor compounds, which fluoresce; the elements themselves are not phosphorescent. So I is correct but II is not.
explanation_text: Phosphorescence is a slow afterglow that continues after the exciting light is removed; fluorescence stops almost at once. Display phosphors must respond instantly, so they are fluorescent. Rare earth ions such as europium (red) and terbium (green) are added as activators to host crystals, and it is these compounds that emit light.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The key treats Statement II as incorrect, so it cannot explain Statement I.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The key treats Statement II as incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is correct; rare earths are used in flat screens.

common_traps: Confusing fluorescence (instant emission, used in displays) with phosphorescence (delayed afterglow).
key_note: Accepted on the official key with doubt. On a loose reading Statement II is true, because rare-earth-doped materials such as europium-doped strontium aluminate are phosphorescent, and that would give option a. The key is defended on the strict reading that the elements themselves are not phosphorescent and that screens use fluorescence.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: the National Rail Plan aims at a 'future ready' railway by 2030, not 2028. Statement II is incorrect: Kavach was developed indigenously by the RDSO with Indian industry, not with Germany. Statement III is correct: Kavach uses RFID tags fixed on the track in station sections to tell the locomotive its exact location. So I and II are not correct.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is correct, so it is not among the 'not correct' ones; statement I is.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is correct; statement II is the other incorrect one.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is correct.

common_traps: The question asks which statements are NOT correct; picking the correct statements reverses the answer.

short_explanation: Axiom-4 supports microgravity research: in 2025 it carried India's Shubhanshu Shukla to the ISS to run microgravity experiments. Gaganyaan supports it: the human spaceflight programme includes microgravity experiments on its missions. SpaDeX does not in the key's reading: it is a docking demonstration of two small satellites. So only two.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Both Axiom-4 and Gaganyaan support microgravity research.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: SpaDeX is a docking technology demonstration, not a microgravity research mission.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Axiom-4 and Gaganyaan both support microgravity research.

common_traps: Counting SpaDeX because its rocket stage (POEM) carried some experiments; the mission's purpose was docking.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. The PSLV stage that launched SpaDeX carried experimental payloads, so a loose reading could count three (option c); the key follows the mission's stated docking purpose.

short_explanation: Pair I is correct: the Dornier-228 is used by the Navy and Coast Guard for maritime patrol. Pair II is incorrect: the IL-76 is a heavy transport aircraft, not a supersonic combat aircraft. Pair III is correct: the C-17 Globemaster III is a strategic military transport aircraft. So only two.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Pairs I and III are both correct.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Pair II is wrong; the IL-76 is a transport aircraft.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Pairs I and III are correctly matched.

short_explanation: Cloud seeding, tried in places such as Delhi to wash pollutants out of the air, disperses silver iodide and potassium iodide (and sometimes dry ice or salt) into clouds. They give water droplets nuclei around which to form ice crystals or grow into raindrops.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Silver nitrate is not a seeding agent.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Potassium nitrate is not a seeding agent.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Neither silver nitrate nor potassium chloride is the standard pair.

topic_name: The President and the Union Executive
short_explanation: Statement I is correct: the Supreme Court (Maru Ram, Epuru Sudhakar) holds that a pardon under Article 72 can be reviewed on limited grounds such as mala fides, arbitrariness or irrelevant considerations. Statement II is incorrect: the President exercises this power on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers. So I only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is incorrect; the President acts on ministerial advice.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is correct; limited judicial review applies.

topic_name: Presiding officers, privileges and office of profit
short_explanation: Statement I is correct: under Article 94 the Speaker stays in office after dissolution until just before the first meeting of the new House. Statement II is incorrect: the Constitution does not require the Speaker to resign from the party. Statement III is correct: Article 94(c) allows removal by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, after at least 14 days' notice. So I and III.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II; resigning from the party is a convention in some countries, not a constitutional rule in India.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II and omits statement I, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II, which is incorrect.

common_traps: Carrying over the British convention that the Speaker gives up party ties; the Indian Constitution has no such rule.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: under paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule, questions of disqualification for defection are decided by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, whose decision is final. The President decides only disqualifications under Article 102(1), on the Election Commission's opinion. Statement II is incorrect: the Tenth Schedule uses the term 'political party' repeatedly. So neither.
explanation_text: Two disqualification routes exist. Under Article 102(1), for grounds such as holding an office of profit, the President decides on the opinion of the Election Commission (Article 103). Under Article 102(2) and the Tenth Schedule, for defection, the Speaker or Chairman decides (paragraph 6), subject to judicial review since Kihoto Hollohan (1992). The Council of Ministers plays no part in either. The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment in 1985, defines and uses 'political party'.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect; the Speaker decides defection cases, and the Council of Ministers has no role.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is incorrect; the Tenth Schedule uses the term 'political party'.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are incorrect.

common_traps: Mixing up the Article 103 route (President on the Election Commission's opinion) with the Tenth Schedule route (Speaker).
key_note: The keyed option a needs Statement I to be correct, but paragraph 6 of the Tenth Schedule gives the decision to the Speaker, not to the President on the Council of Ministers' opinion. Statement II is also false because the Tenth Schedule uses 'political party'. Option d is proposed; the input key may be mis-mapped from another booklet series.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: under Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, State Governments make the rules for granting concessions for minor minerals. Statement II is correct: Section 3(e) lets the Central Government notify any mineral as a minor mineral. So I is not correct but II is.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect; States do make rules for minor minerals.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The reverse holds: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

common_traps: Assuming the Centre controls all mineral concessions; minor minerals (sand, stone, gravel and the like) are regulated by the States.

short_explanation: The Nature Restoration Law is a European Union regulation, adopted in 2024, which requires member states to put restoration measures in place on at least 20% of the EU's degraded land and sea areas by 2030 and on all ecosystems in need by 2050.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The World Bank finances projects but does not enact laws.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The OECD issues guidelines, not binding laws.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The FAO does not legislate for member countries.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: Article 243B lets States with a population not above 20 lakh skip the intermediate level. Statement II is incorrect: the minimum age for Panchayat membership is 21 years (Article 243F). Statement III is incorrect: the State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor under Article 243-I, not the Chief Minister. So all three are not correct.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is also incorrect; the Governor, not the Chief Minister, sets up the Finance Commission.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is also incorrect; small States need not have an intermediate tier.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is also incorrect; the age limit is 21, not 30.

common_traps: The question asks which are NOT correct; candidates who hunt for correct statements find none and panic.
Mixing up 21 (Panchayat membership) with 25 or 30 (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha).

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: BIMSTEC has seven members (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand). Statement II is incorrect: it was founded by the Bangkok Declaration of 1997. Statement III is incorrect: the founders were Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka and Thailand; Nepal joined in 2004. Statement IV is incorrect: in the 2022 reorganisation India leads the security sector, and tourism falls under the people-to-people pillar led by Nepal. So I only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II; the founding document is the Bangkok Declaration of 1997.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements II and III are incorrect, and statement I is omitted.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement IV; India leads security, not tourism.

common_traps: Confusing BIMSTEC's Bangkok Declaration (1997) with SAARC's Dhaka roots.
Assuming Nepal is a founder because it is now a member.

short_explanation: The Gandhi Peace Prize jury is chaired by the Prime Minister and includes the Chief Justice of India and the Leader of the single largest Opposition party in the Lok Sabha, along with eminent persons. The President is not a member. So II, III and IV.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits the Chief Justice of India, who is on the jury.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes the President, who is not on the jury, and omits the Leader of Opposition.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes the President and omits the Prime Minister, who chairs the jury.

common_traps: Assuming the President heads the jury because the President presents many national awards.

short_explanation: GAGAN, built by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India, corrects GPS signals using ground reference stations and geostationary satellites. Statement I is correct: it adds accuracy and integrity. Statement II is correct: it enables more uniform, high-quality air traffic management. Statement III is incorrect: its signals also serve rail, road, shipping, agriculture and survey users. So I and II only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement III; GAGAN benefits other modes of transport too.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement III and omits statement I.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement II; better air traffic management is a stated aim.

common_traps: 'Only in aviation' is the kind of restricting word that makes a statement false.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: the AI Action Summit in Paris in February 2025 was co-chaired by France and India and followed the Bletchley Park (2023) and Seoul (2024) summits. Statement II is incorrect: the United States and the United Kingdom declined to sign the declaration on inclusive and sustainable AI. So I only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is incorrect; the US and UK did not sign.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is correct.

short_explanation: The UN General Assembly designates International Years to draw attention to a theme. Pair I is correct: 2026 is the International Year of the Woman Farmer. Pair II is correct: 2027 is the International Year of Sustainable and Resilient Tourism. Pair III is correct: 2025 is the International Year of Peace and Trust. Pair IV is correct: 2029 is the International Year of Asteroid Awareness and Planetary Defence. So all four.

option_rationales.rationale: All four pairs are correctly matched.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: All four pairs are correctly matched, not two.

option_rationales.rationale: All four pairs are correctly matched, not three.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: Russia chaired BRICS in 2024 and hosted the 16th Summit in Kazan in October. Statement II is correct: Indonesia became a full member in January 2025. Statement III is incorrect: the theme was 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security', not 'Multiculturalism'. So I and II.

option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement III and omits statement I.

option_rationales.label: C

option_rationales.label: D

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 covers public servants in and outside India. Statement II is incorrect: the Chairperson may be a former Chief Justice, a former Supreme Court judge or an eminent person, not necessarily a Chief Justice, and never a sitting one. Statement III is correct: the minimum age is 45 years on assuming office. Statement IV is incorrect: the Lokpal can inquire into a Prime Minister, subject to safeguards such as a full-bench decision and exclusion of certain subjects. So III only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement II; the Chairperson need not be a Chief Justice.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements I and IV are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is correct.

short_explanation: The first Kho Kho World Cup was held at New Delhi's Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in January 2025, and India won both titles, beating Nepal in each final. Statement I is correct. Statements II and III are incorrect because the scores are swapped: the men won 54–36 and the women 78–40. So I only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statements II and III swap the men's and women's final scores.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement III is incorrect; 54–36 was the men's final score.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statements II and III are incorrect.

common_traps: Checking only the winners and not the scores; the statements swap the two finals.
key_note: Final scores taken as men 54–36 and women 78–40; the scores are recalled rather than verified from the scorecards, but the key requires only that statements II and III be wrong.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: Gukesh became the youngest world champion by beating China's Ding Liren in the World Chess Championship in Singapore in December 2024; the 45th Chess Olympiad in Budapest was a team event, which India won. Statement II is correct: Abhimanyu Mishra of the United States became the youngest-ever Grandmaster in 2021, aged 12 years and 4 months. So II only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is incorrect; Gukesh's title came in the World Championship against Ding Liren.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement I, which is incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is correct.

common_traps: Mixing up the Olympiad (a team event India won in 2024) with the individual World Championship.

short_explanation: Raga Bilawal, the parent scale of the Bilawal thaat, uses all natural (shuddha) notes, the Western major scale. Its Carnatic counterpart is Dheerashankarabharanam, the 29th melakarta, which has the same set of notes.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Natabhairavi has a flat third, sixth and seventh; it matches Asavari thaat.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Kamavardhini (Pantuvarali) uses flat second and sharp fourth notes; it is close to Purvi.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Hanumatodi uses flat second, third, sixth and seventh notes; it matches Bhairavi thaat.

common_traps: Mixing up Todi: the Carnatic Hanumatodi matches Hindustani Bhairavi, not Hindustani Todi.

short_explanation: Statement I is not always correct: t + 1/t falls until t = 1 and rises after, so x = 0.5, y = 1 gives 2.5 > 2. Statement II is always correct: √(1 + t²)/t equals √(1/t² + 1), which falls as t grows, so the larger y gives the smaller value. So only II.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I fails for x = 0.5, y = 1 (2.5 is not less than 2).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement I, which is not always correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement II, which always holds.

solution_steps: Statement I: try x = 0.5, y = 1. x + 1/x = 2.5 and y + 1/y = 2, so I fails.
Statement II: √(1 + t²)/t = √(1/t² + 1).
For positive t, 1/t² falls as t rises, so the expression falls.
With y > x, the value at y is smaller: II always holds.
common_traps: Testing I only with x and y both above 1, where it happens to hold; the range allows values below 1.

short_explanation: The Hilton-Young Commission fixed the rupee at 1 shilling 6 pence, a deliberately high rate. Britain adopted it because a strong rupee made it cheaper to remit the Home Charges and other sums to Britain, and it kept India's finances looking sound to its creditors.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Cheaper imports were a side effect, not the reason; Indian nationalists opposed the rate.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: An overvalued rupee made Indian exports, including cotton, costlier abroad.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The question is about a fixed sterling rate, not about preventing depreciation against gold.

common_traps: Thinking a high exchange rate helps exporters; it helps those remitting money out of India and hurts exporters.
tag_note: Topic should be Colonial economic policy and the drain of wealth. The question is about currency and exchange-rate policy, not land revenue.

topic_name: Sets of consecutive and patterned numbers
short_explanation: Fill the 100-litre cylinder three times to get 300 litres, then take out 1 litre twice with the 1-litre cylinder: 5 measurements give 298 litres. Four measurements cannot reach 298.
explanation_text: If only adding were allowed, the fewest measurements would be 12 (for example 2 × 100 + 2 × 25 + 8 × 6), which is not among the options, and the simple greedy method gives 13. The key rests on the fact that a measuring cylinder can also be used to remove water: 100 + 100 + 100 − 1 − 1 = 298.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No four measurements, added or taken away, total 298; the nearest route needs five.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 9; the working gives 5 (three fills of 100, two removals of 1).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 13 is the greedy all-adding count (2 × 100 + 3 × 25 + 3 × 6 + 5 × 1); removing water is allowed and shorter.

solution_steps: 298 is just 2 short of 300 = 3 × 100.
Fill 100 litres three times: 300 litres (3 measurements).
Remove 1 litre twice: 298 litres (2 more).
A check of all combinations of four measurements shows none reaches 298, so 5 is the minimum.
common_traps: Only adding measurements; taking water out with a cylinder also counts as a measurement.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. The key assumes a cylinder can be used to take water out as well as put it in; if only additions were allowed the minimum would be 12, which is not an option.

short_explanation: With 8, 9, 10 or 11 one-kg weights, the rest of 20 kg must come from 2, 5 and 10 kg weights. Counting the ways gives 3, 1, 3 and 1, so 8 ways in all.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Misses one way; the count is 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 8.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 9; the working gives 8.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 10; the working gives 8.

solution_steps: 8 ones: make 12 from 2, 5, 10: 10 + 2, 5 + 5 + 2, six 2s. Three ways.
9 ones: make 11: 5 + 2 + 2 + 2. One way.
10 ones: make 10: 10, 5 + 5, five 2s. Three ways.
11 ones: make 9: 5 + 2 + 2. One way.
common_traps: Missing a split such as 5 + 5 + 2 for 12 kg, or counting orders of the same weights as different ways.
key_note: All weights are taken on one pan against the load; that reading gives the keyed 8.

short_explanation: Inference 1 is correct: coins in the Pali texts and punch-marked silver coins at many sites point to trade and crafts in towns, a mark of urban life. Inference 2 is correct: regular use of named coins for payment shows the shift from barter to a money economy. So both.
explanation_text: The Pali canon of the sixth to fourth centuries BCE, the age of the second urbanisation in the Ganga valley, names coins such as kahapana and nikkha. Archaeology matches it with thousands of punch-marked coins, mostly silver. Coinage, towns and long-distance trade grew together.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits inference 2; coinage is itself the evidence for a money economy.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Omits inference 1; coin use is tied to the growth of towns.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Both inferences follow from the evidence.

topic_name: Area and perimeter — rectangle, square, triangle
short_explanation: Three cuts make at most 8 pieces, and one more flat cut can split at most 7 of the 8 small cubes (a plane cannot pass through all eight), so x₄ is at most 15. 16 is impossible, while 5, 8 and 12 can all be made.
explanation_text: Identical pieces after three cuts can be 4 slabs (three parallel cuts), 6 blocks (one cut one way and two the other way) or 8 small cubes (one cut along each direction). From 4 slabs, a fourth parallel cut through one slab gives 5, and a cross cut through all four gives 8. From 6 blocks, a cut across all six gives 12. From 8 small cubes, a plane can pass through at most 7 of them, so the most is 15. No route reaches 16.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 12 is possible: after one cut one way and two the other (6 identical blocks), a cut across all six gives 12.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 8 is possible: after three parallel cuts (4 slabs), a cut across all four gives 8.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 5 is possible: after three parallel cuts (4 slabs), a fourth parallel cut through one slab gives 5.

solution_steps: Three cuts give at most 8 pieces; identical-piece options are 4, 6 or 8.
A new cut adds one piece for every piece it passes through.
From 8 small cubes, a plane passes through at most 7, giving at most 15.
From 4 or 6 pieces the fourth cut gives at most 8 or 12.
So 16 cannot occur; 5, 8 and 12 can.
common_traps: Doubling 8 to 16 on the assumption that one cut can pass through every piece.
tag_note: Topic should be Cube cutting and spatial reasoning. The item counts pieces made by plane cuts, not area or perimeter.

short_explanation: Temple 1 is not Nagara: the Malegitti Shivalaya at Badami is a Dravida-style temple. Temple 3 is Nagara: the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is an early Nagara temple with a shikhara. Temple 4 is not Nagara: the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal is a classic Dravida temple. So 2 and 3.
explanation_text: The Chalukyan sites of Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal were a workshop where both styles stood side by side. Nagara temples have a curved, beehive-like tower (rekha-prasada). Dravida temples have a stepped, pyramidal vimana. At Pattadakal, Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna are Dravida, while Papanatha and Galaganatha are Nagara.

option_rationales.label: D

common_traps: Assuming every temple in Karnataka is Dravida; the Chalukyan sites also have Nagara temples.

short_explanation: Raising one score by 100 lifts the average by 4, so the class has 100 ÷ 4 = 25 students. Lowering another score by 25 (81 to 56) drops the average by 1, so y = x + 4 − 1 and y − x = 3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 2; the working gives +4 − 1 = 3.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 5 adds the second correction (4 + 1); the score fell from 81 to 56, so the average falls by 1.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 6; the working gives +4 − 1 = 3.

solution_steps: First correction adds 100 marks and lifts the average by 4, so students = 100 ÷ 4 = 25.
Second correction: 56 − 81 = −25 marks, so the average changes by −25 ÷ 25 = −1.
formula_used: Change in average = Change in total ÷ Number of students
common_traps: Treating the second correction as a rise because the recorded score was higher than the true one.

short_explanation: The largest value multiplies the two biggest numbers and adds the next: 5 × 4 + 3 = 23. The smallest multiplies the two smallest and adds the next: 2 × 3 + 4 = 10. So M − N = 13.

solution_steps: Maximum: 5 × 4 = 20, add the largest remaining value 3: M = 23.
Minimum: 2 × 3 = 6, add the smallest remaining value 4: N = 10.

short_explanation: Item 1 supports both statements: the Rigveda mentions the ashma chakra (stone pulley wheel) and ahava (strapped wooden pails) used to lift water from wells. Item 2 does not: axes and sickles are clearing and harvesting tools and say nothing about wells or animal power. Item 3 supports statement II: oxen were already used for ploughing and pulling carts, so draught-animal power was available to draw water. So 1 and 3 only.
explanation_text: The two statements make separate claims: that well irrigation carried farming away from river strips into the Punjab-Haryana plains, and that animals were used to draw the water. Evidence 'supports' them only if it bears on wells or on draught animals. The pulley-and-pail evidence speaks to wells; the long use of the ox speaks to animal traction. Tools for felling and reaping are true facts about Rigvedic farming but are irrelevant to how water was lifted.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 2 (axes and sickles), which says nothing about wells or draught animals, and omits item 3.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes item 2, which is true of the period but does not support either statement.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Omits item 1, the direct evidence of lifting water from wells.

common_traps: Choosing item 2 because it is a true fact about Rigvedic agriculture; the question asks what supports these two statements, not what is true of the period.

short_explanation: Item 1 is not a basis: the Nadi-Sukta of the Rigveda only lists rivers from east to west and cannot record Pleistocene drainage changes. Item 2 is not a basis: Robert Bruce Foote was a geologist and prehistorian who worked mainly in South India, not on the Sutlej and Yamuna. Item 3 is the basis: the same river-dolphin type living in both the Indus and Ganga systems implies the two systems were once connected. So 3 only.
explanation_text: A freshwater dolphin cannot cross the sea between the Indus and Ganga mouths, so its presence in both systems is read as evidence that a river such as the Yamuna or Sutlej once drained into the other system during the Pleistocene, letting the animals pass. The Rigveda dates to a much later period, and Foote's famous work was the 1863 Pallavaram find near Madras.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The Nadi-Sukta is a Vedic hymn listing rivers; it is far too late to record Pleistocene changes.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Foote worked on South Indian prehistory, not on explorations of the Sutlej and Yamuna.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Neither the Nadi-Sukta nor Foote is a basis for this assertion.

common_traps: The Indus and Ganga river dolphins are now often classed as two separate species; the question follows the older treatment of them as one species, which is the basis of the argument.
key_note: Accepted as the official key. Recent taxonomy splits the Indus and Ganga river dolphins into separate species; the question uses the older single-species view on which the argument rests.

short_explanation: Statement I is incorrect: if S is 3rd, T must be 5th, not 2nd. Statement II is incorrect: if Q is 3rd, S must be 5th and T 2nd, not 5th. So neither.
explanation_text: P is 4th and R is 1st, so Q, S and T share ranks 2, 3 and 5. Q is not 5th, so Q is 2nd or 3rd. S is not 2nd, so S is 3rd or 5th. T is not 3rd, so T is 2nd or 5th. Only two orders survive: Q 2nd, S 3rd, T 5th; or Q 3rd, S 5th, T 2nd. In the first, S is 3rd and T is 5th, which breaks statement I. In the second, Q is 3rd and T is 2nd, which breaks statement II.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I fails: with S 3rd, T is 5th.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II fails: with Q 3rd, T is 2nd.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements fail.

solution_steps: P is 4th and R is 1st, so Q, S and T take ranks 2, 3 and 5.
Q can be 2nd or 3rd, S 3rd or 5th, T 2nd or 5th.
Only two orders work: Q 2nd, S 3rd, T 5th; or Q 3rd, S 5th, T 2nd.
S 3rd goes with T 5th, and Q 3rd goes with T 2nd, so both statements are wrong.
common_traps: Checking only whether the rank named in the statement is allowed for T, without fixing all three of Q, S and T together.

Pair 4 is wrong: the Beas was the Vipas (or Vipasa); the Yavyavati is usually identified with a river west of the Indus, such as the Zhob. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes pair 4; the Beas was the Vipas, not the Yavyavati.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Pair 4 is wrong and omits pair 3, which is correct.

common_traps: Swapping Vitasta and Asikni: Vitasta is the Jhelum, Asikni the Chenab.
Taking Yavyavati for the Beas; the Beas is Vipas.

explanation_text: The Amaravati stupa flourished under the Satavahanas and later the Ikshvakus. Its white limestone reliefs, with crowded narrative scenes and slender, lively figures, are one of the three great early schools with Gandhara and Mathura. Many panels are now in the Chennai Government Museum and the British Museum.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; Amaravati was not second in size to Sanchi.

short_explanation: Both are possible, and one arrangement shows both at once. First rod, end to end: P-2, P-3, P-1, P-4, P-5. Second rod: Q-1, Q-5, Q-3, Q-2, Q-4. Here Q-3 is in the middle (statement I) and P-2 is at an end (statement II).
explanation_text: Lay the rods side by side and read them from one end. First rod: P-2, P-3, P-1, P-4, P-5. Second rod: Q-1, Q-5, Q-3, Q-2, Q-4. Check the clues: P-1 and Q-3 are both third, so they match. P-4 is fourth and faces Q-2. Q-4 is fifth and faces P-5. Q-3 (third) and Q-5 (second) are next to each other. Every clue holds, Q-3 sits in the middle portion, and P-2 sits at the end portion, so both statements are possible.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II is also possible: in the arrangement above P-2 is at an end.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I is also possible: in the arrangement above Q-3 is in the middle.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both are possible; the arrangement above satisfies every clue.

solution_steps: P-1 and Q-3 share a portion; put them both in the middle (third) portion.
Q-5 must sit next to Q-3: put it second on the second rod.
P-4 must face Q-1 or Q-2: put P-4 fourth and Q-2 fourth.
Q-4 must face P-3 or P-5: put Q-4 fifth and P-5 fifth; fill in P-3 second, Q-1 first, P-2 first.
Q-3 is in the middle and P-2 at an end, so both are possible.
common_traps: Reading 'possible' as 'must be true'; one valid arrangement is enough to show a statement is possible.
tag_note: Topic should be Arrangement puzzles. The item asks which placements are possible under clues, not for a count of arrangements.

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: the cars carry A, D and F; E and G; and B and C, so no one travels alone. Statement II is incorrect: F travels with A as well as D. Statement III is correct: B's only companion is C. So I and III only.
explanation_text: Car X carries A, D and F. Car Y carries E and G only. Car Z carries B and C. No one is alone, F shares the car with both A and D, and B shares the car only with C.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes II, which fails: F travels with A as well as D.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes II and omits I, which is correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: II is incorrect because F also travels with A.

solution_steps: B is not in Y and cannot share X with A, so B is in Z with C.
E and G must travel together with no one else; X already has A and Z has B and C, so E and G take Y by themselves.
D and F fill the two remaining places in X with A.
No one is alone, F is with A and D, and B is only with C: I and III hold.
common_traps: Reading 'Only D travels with F' as true because D is with F; the word 'only' fails since A is in the same car.

option_rationales.label: C

short_explanation: Statement I is correct: if X is correct, W cannot be correct (a correct W would make X incorrect), and if W is incorrect then Y must be correct. Statement II is incorrect: if Z is correct, X must be correct (an incorrect X would make Z incorrect), and then Y is correct as shown, so Y is necessarily correct. So I only.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: II fails: a correct Z forces X, and then Y, to be correct.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: II is incorrect; Y is necessarily correct once Z is correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: I is correct: X correct rules out W correct, which forces Y correct.

solution_steps: 'If W is correct, X is incorrect' means: if X is correct, W is incorrect.
'If Y is incorrect, W is correct' means: if W is incorrect, Y is correct. So X correct leads to Y correct; statement I holds.
'If X is incorrect, so is Z' means: if Z is correct, X is correct, and then Y is correct.
So Y must be correct whenever Z is; statement II is false. Answer: I only.
common_traps: Reversing a conditional: 'if X is incorrect then Z is incorrect' does not mean 'if Z is incorrect then X is incorrect'; the valid reverse form is 'if Z is correct then X is correct'.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: after the Tripuri crisis Bose could not win Gandhi's confidence and resigned as Congress President. Statement 2 is correct: the Congress Left was divided and did not stand with him. Statement 3 is not accepted as a factor: the Communists had backed Bose in the 1939 election and joined the early Left Consolidation effort, so the blanket claim that they did not support his endeavours is too sweeping. Statement 4 is correct: Royists and socialists like Jayaprakash Narayan put Congress unity first. So 1, 2 and 4.
explanation_text: Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya in the January 1939 presidential election, but the Tripuri session (Pant resolution) asked him to form a Working Committee in line with Gandhi's wishes. Unable to do so, he resigned in April 1939 and formed the Forward Bloc within Congress in May 1939. The socialists who had voted for him chose not to split the Congress.

option_rationales.label: A

short_explanation: In the time Y runs 5 rounds, X runs 7, so X gains 2 rounds and they meet twice. Y then runs the other way at double speed, so they close in at 7 + 10 = 17 rounds per unit of time for the 2 units X needs to finish 21 rounds: 34 meetings, the last of which is the stopping moment. Counting 2 + 33 gives 35.
explanation_text: Take one unit of time as the time Y needs for 5 rounds; X runs 7 rounds in it. In this first stretch X gains 2 rounds on Y, so they meet twice: halfway through and at the end of the unit, when both are back at the start. X needs 3 units in all for 21 rounds, so 2 units remain. Now Y runs the opposite way at 10 rounds per unit, so together they cover 17 rounds per unit and meet once every 1/17 of a unit: 34 times in 2 units. The 34th of these is the instant they stop, which the question excludes (before they finally stopped). Total = 2 + 33 = 35.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 34 counts only the opposite-direction meetings (17 × 2, including the stopping moment) and leaves out the 2 meetings of the first stretch.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 31; the working gives 2 + 33 = 35.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 29; the working gives 2 + 33 = 35.

solution_steps: Unit of time = Y's 5 rounds; X's speed 7, Y's 5 rounds per unit.
Same direction for 1 unit: gap closes at 2 rounds per unit, so 2 meetings.
X needs 21 ÷ 7 = 3 units, so 2 units remain.
Opposite direction: 7 + 10 = 17 rounds per unit, so 17 × 2 = 34 meetings, the last at the stop.
Excluding the stopping moment: 2 + 33 = 35.
formula_used: Meetings = relative distance covered ÷ track length
common_traps: Counting the meeting at the very moment they stop, which gives 36.
Forgetting that Y's speed doubles after the turn.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. The count excludes the meeting at the instant both stop, as the words 'before they finally stopped' suggest; counting it would give 36, which is not an option.

The resulting loss of estates, arms and forts turned the taluqdars against the Company, and this is why Awadh saw some of the most widespread revolt in 1857. short_explanation: Conclusion 1 is not valid: under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 a child aged 16 to 18 can be assessed for trial as an adult only for a heinous offence, not a serious one. Conclusion 2 is valid: the 2021 amendment defines a serious offence by the maximum sentence (more than seven years) where there is no minimum or a minimum below seven years. So 2 only.
explanation_text: The JJ Act, 2015 sorts offences into three classes. Petty offences carry a maximum of up to three years. Serious offences carry three to seven years. Heinous offences carry a minimum of seven years or more. Only for a heinous offence by a child aged 16 to 18 does the Board make a preliminary assessment that may send the case to the Children's Court for trial as an adult. Offences with a maximum above seven years but no minimum, or a minimum below seven years, fitted none of the classes. In Shilpa Mittal v. State (2020) the Supreme Court treated them as serious offences. The 2021 amendment then wrote that into the Act, so the maximum sentence decides the classification.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Rests on conclusion 1; transfer to the adult system is tied to heinous offences, not serious ones.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes conclusion 1, which is not valid.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out conclusion 2, which is valid.

common_traps: Confusing 'serious' with 'heinous' offences; only heinous offences can lead to trial as an adult.
key_note: Passage text not supplied; the answer is corroborated by the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 and its 2021 amendment, which the passage evidently describes.
