explanation_text: The test for 'heinous' is the minimum sentence: seven years or more. An offence such as one punishable 'up to ten years' with no floor therefore cannot be heinous, however long the maximum is. The Supreme Court held this in Shilpa Mittal v. State (2020). The 2021 amendment placed such offences in the serious category.

short_explanation: The second drone flies from 5:02 to 5:05, so the one-way flight is 180 s and the distance is 30 × 180 = 5400 m. Sound took 5400 ÷ 300 = 18 s, and the first drone reached the spot at 5:02, so the explosion was 180 + 18 = 198 s before 5:02: 4:58:42 PM.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 4:59:00 PM subtracts only the drone's 180 s flight and forgets the 18 s the sound took to reach the camp.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 4:59:02 PM; the working gives 5:02:00 − 198 s = 4:58:42 PM.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 4:56:32 PM; the working gives 4:58:42 PM.

solution_steps: Second drone: leaves at 5:02:00, reaches the spot at 5:05:00, so the flight takes 180 s.
Distance = 30 × 180 = 5400 m.
Sound delay = 5400 ÷ 300 = 18 s.
First drone left at 5:02:00 − 180 s = 4:59:00; the sound arrived then, so the blast was 18 s earlier: 4:58:42 PM.
formula_used: Time = Distance ÷ Speed
common_traps: Forgetting that the first drone set off only when the sound reached the camp.

Relationship 3 is incorrect: statements I and III pull in opposite directions, so together they cannot establish one premise. So 1 and 2.

short_explanation: Read as 6 to the power 129 times 7 to the power 307: any power of 6 ends in 6, and 7's powers end in 7, 9, 3, 1 in turn; 307 leaves 3 when divided by 4, so 7 to the power 307 ends in 3. 6 × 3 = 18, so the unit digit is 8.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 2 comes from taking 7 to the power 307 as ending in 7 (6 × 7 = 42), ignoring the four-step cycle.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 4 comes from using the second step of the cycle, 9 (6 × 9 = 54), from a wrong remainder of 2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 6 comes from taking 7 to the power 307 as ending in 1 (6 × 1), as if 307 were a multiple of 4.

solution_steps: Every power of 6 ends in 6.
Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1, repeating every 4.
307 = 4 × 76 + 3, so 7 to the power 307 ends in 3.
6 × 3 = 18, so the unit digit is 8.
formula_used: Unit digit of 7 to the power n follows the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1
common_traps: Multiplying the printed numbers 6129 and 7307 directly; the exponents were lost in printing.
key_note: The stem as printed reads 6129 × 7307, whose literal unit digit is 3 (not an option). The superscripts have been lost: the intended expression is 6 to the power 129 times 7 to the power 307, which gives the keyed 8.

short_explanation: On a salary of 100 he spends 90 and saves 10. After the change he earns 112 and spends 99, so he saves 13, which is 30% more than 10.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 20% comes from the gap of 12% − 10% = 2 points divided by 10; savings must be worked out in rupees, not by subtracting rates.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives a 3% fall; savings rise from 10 to 13.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives a 2% fall; savings rise from 10 to 13, a 30% increase.

solution_steps: Take salary 100: spend 90, save 10.
New salary = 112; new spending = 90 × 1.1 = 99.
New saving = 112 − 99 = 13.
Change = (13 − 10) ÷ 10 = 30% increase.
formula_used: Saving = Income − Expenditure
common_traps: Applying the 10% rise to the whole salary instead of to the 90 spent.

short_explanation: The powers of 2 run 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, so exactly three (128, 256, 512) have three digits.

short_explanation: X takes 12 + 12 + 45 = 69 minutes and Y takes 15 + 12 + 36 = 63 minutes, so Y finishes 6 minutes earlier.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: One weighing cannot single out one cube among 7 with certainty; at best it narrows the search to 3.

solution_steps: Split the 7 cubes into groups of 3, 3 and 1.
Weigh 3 against 3. Balance: the single cube is light (done).

Maximum weighings = 2.
common_traps: Splitting into two halves each time instead of three groups, which uses a balance's three outcomes poorly.

short_explanation: HCF × LCM of two numbers equals their product, so a × b = a³ and b = a². Statement I is correct: a² − a = a(a − 1) is a product of two consecutive numbers, so it is even. Statement II is correct: b = a² is a perfect square. So both.

option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement I; a(a − 1) is always even.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

solution_steps: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: a × b.
a × b = a³, so b = a² (a ≠ 1 as the numbers are distinct).
Difference a² − a = a(a − 1), a product of consecutive integers, which is even.
b = a² is a perfect square. Both hold.
formula_used: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
common_traps: Forgetting the identity HCF × LCM = product and trying to find the numbers by trial.

short_explanation: For 11, the alternate-digit difference of 4x5y790 must be a multiple of 11: (4 + 5 + 7 + 0) − (x + y + 9) = 7 − (x + y). So x + y is 7 or 18, and either way it leaves remainder 7 when divided by 11.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 1; x + y is 7 or 18, both leaving 7.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 3; x + y is 7 or 18, both leaving 7.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 5; x + y is 7 or 18, both leaving 7.

solution_steps: Digits in odd places from the right: 0, 7, 5, 4, sum 16.
Digits in even places: 9, y, x, sum 9 + x + y.
Difference 16 − (9 + x + y) = 7 − (x + y) must be 0 or a multiple of 11.
x + y = 7 or 18; both leave remainder 7 on division by 11.
formula_used: Divisible by 11 when (sum of alternate digits) − (sum of the others) is a multiple of 11
common_traps: Considering only x + y = 7 and missing 18; the remainder is the same, but checking both confirms it.

short_explanation: A − B = 9 × (tens digit − units digit), so for a multiple of 27 the digit gap must be 3 or 6 (9 would need a 0 units digit, making B start with 0). Gap 3 gives 41, 52, 63, 74, 85, 96; gap 6 gives 71, 82, 93: 9 numbers.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 6 counts only a digit gap of 3 and misses 71, 82, 93.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 12 includes 30, 60 and 90, whose reverses (03, 06, 09) are not 2-digit numbers.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 18 counts each qualifying pair twice (A and its reverse), ignoring A > B.

solution_steps: A = 10a + b, B = 10b + a, so A − B = 9(a − b).
9(a − b) a multiple of 27 means a − b is 3, 6 or 9.
B is 2-digit, so b ≥ 1; a − b = 9 is impossible.
a − b = 3: b from 1 to 6, 6 numbers. a − b = 6: b from 1 to 3, 3 numbers. Total 9.
common_traps: Allowing 0 as the units digit of A, which makes B a 1-digit number.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: swarms communicate over ordinary radio bands such as 2.4 and 5.8 GHz; the terahertz band is still largely experimental. Statement 2 is correct: drones in a swarm talk to one another to coordinate. Statement 3 is correct: GPS spoofing, feeding false satellite signals, is a common counter-swarm technique alongside jamming. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; swarms do not normally use the terahertz band.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1 and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

short_explanation: ZERO becomes ADSN by moving the letters alternately one step forward and one step back: Z to A, E to D, R to S, O to N. The same rule turns STOP into T, S, P, O: TSPO.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: SPOT is only a rearrangement of STOP's letters, not the one-forward, one-back shift.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: TSOP shifts only the first two letters and leaves O and P unchanged.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: POST is an anagram of STOP; no letter shift produces it.

solution_steps: Z to A is one step forward (wrapping round), E to D one step back, R to S one step forward, O to N one step back.
Apply the same to STOP: S to T, T to S, O to P, P to O.
The code is TSPO.
common_traps: Spotting that the answer uses the same letters and picking an anagram instead of applying the shift.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: GenomeIndia is an Indian project, separate from the international Human Genome Project that ended in 2003. Statement 2 is correct: it is funded by the Department of Biotechnology. Statement 3 is correct: its main aim is a reference catalogue of Indian genetic variation, from about 10,000 genomes sequenced across population groups. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; GenomeIndia is not part of the Human Genome Project.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1 and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which is incorrect.

topic_name: Area and perimeter — rectangle, square, triangle
short_explanation: The tile lengths 3, 7 and 11 must add to 100. The most tiles is 31 of 3 feet plus 1 of 7 feet (32 tiles); the fewest is 8 of 7 feet plus 4 of 11 feet (12 tiles). So x − y = 20.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 12 is y, the minimum number of tiles, not the difference x − y.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 10; the working gives 32 − 12 = 20.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 7; the working gives 32 − 12 = 20.

solution_steps: Every tile is 3 feet wide, so only lengths matter: 3a + 7b + 11c = 100.
Maximum tiles: use as many 3-foot tiles as possible; 100 = 31 × 3 + 7, so 32 tiles.
Minimum tiles: favour 11-foot tiles; 100 = 4 × 11 + 8 × 7, so 12 tiles (9 × 11 = 99 leaves 1, which no mix fixes with fewer tiles).
common_traps: Taking 9 tiles of 11 feet for the minimum; the leftover 1 foot cannot be covered, so fewer 11-foot tiles are needed.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the National Quantum Mission aims to build intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50 to 1000 physical qubits over eight years. Statement 2 is correct: it is implemented through four Thematic Hubs, in computing, communication, sensing and metrology, and materials and devices, hosted at IISc Bengaluru, IIT Madras, IIT Bombay and IIT Delhi. So both 1 and 2.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 2; the mission does run four T-Hubs.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1; 50-1000 physical qubits is the stated target.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements are correct.

short_explanation: With speed v, the actual trip takes 200/v + 400/(v/2) + 200/(v/8) = 2600/v hours, and the other order takes 200/v + 400/(v/4) + 200/(v/8) = 3400/v. The difference 800/v = 4 hours gives v = 200 km/h.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 190; the working gives 800/v = 4, so v = 200.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 150; the working gives 800/v = 4, so v = 200.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 100 comes from not compounding the second slowdown (taking it as a fraction of the original speed), which makes the time gap 400/v.

solution_steps: Actual: 200 km at v, 400 km at v/2, 200 km at v/8: time 200/v + 800/v + 1600/v = 2600/v.
Other order: 200 km at v, 400 km at v/4, 200 km at v/8: time 200/v + 1600/v + 1600/v = 3400/v.
Difference = 800/v = 4, so v = 200 km/h.
formula_used: Time = Distance ÷ Speed
common_traps: Applying the second slowdown to the original speed instead of to the already reduced speed.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Deep Ocean Mission is run by the Ministry of Earth Sciences, not the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. Statement 2 is correct: Matsya-6000 is a crewed submersible designed to carry three people to 6,000 metres. Statement 3 is correct: Samudrayaan, India's crewed deep-sea programme, falls under this mission. So 2 and 3 only.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; the nodal ministry is Earth Sciences.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1 and omits statement 3.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which names the wrong ministry.

common_traps: Linking an ocean mission to the shipping ministry; it belongs to the Ministry of Earth Sciences.

short_explanation: Weighted scores: candidate 1 scores 5.2, candidate 2 5.1, candidate 3 5.2, candidate 4 4.5 and candidate 5 5.0. To select exactly three (candidates 1, 3 and 2), the cutoff is 5.1.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: A cutoff of 5.2 selects only two candidates (1 and 3).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: A cutoff of 5.3 selects nobody; the top score is 5.2.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: A cutoff of 5.4 selects nobody; the top score is 5.2.

solution_steps: Score = 0.2 × first + 0.3 × second + 0.5 × third component.
Ranked: 5.2, 5.2, 5.1, 5.0, 4.5; the third-highest score, 5.1, is the cutoff.
formula_used: Weighted score = sum of weight × component score
common_traps: Using a simple average of the three components instead of the weights.

short_explanation: Mr. X answered for the public trust placed in him: he reported the wrongdoing to the vigilance authority and stopped the contract for citizens' welfare. Owning responsibility for outcomes and answering to proper oversight is accountability.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Esprit de corps is team spirit and loyalty within a group; Mr. X acted against vested interests, not for group morale.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Equity means fair treatment of all; the case turns on answering for quality and public welfare, not on fair distribution.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Delegation means passing authority to subordinates; nothing was delegated here.

tag_note: Topic should be Ethics, integrity and aptitude (case study). The item tests an officer's ethical conduct in an administrative dilemma; subject and topic are null in the input.

short_explanation: Relationship 1 is incorrect: S3 describes the make-up of environmental activism and how deniers use its extreme voices; it does not argue against S1's claim that protecting the environment is essential. Relationship 2 is incorrect: all three statements concern the climate-change debate, so S3 is connected to both. Relationship 3 is correct: the lack of scientific consensus in S2 leaves room for alarmist and extremist positions, and for deniers to target them, as S3 describes. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes 2; S3 is clearly connected to the climate debate in S1 and S2.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes 1 and 2, both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes 1 and 2 and omits 3, the one correct relationship.

common_traps: Treating S3 as a counterpoint to S1 because it mentions deniers; S3 reports what deniers focus on, it does not deny S1.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. Another reading set aside: relationship 1, since a reader could see S3's criticism of alarmism as cutting against S1's 'existential exigency'; S3 criticises a style of activism, not the need to protect the environment.

short_explanation: Statement 1 helps: acknowledging the tribal community's cultural concerns first builds trust for mediation. Statement 2 does not: pushing ahead and dismissing a community's claims as mere sentiment would escalate the conflict and ignore tribal rights. Statement 3 helps: a joint platform of tribal leaders, experts and municipal officials lets each side hear the other. Statement 4 helps: an independent impact assessment shared openly gives both sides a common set of facts. So 1, 3 and 4 only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which bypasses mediation, and omits statement 1.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2 and omits statements 3 and 4.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which would inflame rather than resolve the dispute.

common_traps: Statement 2 dresses up majority convenience as public interest; a mediator cannot start by ruling one side out.
key_note: Statement 3 is garbled in the stem ('platform tribal leaders'); read as a platform involving tribal leaders.
tag_note: Topic should be Ethics, integrity and aptitude (case study). The item tests an officer's ethical conduct in an administrative dilemma; subject and topic are null in the input.

short_explanation: A captain with the team is informal and firm (1); a judge with lawyers in court is formal and firm (4); a Vice Chancellor with a Deputy Registrar is formal and open-ended (3); peers and coworkers are informal and open-ended (2). So A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2.
explanation_text: Two questions settle each pair. First, formal or informal? Court and university administration are formal settings; a team and colleagues are informal. Second, firm or open-ended? A captain and a judge give instructions or rulings that must be followed, so they are firm. A Vice Chancellor consulting a senior officer and colleagues talking among themselves leave room for discussion, so they are open-ended.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps the judge and the Vice Chancellor: court exchanges are firm, not open-ended.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Makes the captain open-ended and peers firm; a captain directs the team, while peers talk as equals.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Gets all four pairs wrong: the captain is firm, the judge firm, the Vice Chancellor open-ended and peers open-ended.

common_traps: Treating all senior-junior relationships as the same; a judge rules, while a Vice Chancellor consults his administrative officer.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is not advisable: disclosing unproven allegations to the public at once risks defaming the contractor and prejudging the process. Statement 2 is not advisable: recommending removal on unproven claims denies due process. Statement 3 is the right step: a limited disclosure to an oversight committee lets the information be checked without public harm, so 3 only.
explanation_text: Ms. X balances transparency against fairness and confidentiality. Hiding the information, as Mr. Y advises, fails transparency; broadcasting or acting on it before verification fails fairness. Channelling it to a body that can verify it serves both.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which act on unverified claims.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which removes a contractor on unproven allegations.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 1 and 2, which act before the claims are verified.

common_traps: Treating 'transparency' as 'tell everyone now'; the ethical move is disclosure to the proper forum.
key_note: Stem garbled: statement 1 runs on into the text of statement 2. Read statement 1 as 'Immediately disclose the information to the project committee and the public'.
tag_note: Topic should be Ethics, integrity and aptitude (case study). The item tests an officer's ethical conduct in an administrative dilemma; subject and topic are null in the input.

topic_name: Tools of communication and their purpose
short_explanation: A memorandum conveys a directive within an organisation (3); a flyer spreads non-targeted information to anyone who picks it up (4); Bcc sends a copy without other recipients seeing it, so it informs confidentially (2); minutes record the decisions of a meeting (1). So A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Gives minutes' job (recording decisions) to the memorandum and the memorandum's job to minutes.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps memorandum and minutes, and swaps flyer and Bcc.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps flyer and Bcc: a flyer is for everyone, while Bcc hides who else received the message.

common_traps: Confusing Bcc (hidden copy) with Cc; the 'blind' copy is what makes it confidential.

short_explanation: Directive 1 is not appropriate: ordering staff to practise other groups' cultural markers is imposed and can breed resentment. Directive 2 is not appropriate: leaving conflicts to fade on their own is avoidance, not leadership. Directive 3 is appropriate: encouraging people to seek each other's perspectives builds understanding and tackles the cause of conflict. So 3 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes 1, a forced cultural exercise that can deepen friction.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Directive 2 is avoidance and sets a poor precedent.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Includes 2, which leaves conflicts unresolved.

common_traps: Taking directive 1 as good diversity practice; the word 'direct' makes it compulsion, not inclusion.

short_explanation: Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, and custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law. So Y is right that custom is included, and X, by rejecting that, holds a view that is wrong in part.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Article 13 expressly includes custom or usage, so X's rejection of it is wrong.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Y is correct; custom or usage having the force of law is part of the definition.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: X's overall view rejects custom, which Article 13 includes, so X's view is not correct.

common_traps: Accepting 'both correct' because X's list of ordinances, orders and rules was right; X's view also denies custom.
key_note: Accepted as the official key. Another reading set aside: option c, because X's first remarks about ordinances and rules are correct; the key judges X's view as a whole, including the rejection of custom.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Article 393 says 'This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India'. Statement 2 is incorrect: Article 395 repeals the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935. Statement 3 is incorrect: Article 394 says the remaining provisions come into force on the 26th of January, 1950. So no statement is correct.
explanation_text: Article 394 has two parts: some provisions (on citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament and others) came into force on 26 November 1949, and the rest on 26 January 1950, which it names.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: All three statements are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is incorrect; Article 394 names 26 January 1950.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: None of the statements is correct, not one.

common_traps: Remembering Article 394's 26 November 1949 date and forgetting that the same article names 26 January 1950.

short_explanation: A semantic barrier is misunderstanding the meaning of a word (2); a cognitive barrier is information overload, which exceeds the mind's capacity to process (4); an organisational barrier is lack of feedback, arising from structure and channels (1); an affective barrier is fear of social stigma, an emotional block (3). So A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps the semantic and affective barriers, and also the cognitive and organisational ones: word meaning is semantic, overload is cognitive, lack of feedback is organisational and fear of stigma is affective.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps the semantic and affective barriers: word meaning is semantic, fear of stigma is affective.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps the cognitive and organisational barriers: overload is cognitive, lack of feedback is organisational.

common_traps: 'Affective' refers to feelings and emotions (fear, stigma), not to 'effect'.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act was passed in 2016, not 2018. Statement 2 is correct: the Sugamya Bharat (Accessible India) Abhiyan targets the built environment, transport and ICT. Statement 3 is incorrect: NDFDC was set up by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. So 2 only.
explanation_text: The 2016 Act raised the list of disabilities from 7 to 21, set 4% reservation in government jobs and 5% in higher education. NDFDC, set up in 1997, is registered as a not-for-profit company, which is where the Corporate Affairs confusion arises.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 1, which gets the year of the Act wrong.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; the Act dates from 2016.

common_traps: The Act came into force in 2017 and was passed in 2016; 2018 is wrong on both counts.
NDFDC is a company under the Companies Act but set up by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
tag_note: Topic should be Welfare of vulnerable sections (persons with disabilities). The question tests a statute, a scheme and a corporation, not Part III rights.

topic_name: Tools of communication and their purpose
short_explanation: Head 1, size of family, belongs: a family-oriented resort must know the size of the groups it will serve. Head 2, budget, belongs: feasibility depends on what visitors will spend. Head 3, number of earners, does not: it is intrusive, and the budget already captures ability to pay. Head 4, food allergies, does not: it is an operating detail for a running resort, not a feasibility question. So 1 and 2 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes head 3; the number of earners adds nothing that the budget does not already show.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Includes head 4; dietary restrictions matter once a resort is running, not for judging whether to build it.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits head 1 and includes head 3.

common_traps: Including every question that seems useful; a feasibility questionnaire should ask only what bears on the decision, briefly and without intruding.

topic_name: Special provisions for states and areas
short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram are governed by the Sixth Schedule, not the Fifth. Statement 2 is correct: under Section 10(26) of the Income-tax Act, Scheduled Tribe members living in specified north-eastern areas and Ladakh are exempt on income from those areas. Statement 3 is correct: Article 243D(2) reserves not less than one-third of SC and ST seats in Panchayats for SC and ST women. So two correct statements, including statement 2.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; these states are under the Sixth Schedule.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Two statements, 2 and 3, are correct.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect.

common_traps: Confusing the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas in other states) with the Sixth Schedule (tribal areas of the four north-eastern states).

topic_name: Tools of communication and their purpose
short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: a circular letter goes to a group of people. Statement 2 is not correct: circulars carry standard, identical content, not customised content. Statement 3 is not correct: appraisals and increments are personal and go in individual letters. Statement 4 is not correct: circulars are more cost-effective than individual letters. So 1 only.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2; circular content is standard, not customised.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 2 and 4 are both incorrect.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 3 and 4; appraisals are individual matters and circulars save cost.

common_traps: Statement 4 reverses the main advantage of circulars: one text for many readers is cheaper.

topic_name: Cost price, selling price and margin
short_explanation: Profit shares follow capital × time: A gets 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9, B gets 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, and C, with the remaining 5/12 for the full period, gets 5/12. In 144ths that is 16 : 9 : 60, so C gets 60/85 × 17,000 = ₹12,000.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives ₹10,000; the working gives 60/85 × 17,000 = ₹12,000.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives ₹12,500; the working gives ₹12,000.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives ₹10,750; the working gives ₹12,000.

solution_steps: Capital × time: A 1/9, B 1/16, C 5/12.
Multiply by 144: A 16, B 9, C 60; total 85.
formula_used: Profit share ∝ Capital × Time
common_traps: Sharing profit by capital alone, which gives C only 5/12 of ₹17,000.
tag_note: Topic should be Partnership. Profit is shared by capital and time, not a cost-price or margin calculation.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: unstarred questions get a written answer. Statement 2 is incorrect: starred questions get an oral answer in the House. Statement 3 is correct: since there is no oral answer to an unstarred question, no supplementary question can be asked on it. So only one statement is correct.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 2 swap the meanings of starred and unstarred questions.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is incorrect; starred questions are answered orally.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is correct.

common_traps: Swapping starred and unstarred: the star marks a question for oral answer, which allows supplementaries.

short_explanation: Each replacement keeps 9/10 of chemical A. After three, A is 10 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 7.29 litres, so B is 2.71 litres, about 27% of the 10 litres.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 25%; the working gives 1 − 0.729 = 27.1%.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 29%; the working gives 27.1%.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 31%; the working gives 27.1% (simply adding 10% three times would give 30%, not 31%).

solution_steps: After each step the fraction of A left is multiplied by 9/10.
After three steps: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729, so A = 7.29 litres.
B = 10 − 7.29 = 2.71 litres, about 27%.
formula_used: Remaining A = Initial × (1 − removed/total) to the power of the number of replacements
common_traps: Adding 1 litre of B per step to get 3 litres (30%), forgetting that later removals take out some B too.
tag_note: Topic should be Mixtures and replacement. The item is a repeated-replacement problem, not a percentage change.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Statement 2 is incorrect: 20 members come from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha. Statement 3 is incorrect: no Minister, without exception, can be a member. Statement 4 is incorrect: members' term does not exceed one year. So no statement is correct.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: All four statements are incorrect.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 reverses the numbers; the Lok Sabha elects 20 and the Rajya Sabha 10.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect; the Speaker appoints the Chairperson.

common_traps: Reversing the 20:10 split between the two Houses.
The exception in statement 3 is invented: no Minister may be a member.

short_explanation: Mission Sudarshan Chakra, announced on Independence Day 2025, is a planned national air and missile defence shield. Statement 1 is correct: it covers air defence, ballistic missile defence and a capability to strike back. Statement 2 is correct: it seeks rapid, precise and powerful responses that support strategic autonomy. Statement 3 is correct: it aims to extend a nationwide security shield over strategic, civilian and public places by 2035. So 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3; the 2035 nationwide shield is part of the stated aim.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is also correct.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statements 2 and 3, which are also correct.

key_note: Accepted as the official key; the mission's detailed scope rests on announcements that could not all be independently corroborated.

topic_name: Cost price, selling price and margin
short_explanation: He earns 5 per delivery plus 2 per km. With 80, 85 or 90 deliveries the delivery money is only ₹400, ₹425 or ₹450, so crossing ₹500 depends on the distance, which is not given (he needs at least 101 deliveries to be sure regardless of distance).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 80 deliveries give ₹400; he also needs more than 50 km, which is not certain.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 85 deliveries give ₹425; he also needs more than 37.5 km, which is not certain.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 90 deliveries give ₹450; he also needs more than 25 km, which is not certain.

solution_steps: Earnings = 5 × deliveries + 2 × km.
For a guaranteed target without knowing the distance, 5 × deliveries must alone exceed 500, which needs 101 deliveries.
None of 80, 85, 90 reaches that; each still depends on the unknown distance.
So the data are insufficient.
formula_used: Earnings = 5n + 2d
common_traps: Assuming he always travels the full 100 km; the 100 km is only an upper limit.
key_note: Accepted as defensible. One could argue that deliveries need some travel, but the stem gives no minimum distance, so none of the listed counts is certain to cross ₹500.
tag_note: Topic should be Linear inequalities (earnings conditions). There is no cost price, selling price or margin in the item.

short_explanation: Statement I alone is not enough: m = 32 (2 + 10 + 20) is not prime and has no 5-coin, while m = 8 (1 + 2 + 5) is not prime and has one. Statement II alone is enough: the totals with digit sum above 5 are 8, 16, 17, 26, 27 and 35, and every one of them includes the 5-coin. So one statement (II) alone answers it.
explanation_text: The ten possible sets of three different coins give totals 8, 13, 23, 16, 26, 31, 17, 27, 32 and 35. short_explanation: Statement I alone says only that x or y is even, and Statement II alone says only that x and y have the same parity. Together they force both to be even, so x is even: both statements are needed.
explanation_text: Statement I: x²y² is even exactly when xy is even, that is when at least one of x and y is even. x could be odd with y even, so I alone is not enough. Statement II: 1 + x² + y² is odd means x² + y² is even, so x and y are both even or both odd. Either case is possible, so II alone is not enough. Together: they share the same parity and at least one is even, so both are even and x is even.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Neither statement alone settles it: I allows x odd with y even, and II allows x and y both odd.

option_rationales.label: b

solution_steps: Statement I: x²y² even means xy even, so at least one of x, y is even. x = 1, y = 2 and x = 2, y = 1 both fit: not sufficient.
Statement II: 1 + x² + y² odd means x² + y² even, so x and y have the same parity. x = y = 1 and x = y = 2 both fit: not sufficient.
Together: same parity and at least one even, so both are even. x is even: sufficient.
formula_used: odd × odd = odd; even + even = even; odd + odd = even
common_traps: Reading Statement I as 'x is even'; x²y² is even whenever just one of x and y is even.

Statement II: (p − 1)q is odd only when p is even and q is odd; so the condition fails exactly when T mixes an even and an odd number. It too says only that T is all odd or all even. T = {1, 3} and T = {2, 4} satisfy both statements, yet only the second is entirely from Y.

option_rationales.rationale: Neither statement alone is enough: each allows T to be all odd.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Neither statement alone is enough: each allows T to be all odd.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Both statements together give the same information (same parity throughout), so an all-odd T is still possible.

solution_steps: Statement I: an even sum for every pair means no odd number is paired with an even one, so T is all odd or all even.
Statement II: (p − 1)q is odd only when p is even and q is odd, so T cannot mix parities; again all odd or all even.
Both statements together still allow T = {1, 3} (all from X) and T = {2, 4} (all from Y), so the question cannot be answered.
formula_used: (p − 1)q is odd only when p − 1 and q are both odd
common_traps: Assuming an even sum means the numbers are even; two odd numbers also add to an even number.

Below 199, the next common mark would be 139, which is outside the range. Upwards: 199 + 60k ≤ 1000 gives k ≤ 13, so k = 0, 1, ..., 13, which is 14 marks (199 to 979). The 'by 9 AM' clause only confirms all three do pass 1000'.

solution_steps: LCM of 4, 6 and 5 = 60, so the common marks are 60 feet apart, starting from 199.
The one before 199 is 139, below 195, so the first common mark in range is 199.
Largest: 199 + 60k ≤ 1000 gives k ≤ 13, so the last is 199 + 780 = 979.
Count k = 0 to 13: 14 marks.
formula_used: Common marks = 199 + LCM(4, 6, 5) × k = 199 + 60k
common_traps: Forgetting to count the starting mark 199', which gives 13.

short_explanation: Each blue strip must sit in a corner with its 8' side along the 10' edge (8' is longer than the 6' edge), which gives four possible corner strips. Strips in the two corners of the same long edge overlap, so the non-overlapping pairs are 4.
explanation_text: Sharing exactly two sides with the table's edges means a blue strip sits in a corner. Its 8' side cannot run along the 6' edge, so it runs along a 10' edge and covers 2.5' of the 6' width. There are four corners, so four possible strips. Two strips on the same 10' edge would cover 16' of a 10' edge and overlap. Two strips on opposite 10' edges leave a 1' white band between them (2.5 + 2.5 = 5 is less than 6), so these pairs work: both strips starting at the left end, both at the right end, or one at each end in the two diagonal ways. That is 4 patterns. Because the table is fixed, turning it round does not merge any of them.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 2 counts patterns as if the table could be turned or flipped, merging mirror-image layouts; the table is fixed.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 6 is every pair of corners, including the two pairs on the same long edge that would overlap.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 8 counts the two blue strips as distinguishable (ordered pairs); from above, two identical blue strips give only 4 patterns.

solution_steps: A strip sharing two sides with the table's edges sits in a corner; its 8' side must lie along a 10' edge, since the other edge is only 6'.
Four corners give four possible strips, and choosing two gives 6 pairs.
Two strips on the same 10' edge overlap (8 + 8 is more than 10), which rules out 2 pairs.
Strips on opposite long edges fit (2.5 + 2.5 is less than 6), leaving 4 patterns.
formula_used: Valid pairs = 4C2 − overlapping pairs = 6 − 2
common_traps: Placing the 8' side along the 6' edge, which cannot fit.
Counting the overlapping same-edge pairs.
key_note: Accepted on the natural reading that the two blue portions do not overlap and are identical when seen from above.
tag_note: Topic should be Counting and arrangements (geometric placement). It counts placements of rectangles on a table top; no number series is involved.

short_explanation: A Silver Notice seeks to identify and trace criminal assets. A Blue Notice gathers more information about a person's identity, location or activities in a criminal investigation. A Black Notice seeks information on unidentified bodies. A Green Notice warns about a person's criminal activities where they may threaten public safety. So the code is 4, 2, 1, 3.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Gives the Silver Notice the Green Notice's warning role and swaps Blue and Black.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Gives the Silver Notice the Green Notice's role and the Green Notice the asset role.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Swaps the Blue and Black notices; Black is for unidentified bodies.

common_traps: Taking the Blue Notice for unidentified bodies; that is the Black Notice.
The Silver Notice is new (piloted from 2025) and deals with assets, not persons.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: if output prices and quantities stay the same and oil prices fall, the real value of output should not change. Deflating inputs and outputs separately (double deflation) is what keeps it steady. Statement 2 is not correct: 'universally adopted by all economies' overstates; India, for example, uses single deflation for much of its GVA. So 1 only.
explanation_text: Real gross value added is output minus inputs, both at constant prices. Suppose output prices and quantities are unchanged but oil, an input, gets cheaper. Nominal value added rises because the input bill falls. If only the output price is used to deflate (single deflation), that rise looks like real growth. Double deflation deflates inputs by their own falling price and shows no change in real value, which is the correct answer when nothing real has changed. Many economies still use single deflation for some sectors, which is why statement 2's 'universally' fails.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 overreaches with 'universally adopted by all economies'.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which is not correct.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is correct.

common_traps: An 'all' or 'universally' claim: separate deflators are good practice but not what every economy does.
key_note: Passage text not supplied; the answer is corroborated by the standard single-versus-double deflation argument, which the passage evidently makes.

Statement 3 is correct as keyed: Capacity Development Support is led by the Indian Institute of Forest Management, Bhopal. So 1 and 3 only.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is valid: the argument rests on the idea that the way output is deflated can make manufacturers' real performance look better than it is. Statement 2 is not valid: double deflation means deflating output by output prices and inputs by input prices separately; deflating both against a single price is a form of single deflation. So 1 only.
explanation_text: Real value added can be measured by single deflation, where one price index is applied to nominal value added, or by double deflation, where output and inputs are each deflated by their own price indices and the difference taken. When input prices fall faster than output prices, single deflation can overstate real manufacturing growth, which is the concern behind statement 1.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 misdescribes double deflation, which uses separate price indices for output and inputs.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 2, which misdescribes double deflation.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is valid.

common_traps: Statement 2 names the right term but attaches the wrong definition; double deflation is defined by using two separate indices.
key_note: The passage text is not included in this input row, so the explanation paraphrases the argument the keyed option summarises and does not quote the passage.

Statement 2 is an outcome: a youth hockey development MoU between Hockey India and the German Hockey Federation. topic_name: Number series — arithmetic and difference patterns
short_explanation: The 15-character string splits into three blocks of five, and the known letters fit only the block 'abbab' repeated three times. So the 7th and 8th characters are b and b.
explanation_text: Write the string in three blocks of five characters. Block one: blank, b, blank, a, blank. Block two: a, blank, blank, a, blank. Block three: a, blank, b, a, b. Matching the same place in each block: the first place is a (from blocks two and three), the second is b (block one), the third is b (block three), the fourth is a (all three), the fifth is b (block three). So each block is 'abbab', and the full string is abbab abbab abbab. The 7th and 8th characters are the second and third of block two: b and b.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The pattern 'abbab' puts b in both the 7th and 8th places, not a and a.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The 7th character is b, not a.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The 8th character is b, not a.

solution_steps: The string has 15 characters; try a repeating block of 5 (three copies).
Match known letters place by place across the blocks: first a, second b, third b, fourth a, fifth b.
The block is 'abbab', with no clash anywhere in the string.
The 7th and 8th characters are the 2nd and 3rd of the second block: b and b.
common_traps: Trying to spot a pattern by eye instead of lining the string up in equal blocks.
key_note: The blanks are printed as × in the stem; the reading is otherwise clear.
tag_note: Topic should be Letter series and repeating patterns. The string is a letter pattern, not a number series.

short_explanation: Read the stem as 10^m × 1000 × n = 75^25 × 25^32 × 32^75. The right side has 2^375 and 5^(50 + 64) = 5^114, so it holds exactly 10^114; since n has no factor 10, m + 3 = 114 and m = 111.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 101; the working gives 111 (m + 3 = 114).

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 121; the working gives 111 (m + 3 = 114).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 131; the working gives 111 (m + 3 = 114).

solution_steps: Powers of 5: 50 + 64 = 114; powers of 2: 375. Complete tens = the smaller, 114.
n is not divisible by 10, so all 114 tens sit in 10^m × 1000: m + 3 = 114, m = 111.
formula_used: Number of factors of 10 = min(power of 2, power of 5)
common_traps: Forgetting to subtract the 3 tens in the factor 1000, which gives 114 (not an option).
Counting only one 5 in each 75, which gives 5^25 instead of 5^50.
key_note: The stem has lost its superscripts; it is read as 10^m × 1000 × n = 75^25 × 25^32 × 32^75, which gives exactly one of the options.

option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; no Russian institute was involved in developing the standard.

short_explanation: Same direction: relative speed 96 km/h for 15 s gives train length 96 × 5/18 × 15 = 400 m. Opposite direction: relative speed 104 km/h, so time = 400 ÷ (104 × 5/18) = 13.85 s.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 13.51; the working gives 15 × 96 ÷ 104 = 13.85.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 13.65; the working gives 15 × 96 ÷ 104 = 13.85.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 14.05; the working gives 15 × 96 ÷ 104 = 13.85. (Using the train's own 100 km/h for the length gives 14.42, which is not offered.)

solution_steps: Same direction: relative speed = 100 − 4 = 96 km/h = 96 × 5/18 = 80/3 m/s.
Train length = 80/3 × 15 = 400 m.
Opposite direction: relative speed = 100 + 4 = 104 km/h = 104 × 5/18 m/s.
formula_used: Time = Length ÷ Relative speed; 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s
common_traps: Adding the speeds for the same-direction case, or using the train's speed alone to find its length.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: permissioned views let stakeholders see records while the ledger resists alteration. Statement 2 is correct: every node keeps a full copy of the ledger, which syncs quickly across the network. Statement 3 is incorrect: a blend of public and private chains is a hybrid blockchain; a consortium blockchain is a permissioned chain run jointly by a group of organisations. Statement 4 is correct in the key's sense: cryptographic hashing and consensus make recorded data practically unchangeable. So 1, 2 and 4.
explanation_text: Four types are usually distinguished: public (anyone can join), private (one organisation controls it), consortium (a group of organisations shares control) and hybrid (a private network with some data made public). Statement 3 describes the hybrid type under the consortium name.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statements 2 and 3, both incorrect.

common_traps: Statement 2 fails on 'All': NBFCs regulated by SEBI, IRDAI or state governments are exempt from RBI registration.

short_explanation: Statement 1 is correct: both the global MPI and NITI Aayog's national MPI use the Alkire-Foster method. Statement 2 is correct: NITI Aayog's MPI has 12 indicators. Statement 3 is incorrect: maternal health and bank account are the two indicators NITI Aayog added; the UNDP-OPHI global MPI has only 10 indicators and includes neither. So 1 and 2 only.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3; maternal health and bank account are not in the UNDP index.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and omits statement 2.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 1, which is also correct.

common_traps: The two extra Indian indicators are exactly what statement 3 wrongly calls 'common'.
